<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Here are two examples of jump rates $c_{0,e_1}(\cdot)$ satisfying
\eqref{11}:
\begin{equation*}
c_{0,e_1}(\eta) \,=\, a \,+\, [\,\eta_{-e_1} + \eta_{2e_1}\,]\,,
\quad
c_{0,e_1}(\eta) \,=\, a \,+\, [\,\eta_{e_2}  + \eta_{e_1+e_2}  +
\eta_{-e_2}  + \eta_{e_1-e_2} \,]
\end{equation*}
where $a>0$ to guarantee that the jump rates are strictly positive. In
the first case,
\begin{equation*}
h_{1,1}(\eta) \,=\, a \, \eta_0 \,-\, \eta_{-e_1}\eta_{e_1} \,+\, 
\eta_{-e_1} \eta_0 \,+\, \eta_0 \eta_{e_1}\,, \quad
h_{1,k}(\eta) \,=\, 0\,, \;\; 2\le k\le d\,.
\end{equation*}
In the second one, 
\begin{equation*}
h_{1,1}(\eta) \,=\, a \, \eta_0 \,+\, \eta_{-e_2}\eta_{0} \,+\,
\eta_{0}\eta_{e_2}\,, \;\;
h_{1,2}(\eta) \,=\, \eta_{e_1-e_2}\eta_{0} \,-\,
\eta_{e_1}\eta_{-e_2} \,, \quad
h_{1,k}(\eta) \,=\, 0\,, \;\; 3\le k\le d\,.
\end{equation*}
Mind that ${\mathtt p}_{h_{j,k}} (\alpha) = 0$ for all $0\le \alpha\le 1$,
$j\neq k$. This seems to be a common feature of all gradient models.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{t1}
Let $d\le 3$. Fix $T>0$, a density profile
$u_0\colon {\mathbb T}^d\to (0,1)$, and a sequence of probability measures
$\mu_n$ on $\Omega_n$. Assume that

\begin{itemize}
\item [(a)] $H_n(\mu_n \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}) = o(n^{d/2})$;

\item [(b)] there exist ${\mathtt r}_0 > d/2$ and a random
${\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}_0}$-valued density field $X_0$ such that $X^n_0$
converges weakly  to $X_0$ in ${\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}_0}$;

\item [(c)] the density profile $u_0$ belongs to
$H^{p+\beta}({\mathbb T}^d)$, for some integer $p\ge \max\{4, {\mathtt r}_0 + d/2
+ 2\}$, $0<\beta<1$, and satisfies \eqref{255a}. 

\end{itemize}
Let \begin{equation}
\label{242b}
{\mathtt r} \;>\; {\color{blue} {\mathtt r}^\star } \,:=\, 
\max\Big\{\, 6 \,+\, (3d+1)/2\,,\;\;
{\mathtt r}_0 \,+\, d\,+\,4 \,\Big\}\;.
\end{equation}
Then, the sequence of probability measures ${\mathbb Q}_{\mu_n}$ converges
weakly in $L^1( 0, T ;{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})$ to the measure ${\mathbb Q}$ induced by
the solution to  the equation
\begin{equation}
\label{58}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
& \partial_t Y_t \;=\; {\mathcal A}^*_t \, Y_t   \;+\;  \sum_{j=1}^d
\partial_{x_j} \Big(\, \sqrt{2\, \chi(u(t))\, D_j(u(t)) }
\, \xi^j_t \,\Big)\;, \\
& Y_0\;=\; X_0\;.
\end{aligned}
\right.
\end{equation}
In this formula, ${\color{blue} \chi(\rho) := \rho(1-\rho)}$ is the static
compressibility of the exclusion dynamics,
$\xi = (\xi^1, \dots, \xi^d)$ is a $d$-dimensional standard space-time
white noise, ${\mathcal A}_t$, $t\ge 0$, is the second-order linear
elliptic operator defined by
\begin{equation}
\label{41}
{\color{blue} ({\mathcal A}_t \, F)(x)} \; :=\; \sum_{j=1}^d  D_{j} (u(t,x))\,
\partial^2_{x_j} F (x) \;,\quad x\in {\mathbb T}^d\,, 
\end{equation}
for functions $F$ in $C^2({\mathbb T}^d)$, and ${\mathcal A}^*_t$ stands for its
adjoint, so that \eqref{58} has to be understood in the
weak sense:
\begin{equation*}
d Y_t (F) \;=\; Y_t({\mathcal A}_t F)   \, dt \;+\;  \sum_{j=1}^d
\int_{{\mathbb T}^d} \sqrt{2\, \chi(u(t))\, D_j(u(t)) }\, 
(\partial_{x_j} F) (x) \, \xi^j (dt, dx) \;,
\end{equation*}
$F\in {\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
It follows from the assumption
$\lim_{n\to \infty} n^{-d/2} H_n(\mu_n \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}) =0$
and the entropy inequality 
that under $\mu_n$ the empirical measure $\pi^n$ converges to
$u_0(x)\, dx$ in ${\mathscr M}({\mathbb T}^d)$.

One may view the process $Y_t$ as a time-dependent form of a
generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{t02}
Fix $d\le 3$. Assume that the initial condition $u_0$ satisfies
\eqref{255a}, and belongs to $H^{4+\beta}$ for some $0<\beta<1$.
Let $u(t,x)$ be the solution of the hydrodynamic equation \eqref{127}, and
$\mu_n$ be a sequence of probability measures on $\Omega_n$ such
that $H_n(\mu_n \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)} ) = o(n^{d/2})$. Then,
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} G (s, x/n)\,
\Pi_{u(s, \cdot), h}  (x,\eta^n(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \, \Big] \;=\; 0
\end{equation*}
for all $t>0$, functions $G$ in $C^{0,2}([0,t] \times {\mathbb T}^d)$, and
cylinder functions $h\colon \{0,1\}^{{\mathbb Z}^d} \to {\mathbb R}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The bound of order $n^{(d/2)-2}$ for ${\mathtt D}^{(n)}_s(F) $ in
\eqref{145} is bad in dimension $d\ge 4$.  In dimension $d\ge 4$, it
might be necessary to take the density profile $u(t, \cdot )$ as the
solution of a semi-discrete in space PDE, and to consider a higher
order expansion of $E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}} \, [\, h_j \,]$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{t01}
Fix $T>0$. Assume that the initial condition $u_0$ satisfies
\eqref{255a}, and belongs to $H^{4+\beta}$ for some $0<\beta<1$.  Let
$u(t,x)$ be the solution of the hydrodynamic equation
\eqref{127}. Then, in dimension $d=1$, $2$, there exists a finite
positive constant $C_1$, depending only on ${\mathfrak r}$, $h_j$,
$c_{0, e_j}$, $1\le j\le d$, $\Vert u \Vert_{T,4}$, and $T$, such that
\begin{equation}
\label{133}
H_n(f_t | \nu^n_{u(t, \cdot) }) \,+\,
\int_0^t   n^2\, I_n  (f_s;  \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot) } ) \; ds
\,\le\,  \big\{ H_n(f_0 | \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot) }  ) \, +\, C_1\,
\varkappa_n^{(d)}\,\big\} \, e^{C_1\,  t}
\end{equation}
for all $0\le t\le T$, $n\ge 1$.  In dimension $1$, a constant
$0<b<1/6$ is fixed, $\varkappa_n^{(1)} = n^{(1/3) +b}$, and the
constant $C_1$ may depend on $b$. In dimension $2$,
$\varkappa_n^{(2)} = n^{4/5}$.

In dimension $3$, fix $\kappa>1$.  Then, there exists a finite
positive constant $C_1$, depending only on ${\mathfrak r}$, $h_j$,
$c_{0, e_j}$, $1\le j\le d$, $\Vert u \Vert_{T,4}$, and $T$, and an
integer $n_0$ depending on the previous variables and on $\kappa$ for
which \eqref{133} holds for all $n\ge n_0$, $0\le t\le T$, where
$\varkappa_n^{(3)} = n^{3/2}/\kappa^3$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The proof of this result is based on a block lemma which allows one to
replace space averages of a local function $h$ by a function of the
particles' empirical density over mesoscopic cubes.  The method
presented in the next sections allows one to reach cubes of width
\begin{equation*}
n^{(2/3)-b} \;\;\text{in dimension $d=1$,}\quad
n^{3/5} \;\;\text{for $d=2$, }\quad
\kappa\, n^{1/2} \;\;\text{for $d=3$}\,,
\end{equation*}
where $\kappa\to\infty$ after $n$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{c-t01}
Assume that $d=3$ and that
$H_n(f_0 | \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot) } ) = o(n^{d/2})$. Then, under the
hypotheses of Theorem \ref{t01}, there exists an increasing sequence
$(\alpha_n)_{n\ge 1}$ such that $\alpha_n\to\infty$, and
\begin{equation*}
\limsup_{n\to \infty} 
\frac{\alpha_n }{n^{d/2}}
\,\Big\{\, \sup_{0\le t\le T} H_n (f_t \,|\, \nu^n_{u (t, \cdot)}  )
\,+\, \int_0^T   n^2\, I_n  (f_s;  \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot) } ) \; ds\, \Big\}
\,=\, 0\,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{t01}, the result holds if we set $\alpha_n=1$ for all
$n\ge 1$, letting $\kappa\to\infty$ after $n\to\infty$.  If
$(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ is a sequence of real numbers converging to $0$, it
is easy to show that there exists a sequence $(\alpha_n)_{n\ge 1}$
satisfying the conditions of the corollary and such that
$\alpha_n\, a_n \to 0$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{l03}
For all $t\ge 0$,
\begin{equation}
\label{2-22}
\frac{d}{dt}\, H_n(f_t | \nu^{n,t}_{\rm ref}) \;\leq\; -\,2\,  
n^2\, I_n(f_t ; \nu^{n,t}_{\rm ref})
\;+\;  \int
\big\{ L^{{\rm ref}, *}_{n,t} \, {\boldsymbol 1} \, -\, \partial_t   \ln \psi^{\rm ref}_t \,\big\}
\; f_t \, d \nu^{n,t}_{\rm ref} \;,
\end{equation}
where, recall, ${\boldsymbol 1} \colon \Omega_n \to {\mathbb R}$ is the constant
function equal to $1$, and ${\color{blue} L^{{\rm ref}, *}_{n,t}}$ represents the
adjoint of $L_n$ in $L^2(\nu^{n,t}_{\rm ref})$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{s41}
Recall that $u$ is the solution of the parabolic equation
\eqref{127}. Then,
\begin{equation*}
L_{n,t}^{*} \, {\boldsymbol 1}  \,-\, \partial_t   \ln \psi^n_t  \, =\,
{\mathfrak W}_t \, +\, I_n (t)\,+\,  {\mathfrak R}^{(4)}_{t,n} \, n^{d-2} \;,
\end{equation*}
where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
{\mathfrak W}_t \, & =\,
\sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x\in{\mathbb T}^d_n}
\frac{(\partial^2_{x_j} u)  (t,x/n)}
{\chi(u  (t,x/n)) }\,  \Pi_{u  (t,\cdot) , h_j} (x, \eta)
\\
& +\, \frac{1}{2}\, 
\sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x\in{\mathbb T}^d_n}
\Big(\, \frac{(\partial_{x_j} u)  (t,x/n)}
{\chi(u  (t,x/n)) }\Big)^2
\, \Pi_{u  (t,\cdot) , g_j} (x, \eta) 
\\
& -\, \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x\in{\mathbb T}^d_n}
\Big(\, \frac{(\partial_{x_j} u)  (t,x/n)}
{\chi(u  (t,x/n)) }\Big)^2 \, [1-2 u  (t,x/n)] \,
\, \Pi_{u  (t,\cdot) , h_j} (x, \eta)  \,,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
$I_n(t)$ is given by \eqref{106c} and satisfies the
bound \eqref{108}, and ${\mathfrak R}^{(4)}_{t,n}$ is a remainder
satisfying the bound \eqref{106d}.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Recall equation \eqref{106} for $L_{n,t}^{*} \, {\boldsymbol 1}$, and the
estimate \eqref{108} for $I_n(t)$. We turn to the first two sums in
\eqref{106}. Since
$\partial^2_{x_j} U = \chi(u)^{-1}\, \partial^2_{x_j} u -
(1-2u)\, \chi(u)^{-2}\, [\partial_{x_j} u]^2$, and
$\partial_{x_j} U = \chi(u)^{-1}\, \partial_{x_j} u$, equation
\eqref{106} can be rewritten as 
\begin{align}
\label{129}
L_{n,t}^{*} \, {\boldsymbol 1} \,  &=\,
\sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x\in{\mathbb T}^d_n}
\frac{(\partial^2_{x_j} u)  (t,x/n)}
{\chi(u  (t,x/n)) }\,
\, \{\, \tau_x h_j -
E_{\nu^{n}_{u(t, \cdot)}}[\tau_x h_j ]  \,\}
\\
& +\, \frac{1}{2}\, 
\sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x\in{\mathbb T}^d_n}
\Big(\, \frac{(\partial_{x_j} u)  (t,x/n)}
{\chi(u  (t,x/n)) }\Big)^2
\{\,  \tau_x g_j - E_{\nu^{n}_{u(t, \cdot)}}[\tau_x g_j]
\,\}
\nonumber
\\
& -\, \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x\in{\mathbb T}^d_n}
\Big(\, \frac{(\partial_{x_j} u)  (t,x/n)}
{\chi(u  (t,x/n)) }\Big)^2 \, [1-2 u  (t,x/n)] \,
 \{\, \tau_x h_j - E_{\nu^{n}_{u(t, \cdot)}}[\tau_x h_j ] \,\}
\, +\, I_n (t)\,+\,  {\mathfrak R}^{(4)}_{t,n} \, n^{d-2}\;,
\nonumber
\end{align}
where ${\mathfrak R}^{(4)}_{t,n}$ satisfies the bound stated in the lemma.

The first line of the previous expression combined with the first line
of \eqref{107} yields $\Pi_{u(t, \cdot), h_j} (x, \eta)$. By
\eqref{125}, ${\mathtt p}_{h_j}'(\alpha) = D_j(\alpha)$, so that
${\mathtt p}_{h_j}''(\alpha) = D'_j(\alpha)$. By \eqref{126},
$(1/2)\, {\mathtt p}_{g_j}' (\alpha) - (1-2\alpha) D_j(\alpha) =
\chi(\alpha) D_j' (\alpha)$. Therefore, the difference of the second
and third lines of the previous formula combined with the second line
of \eqref{107} yields the second and third lines of the statement of
the lemma. This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The expression $L_{n,t}^{*} \, {\boldsymbol 1} \,-\, \partial_t \ln \psi^n_t$
reveals the equation that $u$ has to satisfy. Indeed, choose a product
reference measure associated with a time-dependent density profile
$u(t,x)$, and compute $L_{n,t}^{*} \, {\boldsymbol 1}$ as in equation
\eqref{106}, expressing it in terms of the local functions $h_j$,
$g_j$ and the spatial derivatives of $u$. Next, compute
$\partial_t \ln \psi^n_t$, which is expressed in terms of the time
derivative of $u$ and the linear function $\eta_x - u(t,x/n)$. It then
remains to determine the PDE that $u$ must satisfy for the difference
$L_{n,t}^{*} \, {\boldsymbol 1} \,-\, \partial_t \ln \psi^n_t$ to become a
function of $\Pi_{u(t, \cdot), h} (x,\eta)$, $h$ a cylinder function.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{s47}
Fix a local function $h\colon \{0,1\}^{{\mathbb Z}^d} \to {\mathbb R}$, a
function ${\mathfrak a} \colon {\mathbb T}^d_n \to {\mathbb R}$ and let
$\Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty := \max_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} |{\mathfrak a}(x)|$.
Then,
\begin{equation*}
\int  \Big  | \, \sum_{x \in {\mathbb T}^d_n} {\mathfrak a} (x) \,
\big( \, \tau_x  h - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x h] \, \big)\,\Big |
\, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\,\le \, \frac{1}{\gamma}\, \Big\{\, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}
)  \,+\, \ln(2) \, \Big\} \,+ \, c_1\, \gamma\, e^{c_2 \, \gamma}\, n^d
\end{equation*}
for all $\gamma>0$, and density $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} $. In this formula,
\begin{equation*}
c_1 \,=\,  2\, (2\ell_h + 1)^d \, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty^2
\, \Vert h \Vert_\infty^2 \,, \quad
c_2\,=\,  2 \, (2\ell_h + 1)^d \, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty
\, \Vert h \Vert_\infty \, .
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By the entropy inequality, the expression appearing on the left-hand
side of the statement of the lemma is bounded above by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )  \,+\,
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, 
\ln \int  \exp\Big\{ \, \gamma\, \Big  | \, \sum_{x \in {\mathbb T}^d_n} {\mathfrak a} (x) \,
\big( \, \tau_x  h   - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x  h  ] \, \big)\,\Big
|\, \Big\}  \; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\end{equation*}
for all $\gamma>0$.  Since $e^{|y|}\leq e^{y} + e^{-y}$, for any
bounded random variable $X$,
\begin{equation}
\label{154}
\ln {\mathbb E} \big [ \,e^{|X|} \, \big] \,\leq \,
\ln {\mathbb E} \big[ \, e^{X} + e^{-X} \big ] \,\leq \,
\ln \Big(\,  2 \, \max_{b=\pm 1} \,
{\mathbb E} \big[ \, e^{b X} \, \big ] \,\Big ) \,=\, 
\ln(2) \,+\,
\max_{b=\pm 1} \, \ln
{\mathbb E} \big[ \, e^{b X} \, \big ] \,.
\end{equation}
Therefore, the expression in the penultimate displayed equation is
bounded by
\begin{equation}
\label{155}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, \Big\{\, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}
)  \,+\, \ln(2) \, \Big\}  \,+\,
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, 
\max_{b=\pm 1} \,  \ln \int
\exp \Big\{  b\, \gamma\, \sum_{x \in {\mathbb T}^d_n}
{\mathfrak a} (x) \,
\big( \, \tau_x  h   - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x  h  ] \, \big)
\Big\}  \; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,.
\end{equation}

Recall the definition of $\ell_h$, introduced just before the
statement of the lemma, and write
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{x \in {\mathbb T}^d_n}
{\mathfrak a} (x) \,
\big( \, \tau_x  h   - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x  h  ] \, \big)
\,=\,
\sum_{y\in {\Sigma_{\ell_h}}} \sum_{z\in B_{n,y}}
{\mathfrak a} (x(y,z)) \,
\big( \, \tau_{x(y,z)}  h   - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_{x(y,z)}
h  ] \, \big)\,. 
\end{equation*}
In this equation, $x(y,z) = y + (2\ell_h + 1) z$, and the second sum
is carried over all $z\in {\mathbb Z}^d$ such that
$y + (2\ell_h + 1) z \in \Sigma^+_n$.  By H\"older inequality, the
last term in the penultimate displayed equation is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\max_{b=\pm 1} \,  \frac{1}{\gamma \, (2\ell_h + 1)^d}
\sum_{y\in {\Sigma_{\ell_h}}}  \ln \int
\exp \Big\{  b\, \gamma\, (2\ell_h + 1)^d\, \sum_{z\in B_{n,y}} 
{\mathfrak a} (x(y,z)) \,
\big( \, \tau_{x(y,z)}  h   - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_{x(y,z)} h  ] \, \big)
\Big\}  \; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,.
\end{equation*}
Clearly, if $z\neq z'$, then $x(y,z)-x(y,z')$ does not belong to
$\Sigma_{2 \ell_h}$, which implies that
$\{\tau_{x(y,z)} h: z\in B_{n,y}\}$ are independent random variables
with respect to any product measure. The previous expression is thus
equal to
\begin{equation*}
\max_{b=\pm 1} \,  \frac{1}{\gamma \, (2\ell_h + 1)^d}
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n}  \ln \int
\exp \Big\{  b\, \gamma\, (2\ell_h + 1)^d\, 
{\mathfrak a} (x) \,
\big( \, \tau_x  h   - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x  h  ] \, \big)
\Big\}  \; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,.
\end{equation*}
Since $e^r \le 1 + r + (1/2) \, r^2 \, e^{|r|} $ for all $r\in {\mathbb R}$,
$\tau_x h - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x h ] $ has mean zero with
respect to $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}$, and $\ln (1+c) \le c$ for $c>0$,
the previous expression is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{\gamma}{2}\, e^{2\, \gamma\, (2\ell_h + 1)^d
\Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty \, \Vert h \Vert_\infty }\,
\sum_{x \in {\mathbb T}^d_n} (2\ell_h + 1)^d \, {\mathfrak a} (x)^2\, 
\int \big( \, \tau_x  h   - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x  h  ] \, \big)^2
\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,.
\end{equation*}
To complete the proof of the lemma, it remains to estimate
$|\, \tau_x h - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [\tau_x h ] \,|$ by
$ 2 \Vert h\Vert_\infty$, and to recollect all previous estimates.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{s51b}
Fix a function $J\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to {\mathbb R}$ of class
$C^2({\mathbb T}^d)$, and let
\begin{equation*}
W_J \,:=\,
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n}  J(x/n)\, \big[\, \eta(x) - \rho (x/n) \,\big] \,
- \,
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} J (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})
\big\{\, {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  
-  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}[ {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  ]  \,\big\}\,.
\end{equation*}
Then, 
\begin{align*}
& \int \big| \, W_J  \,\big | \, 
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\,\le \,
H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )  \,+\, \ln(2) \,+\,
\Vert J \Vert^2_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)} \,
e^{\Vert J \Vert_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)} \, (r_1/n)^2} \,
\Big( \frac{r_1}{n}\Big)^4  \, n^d 
\end{align*}
for all density $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix a function $J\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to {\mathbb R}$ of class $C^2({\mathbb T}^d)$,
and a density $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$. Recall that
$r_1 = 2b_1 +1$, and let
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue}  J^{(2)} (x+ \Sigma_{b_1}) } :=
\frac{1}{|\Sigma_{b_1}|}\,
\sum_{y\in \Sigma_{b_1}} J(x - y + \Sigma_{b_1})\,,
\end{equation*}
where $J(x+ \Sigma_{b_1})$ has been introduced in \eqref{156}.  As $J$
is of class $C^2({\mathbb T}^d)$, the absolute value of the difference
$J(x/n)\, -\, J^{(2)}(x+ \Sigma_{b_1}) $ is bounded by
$2\, \Vert J \Vert_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)} \, (b_1/n)^2$ uniformly in
$x$. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{s47} with $\gamma=1$, $\ell_h=0$,
$\Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty = 2\, \Vert J \Vert_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)} \,
(b_1/n)^2$,
\begin{align*}
& \int \Big | \, \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} 
\big[ \, J(x/n)\, -\,  J^{(2)} (x+ \Sigma_{b_1}) \, \big]
\big[\, \eta(x) - \rho(x/n) \,\big] \,\Big| \, 
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\\
&\quad
\,\le \,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )  \,+\, \ln(2)\,+\,
C_1(J)\, \Big( \frac{r_1}{n}\Big)^4  \, n^d\, e^{C_2 (J) \, (r_1/n)^2} \,,
\end{align*}
where $C_1(J) = \Vert J \Vert^2_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)}$,
$C_2(J) = \Vert J \Vert_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)} $. Here we used the fact
that $b_1 \le r_1/2$.  A summation by parts yields that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} 
J^{(2)} (x+ \Sigma_{b_1}) \, \big[\, \eta(x) - \rho(x/n) \,\big]
\,=\, \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} J (x+ \Sigma_{b_1})
\big\{\, {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma_{b_1})  
-  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}[ {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma_{b_1})  ]  \,\big\} \,, 
\end{equation*}
where ${\textsf m} (x+ B)$ has been introduced in \eqref{156}.  As
$\Sigma_{b_1} = -\, (b_1, \dots, b_1) + \Sigma^+_{r_1}$, this last sum
is equal to
\begin{align*}
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} J (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})
\big\{\, {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  
-  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}[ {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  ]  \,\big\} \,.
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{s52b}
Fix two functions $F$, $G\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to {\mathbb R}$ of class
$C^2({\mathbb T}^d)$. Let
\begin{align*}
W_{F,G} \,=\,
& \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} 
F(x/n)\, G(x/n)\,  \big[\, \eta(x) - \rho( x/n) \,\big]
\\
& \,-\,
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} F (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})\, G (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})\, 
\big\{\, {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  
-  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}[ {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  ]  \,\big\}  \,.
\end{align*}
Then,
\begin{equation*}
\int \big |\,  W_{F,G}  \,\big | \,  f\, d\nu^n_{\rho( \cdot)}
\,\le\,
2\, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )  \,+\, 2\, \ln(2) \,+\,
C_1\, \Big( \frac{r_1}{n}\Big)^4  \, n^d
\end{equation*}
for all density $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho( \cdot)}$.
In this formula,
\begin{align*}
C_1 \,:=\, \Vert F\, G \Vert^2_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)} \,
e^{\Vert  F\, G \Vert_{C^2({\mathbb T}^d)} \, (r_1/n)^2}
\,+\, 2\,   \Vert F\Vert^2_{C^1({\mathbb T}^d)} \,
\Vert G\Vert^2_{C^1({\mathbb T}^d)} 
\, \exp\{ 2\,  \Vert F\Vert_{C^1({\mathbb T}^d)} \,
\Vert G\Vert_{C^1({\mathbb T}^d)} \, (r_1/n)^2 \}\,.
\end{align*}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Fix two functions $F$, $G$ in $C^2({\mathbb T}^d)$, and let $J = F\, G$.  We
use the triangle inequality to estimate $W_{F,G} $ summing and
subtracting the term
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{W}_{F,G} \,:=\,
\sum_{x\in  {\mathbb T}^d_n} J (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})\,
\big\{\, {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  
-  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}[ {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  ]  \,\big\}  \,.
\end{equation*}
The previous lemma provides an estimate for the difference between the
first term on the right-hand side of the definition of $W_{F,G} $ and
$\widetilde{W}_{F,G}$.

The difference between $\widetilde{W}_{F,G}$ and the second term on
the right-hand side of the definition of $W_{F,G} $ is equal to
\begin{equation}
\label{157}
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} H (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})\,
\big\{\, {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  
-  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}[ {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  ]  \,\big\}
\,,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{align*}
H(B)  & =\, \frac{1}{| B|} \,  \sum_{x\in B}
F(x/n) \, G(x/n) \,-\, F(B) \, G(B)
\\
\, &=\, \frac{1}{| B|} \,  \sum_{x\in B}
\big\{\, F(x/n) - F(B)\big\}\,
\big\{\, G(x/n) - G(B)\big\} \,.
\end{align*}
As $F$, $G$ are Lipschitz-continuous,
$|H( B)|\le \Vert F\Vert_{C^1({\mathbb T}^d)} \, \Vert
G\Vert_{C^1({\mathbb T}^d)}\, (r_1/n)^2$.

Write \eqref{157} as
\begin{align*}
& \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} H (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})\,
\frac{1}{| \Sigma^+_{r_1} |} \,
\sum_{y\in \Sigma^+_{r_1}}  \,[\, \eta_{x+y} - \rho((x+y)/n)\,]
\\
& \quad \,=\,
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} \,[\, \eta_{x} - \rho(x/n)\,] \,
\frac{1}{| \Sigma^+_{r_1} |} \,
\sum_{y\in \Sigma^+_{r_1}}  
H (x - y+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})\,
\,,
\end{align*}
where we performed the change of variables $x'=x+y$ and used the fact
that the torus ${\mathbb T}^d_n$ has periodic boundaries.  Let
\begin{align*}
{\mathtt a} (x) \,=\,
\frac{1}{| \Sigma^+_{r_1} |} \,
\sum_{y\in \Sigma^+_{r_1}}  
H (x - y+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})
\quad\text{so that}\;\;
\max_{z\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} 
\big|\, {\mathtt a}(z)  \, \big| \,\le\, 
\Vert H\Vert_\infty\,.
\end{align*}
In consequence, by Lemma \ref{s47} with $\gamma =1$, $\ell_h=0$,
$h(\eta)=\eta_0$,  ${\mathfrak a} (\cdot)= {\mathtt a}(\cdot)$,
\begin{equation*}
\int \Big|\, \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} H (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})\,
\big\{\, {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  
-  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}[ {\textsf m} (x+ \Sigma^+_{r_1})  ]  \,\big\}
\, \Big | \, 
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho( \cdot)} \,\le \, 
H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )  \,+\, \ln(2) \,+\,
C_2 \, n^d
\end{equation*}
for all density $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} $.  In this
formula, $C_2= 2 \, \Vert H\Vert^2_\infty \, \exp\{ 2\, 
\Vert H\Vert_\infty\}$.  
To complete the proof of the corollary, it remains to recollect the
previous estimates.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{s32}
Fix a function $F$ in $C^1([0,1])$, and a function
${\mathfrak a} \colon \Sigma^+_{r_2} \to {\mathbb R}$.  Then,
\begin{equation*}
\int \Big | \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} {\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) \,
\big\{ \, F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}})
- E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}) ] \, \big\}\, \Big|
\, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\,\le \,  \frac{1}{\gamma}\, \Big\{\,
H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )  \,+\, \ln (2) \, \Big\} \,+\,
c_0 \gamma\, e^{c_1 \gamma}\, 
\Big( \frac{n}{r_1^{2}} \Big)^d 
\end{equation*}
for all $\gamma>0$, and density $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} $. In this formula,
\begin{equation*}
c_0 \,=\,  \frac{1}{4}   \, 
\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty^2 \, \Vert F'\Vert^2_\infty\,
\quad\text{and}\quad
c_1 \,=\, 2 \,  \Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty
\, \Vert F\Vert_\infty\,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The proof is the same as the one of Lemma \ref{s47} up to equation
\eqref{155}. At that point we need to estimate the second term.  As
$\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}$ is a product measure, this term is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
\ln \int 
\exp\Big\{\, b\, \gamma\, {\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) \,
\big[ \, F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}) - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}) ] \,
\big]  \,\Big\}\, d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}\,.
\end{equation*}
The expression inside braces is bounded by
$2 \, \gamma\, \Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty \, \Vert F\Vert_\infty$. Since
$e^x \le 1 + x + (1/2) x^2 e^{|x|} $ for all $x\in{\mathbb R}$, the previous
expression is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\,  \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} \ln \Big\{\, 1
\,+\, \frac{1}{2}   \, \gamma^2\,
\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty^2 \,
e^{2 \, \gamma\,
\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty  \, \Vert F\Vert_\infty}\,
\int \big\{ \, F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}})
- E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}) ] \,\big\}^2
\, d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}\,\Big\}
\end{equation*}
because
$F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}) - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}) ] $
has zero mean. As $\ln (1+a) \le a$, the previous expression is less
than or equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2}   \, \gamma\,
\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty^2 \,
e^{2 \, \gamma\,
\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty  \, \Vert F\Vert_\infty}\,
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} 
\int \big\{ \, F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}})
- E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}) ] \,\big\}^2
\, d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,.
\end{equation*}
Introduce $F({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}})$ inside the expectation and apply
Schwarz inequality.  Since $F(\cdot)$ is Lipschitz continuous, the
previous expression is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2}   \, \gamma\,
\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty^2 \, \Vert F'\Vert^2_\infty\,  
e^{2 \, \gamma\,
\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty  \, \Vert F\Vert_\infty}\,
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} \int \,\int 
\Big\{ \, \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|} \sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt i}}} \eta_x
\,-\,
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|} \sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt i}}} \xi_x
\,\Big\}^2
\, d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} (\eta)  \, d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} (\xi)\,.
\end{equation*}
The double integral is twice the variance of
$|B_{{\mathtt i}}|^{-1}\, \sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt i}}} \eta_x$. To complete the
proof, recall that $\chi(\rho) = \rho (1-\rho) \le 1/4$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{l02}
Fix $J\colon \Sigma^+_{r_2} \to {\mathbb R}$, and let
$\Vert J\Vert_\infty = \max_{{\mathtt i} \in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} |J({\mathtt i})|$.
Then,
\begin{equation*}
\int \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} J({\mathtt i}) \,
r_1^d\, ( {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - \bar \rho_{{\mathtt i}} )^2
\, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\,\le \, 8\, \|J\|_\infty \, \Big\{   \, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )  \,+\,
\Big( \frac{n}{r_1}\Big)^d\, \Big\}
\end{equation*}
for all density $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} $.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By the entropy inequality, the left-hand side of the displayed
equation appearing in the statement of the lemma is bounded above by 
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}   \, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\,
\frac{1}{\gamma}  \ln \int \exp\Big\{\,
\gamma\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} J({\mathtt i}) \,
r_1^d\, ( {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - \bar \rho_{{\mathtt i}} )^2 \,\Big\}\,
d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}
\end{equation*}
for all $\gamma>0$. As $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}$ is a product measure,
the second term is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}  \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
\ln \int 
e^{\gamma\, J({\mathtt i}) \,
r_1^d\, ( {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - \bar \rho_{{\mathtt i}} )^2} \,
d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,.
\end{equation*}
By Hoeffding's inequality \cite[Lemma 2.2]{BLM13},
$\sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt i}}}
[\eta_x - \rho(x/n)]$ is an $r_1^d$-sub-Gaussian random variable. Thus,
by \cite[Proposition B.1]{jm1},
\begin{equation*}
\int  e^{\gamma\, J({\mathtt i}) \,
r_1^d\, ( {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - \bar \rho_{{\mathtt i}} )^2} \,
d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,\le\, e^{8 \gamma \Vert J\Vert_\infty }
\end{equation*}
provided $\gamma \Vert J\Vert_\infty < 1/4$. To complete the proof of
the lemma, it remains to choose $\gamma = 1/ (8\Vert J\Vert_\infty)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{s19}
Fix $T>0$ and let $(f^{(n)}_t : 0\le t\le T)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence
of densities with respect to the measures
$(\nu^{n}_{u(t)} : 0\le t\le T)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{n\to \infty}  \int_0^T \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
H_n(f^{(n)}_s | \nu^{n}_{u(s, \cdot)})
\, ds \, = 0\,.
\end{equation*}
Then,
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{n\to \infty}  \int_0^T  ds\,
\int \frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} J_n(s,{\mathtt i}) \,
r_1^d\, ( {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - \bar u(s, {\mathtt i}) )^2
\, f^{(n)}_s \; d\nu^n_{u (s, \cdot)} \,=\, 0
\end{equation*}
for every uniformly bounded sequence
$J_n\colon [0,T]\times \Sigma^+_{r_2} \to {\mathbb R}$ {\rm
(}$\sup_{n\ge 1} \sup_{0\le s\le T} \max_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2} }
|J_n(s,{\mathtt i})| < +\infty${\rm )}, and sequence $r_1$ such that
$\sqrt{n}/r_1 \to 0$. In this equation,
$\bar u(s, {\mathtt i}) = |B_{{\mathtt i}}|^{-1} \sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt i}}}
u(s,x/n)$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{s45}
Fix an integer $p\ge 1$, and a function
${\mathfrak a} \colon \Sigma^+_{r_2} \to {\mathbb R}$.  Suppose that
$\Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty \le {\mathfrak c}_0 \, r_1^{d/2}$ for some finite
constant ${\mathfrak c}_0$.  Then, there exists a finite constant $C_p$
depending only on $p$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\int  \Big|\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} {\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) \,
\big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}^p
- E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}^p ] \, \big\} \,\Big|
\, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\,\le \,
C_p\,  \Big\{\, {\mathfrak c}_0\, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\, \, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty\,
\Big(\frac{n}{r_1^{3/2}} \Big)^d \,\Big\} 
\end{equation*}
for all density $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} $.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose that $p=1$. In this case, by Young's inequality, the
expression on the left-hand side of the statement of the lemma is
bounded above by
\begin{equation}
\label{113}
\frac{1}{2\gamma}\,
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} {\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i})^2 \, +\, 
\frac{\gamma}{2}\,
\int
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
\big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ]  \, \big\}^2
\, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\end{equation}
for every $\gamma>0$. The first term is bounded by
$\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty^2 r_2^d / (2\gamma)$. By the entropy
inequality, the second term is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\beta}\,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\,
\frac{1}{\beta}\,   \ln \int \exp\Big\{\,
\frac{\beta \,\gamma}{2} \, 
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
\big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ] \, \big\}^2
\,\Big\}\,
d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}
\end{equation*}
for every $\beta>0$.
Since $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}$ is a product measure and the cubes
$B_{{\mathtt i}}$ are disjoint, this sum is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\beta}\,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\,
\frac{1}{\beta}\,   \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
\ln \int \exp\Big\{\,
\frac{\beta \,\gamma}{2} \, 
\big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ] \, \big\}^2
\,\Big\}\,
d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}\,.
\end{equation*}
By Hoeffding's inequality \cite[Lemma 2.2]{BLM13} (see \cite[Lemma
4.4]{jl23})
${\textsf M}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf M}_{{\mathtt i}} ]$ is
A-subgaussian, where $A= (1/4) |B_{{\mathtt i}}|$. Therefore, by
\cite[Proposition B.1]{jm1}, the previous expression is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\beta}\,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\,
\frac{1}{\beta}\,   \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
\frac{\beta \,\gamma}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|} \,
\,=\,
\frac{1}{\beta}\,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\,
\frac{n^d}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|} \,
\frac{\gamma}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|} \, 
\end{equation*}
provided $\beta \,\gamma < 2\, |B_{{\mathtt i}}|$.

Set $\gamma = \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty\, r_1^{d/2}$ and
$\beta = 1/{\mathfrak c}_0$, where ${\mathfrak c}_0$ appeared in the hypotheses
of the lemma.  With these definitions,
$\beta \,\gamma = (1/{\mathfrak c}_0)\, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty\, r_1^{d/2} \le
(1/{\mathfrak c}_0)\, {\mathfrak c}_0 \, r_1^{d} = |B_{{\mathtt i}}| < 2\, |B_{{\mathtt i}}|$.
Therefore, $\beta \,\gamma$ is less than $2\, |B_{{\mathtt i}}|$, as
required. With these values the last displayed equation becomes
\begin{equation*}
{\mathfrak c}_0 \,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty\,
\frac{n^d}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|^{3/2}} \, .
\end{equation*}
Adding the first term in \eqref{113} with
$\gamma =\Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty\, r_1^{d/2}$ yields that
\begin{equation}
\label{114}
\int  \Big|\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} {\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) \,
\big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ] \, \big\} 
\, \Big| \, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\,\le \,
{\mathfrak c}_0 \,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\, 2\, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty\,
\frac{n^d}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|^{3/2}} \,,
\end{equation}
as claimed.

We turn to the case $p\ge 2$. As $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} $ is a product
measure, $E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}^p] = E_{\nu^n_{\rho
(\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}]^p + {\mathfrak R}_n$, where $|{\mathfrak R}_n|\le C_p / |B_{{\mathtt i}}|$ for some finite constant $C_p$ depending only on $p$. The
integral we wish to bound is thus less than or equal to
\begin{equation*}
\int  \Big|\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}} {\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) \,
\big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}}^p
- E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ] ^p \, \big\} \,\Big|
\, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\, +\, C_p \, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty\,
\frac{n^d}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|^{2}} \,\cdot
\end{equation*}
Let $f_p(x) = x^p$. Add and subtract $f_p'(\,E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}}
[{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ]\,) \, \{\, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}}
[{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ]\,\}$ inside the sum.  The linear term has been taken
care of in the first part of the proof. It is enough to remark that
$\sup_{0\le \rho\le 1} | f_p'(\rho)| \le C_p$ to obtain the bound
\eqref{114} with an extra multiplicative factor $C_p$.

On the other hand, by a Taylor expansion, the non-linear term is
bounded by
\begin{equation*}
C_p\,  \int  \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
|\, {\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) \,| \,
\big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ] \, \big\}^2
\, f\; d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,.
\end{equation*}
Repeating exactly the same steps as in the first part of the proof
yields that this expression is less than or equal to
\begin{equation*}
C_p\,  \Big\{\, \frac{1}{\beta}\,  H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\,
\frac{1}{\beta}\,   \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}}
\frac{2\, \beta \, |{\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i})|}{|B_{{\mathtt i}}|} \, \Big\} 
\end{equation*}
provided $\beta \, \Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty < |B_{{\mathtt i}}|$. Choose
$\beta = 1/{\mathfrak c}_0$, and recollect all previous estimates to complete
the proof.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
It is the linear term
${\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) \, \{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} - E_{\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}}
[{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} ] \, \}$ which gives a bound of order
$\Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty \, (n/r_1^{3/2})^d$. All the other terms
are bounded by $\Vert {\mathfrak a} \Vert_\infty \, (n/r_1^{2})^d$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{s23}
Assume that $V_{{\mathtt i}}$, ${\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }$, is measurable
with respect to $\{\eta_x : x\in B_{{\mathtt i}} \}$, that there exists a
finite constant $C_1$ such that
$ \Vert V_{{\mathtt i}} \Vert_\infty \le C_1(n/r_1)^2$ for all
${\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }$, and that $V_{{\mathtt i}}$ has zero-mean with
respect to all canonical measures:
\begin{equation*}
\int V_{{\mathtt i}} \;  d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \,=\, 0
\quad
\text{for all ${\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }$, $0\le {\textsf M} \le r_1^d$}\,.
\end{equation*}
Then,  
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }} 
\int V_{{\mathtt i}}  \, f \, d  \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} \,\le\,
\delta\, n^2 \,  I_n  ( f \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} ) \,+\,
C_2\, \Big(\frac{r_1}{n}\Big)^2\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }} 
\max_{0\le {\textsf M} \le r_1^d} \int V^2_{{\mathtt i}} \;
d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} 
\end{equation*}
for all $\delta>0$, and density $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} $. In this formula,
$C_2 = ({\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS} / 2 \delta)\, \exp\{C_1 {\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}
/\delta\}$, and ${\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}$ is the logarithmic Sobolev constant
appearing in Theorem \ref{s83}.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The proof is divided into several steps. 

\smallskip\noindent{\bf Step 1: Projecting on $\Omega_{{\mathtt k}} $.}
Denote by $\mu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_f$, ${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}$, the
marginal of the measure $f(\cdot) \, \nu^{n}_{\rho (\cdot)} (\cdot)$
on the set $\Omega_{{\mathtt k}} $:
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue}  \mu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_f (\xi) } \,:=\, \int {\mathtt 1}
\{\eta \in \Omega_n : \eta_x = \xi_x\;\forall
\,x\in B_{{\mathtt k}}\}\, f(\eta) \, d\nu^{n}_{\rho (\cdot)} (
\eta)\,, 
\quad
\text{for all}\; \xi \in \Omega_{{\mathtt k}}  \,.
\end{gather*}
In this formula and below, ${\color{blue} {\mathtt 1}\{A\}}$ represents the indicator
function of the set $A$.

Fix ${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}$. Since $V_{{\mathtt k}}$ depends only on the
variables $\{\eta_x: x \in B_{{\mathtt k}}\}$,
\begin{equation}
\label{01c}
\int V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} \,=\,
\int V_{{\mathtt k}}  \, f_{{\mathtt k}} \, d\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)} \,,
\end{equation}
where $f_{{\mathtt k}} $ represents the density (the Radon-Nikodym
derivative) of the measure $\mu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_f$  with respect to
$\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}} }_{\rho(\cdot)}$:
\begin{equation}
\label{06c}
{\color{blue}  f_{{\mathtt k}}   (\xi)}  \,:=\, \frac{\mu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_f  (\xi)}
{\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}} } _{\rho (\cdot)}(\xi)} \,, 
\quad
\xi \in \Omega_{{\mathtt k}}  \,.
\end{equation}

\smallskip\noindent{\bf Step 2: Projecting on hyperplanes.}  
Decomposing the expectation on the right-hand side of \eqref{01c}
according to the total number of particles yields that
\begin{equation}
\label{04b}
\int V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f_{{\mathtt k}} \, d\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)} 
\; =\; 
\sum_{{\textsf M} =0}^{| B_{{\mathtt k}}|}
\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)}  (\Omega_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}})\,
\< f_{{\mathtt k}} \>_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \,
\int V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \, d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}
\;,
\end{equation}
where $\< f_{{\mathtt k}} \>_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} $ is the expectation of
$f_{{\mathtt k}}$ with respect to the measure
$\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$, and $f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} $ is the
density (with respect to the measure $\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$)
given by
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue}  \< f_{{\mathtt k}} \>_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} }  \, :=\,
\int  f_{{\mathtt k}} \, d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}\,,
\quad
{\color{blue}  f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} (\xi) } \, :=\, \frac {f_{{\mathtt k}} (\xi)}
{\< f_{{\mathtt k}} \>_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}} \,, \quad \xi \in
\Omega_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}\,.
\end{gather*}
With this notation, the expression appearing in the statement of the
lemma is equal to
\begin{equation}
\label{93}
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }} 
\sum_{{\textsf M} =0}^{| B_{{\mathtt i}} |}
\nu^{B_{{\mathtt i}}}_{\rho (\cdot)}  (\Omega_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}})\,
\< f_{{\mathtt i}}  \>_{{\mathtt i} , {\textsf M}} \,
\int V_{{\mathtt i}}  \,
\, f_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \, d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \,.
\end{equation}

Fix ${\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }$, $0\le {\textsf M} \le r_1^d$.  By the
entropy inequality,
\begin{equation}
\label{69}
\int V_{{\mathtt i}}  \,
\, f_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \, d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}}
\,\le\,
\frac{1}{\gamma} H_{B_{{\mathtt i}}}
(f_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \,|\,  \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} )
\,+\, \frac{1}{\gamma}  \ln \int e^{ \gamma\,  V_{{\mathtt i}} }\;
d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}}  
\end{equation}
for all $\gamma>0$. In this formula and below, for a cube $B$
contained in ${\mathbb Z}^d$, a probability measure $\nu$ defined on
$\{0,1\}^B$, and a density $g\colon \{0,1\}^B \to {\mathbb R}_+$ with
respect to $\nu$, ${\color{blue} H_{B} (g \,|\, \nu)}$ represents the entropy of
the measure $g\, d\nu$ with respect to $\nu$. Similarly,
${\color{blue} I_{B} (g \,;\, \nu)}$ stands for the carr\'e du champ of $g$
averaged with respect to $\nu$:
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} I_{B} (g \,;\, \nu) }
\;:=\; \frac{1}{2}\, \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x} 
\int  c_{x,x+e_j} (\eta)\,  \Big[\,  \sqrt{g (T_{x,x+e_j} \eta )} \,-\,
\sqrt{g(\eta)}\, \Big]^2 \;  \nu (d\eta) \;.
\end{equation*}
In this equation, the second sum is performed over all $x\in {\mathbb Z}^d$
such that $\{x, x+e_j\}\subset B$.


By the logarithmic Sobolev inequality stated in Theorem \ref{s83}, 
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma} H_{B_{{\mathtt i}}}
(f_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \,|\,  \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} )
\,\le\, 
\frac{1}{\gamma} \, {\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}\, r_1^2\, 
I_{B_{{\mathtt i}}}
( f_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \,;\,  \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} )\,,
\end{equation*}
where ${\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}$ represents the logarithmic Sobolev constant. An
elementary computation yields that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2 }} 
\sum_{{\textsf M} =0}^{| B_{{\mathtt i}} |}
\nu^{B_{{\mathtt i}}}_{\rho (\cdot)}  (\Omega_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}})\,
\< f_{{\mathtt i}}  \>_{{\mathtt i} , {\textsf M}} \, I_{B_{{\mathtt i}}}
( f_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \,;\,  \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}}  ) \,\le\,
I_n  ( f \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} ) \,.
\end{equation*}
Hence, the sum over ${\mathtt i}$ and ${\textsf M}$ of the first term on the
right-hand side of \eqref{69} multiplied by
$\nu^{B_{{\mathtt i}}}_{\rho (\cdot)} (\Omega_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}})\, \<
f_{{\mathtt i}} \>_{{\mathtt i} , {\textsf M}} $ is bounded by
${\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}\, r_1^2\, \gamma^{-1} \, I_n ( f \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho
(\cdot)} )$. Choose $\gamma = {\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}\, r_1^2 / (\delta n^2)$ to
get the first term on the right-hand side of the statement of the
lemma.

We turn to the second term on the right-hand side of \eqref{69}.  As
in the previous proofs, since $e^x \le 1 + x + (1/2) x^2 e^{|x|}$ for all
$x\in {\mathbb R}$, and since $|V_{{\mathtt i}}| \le C_1 (n/r_1)^2$,
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}  \ln \int e^{ \gamma\,  V_{{\mathtt i}} }\;
d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}}   \,\le\, 
\frac{1}{\gamma}  \ln \Big\{\, 1
\,+\, \gamma \int V_{{\mathtt i}} \;
d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}}   
\,+\,  \frac{1}{2}\, e^{\gamma C_1 (n/r_1)^2}\,
\gamma^2  \int V^2_{{\mathtt i}} \;
d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}} \, \Big\}\,.
\end{equation*}
As $V_{{\mathtt i}}$ has zero-mean and $\ln (1+a) \le a$, by the choice of
$\gamma$, this expression is less than or equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2}\, \gamma \, 
e^{\gamma C_1 (n/r_1)^2}\,\int V^2_{{\mathtt i}} \;
d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}}
\,=\,
\frac{{\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}}{2}\, \frac{1}{\delta}\, 
e^{C_1 {\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS} /\delta}\,
\Big(\frac{r_1}{n}\Big)^2 \,  \int V^2_{{\mathtt i}} \;
d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt i}, {\textsf M}}
\,.
\end{equation*}
To complete the proof, it remains to maximize over ${\textsf M}$, and to sum
over ${\mathtt i}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{s07b}
Fix $0<{\mathfrak a}_0<{\mathfrak r}$. Then, there exists a positive and finite
constant ${\mathfrak a}_1 = {\mathfrak a}_1({\mathfrak a}_0, {\mathfrak r})$, depending only on ${\mathfrak a}_0$,
${\mathfrak r}$, such that
\begin{equation*}
\int \sum_{ {\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2} }  r_1^d\, 
{\mathtt 1}\{ {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} \not\in ({\mathfrak a}_0, 1-{\mathfrak a}_0) \}\,
f (\eta) \,  d \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} (\eta)
\,\le\,
{\mathfrak a}_1  \, \Big\{\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {r_1} \Big)^d\, 
e^{-r_1^d/{\mathfrak a}_1} \,\Big\}
\end{equation*}
for all density $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By the entropy inequality the expression on the left-hand side of the
statement of the lemma is bounded above by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\,
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, \ln
E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}\Big[
\, \exp\Big\{ \,\gamma\, 
\sum_{ {\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2} }  r_1^d\, 
{\mathtt 1} \big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} \not\in ({\mathfrak a}_0, 1-{\mathfrak a}_0) \,\big\}\,
\,  \Big\} \,\Big]
\end{equation*}
for every $\gamma>0$. Since $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$ is a product measure
and the cubes $B_{{\mathtt i}}$ are disjoint, the second term of the
previous expression is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, \sum_{ {\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2} }  \, \ln
E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}}\Big[
\, \exp\Big\{ \,\gamma\, r_1^d\, 
{\mathtt 1} \big\{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} \not\in ({\mathfrak a}_0, 1-{\mathfrak a}_0) \,\big\}\,
\,  \Big\} \,\Big]\,.
\end{equation*}

Since the density profile $\rho(\cdot)$ takes values in the interval
$[{\mathfrak r}, 1-{\mathfrak r}]$ and $0<{\mathfrak a}_0<{\mathfrak r}$, there exists a positive
constant $c_1 = c_1({\mathfrak a}_0,{\mathfrak r})$ such that
$\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} \{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} \not\in ({\mathfrak a}_0, 1-{\mathfrak a}_0) \, \}
\le e^{- c_1 r_1^d}$ for all ${\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}$. The
previous expression is thus less than or equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\,  \sum_{ {\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2} } \,
\ln \Big \{ 1 \,+\,  \Big( e^{\gamma r_1^d} - 1\Big) \,
\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} \{ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt i}} \not\in ({\mathfrak a}_0, 1-{\mathfrak a}_0) \,\}
\Big\}
\,\le\,
\frac{1}{\gamma}\, \Big( \frac{n} {r_1}\Big)^d\,
e^{\gamma r_1^d}  \,  e^{- c_1 r_1^d}
\end{equation*}
because $\ln (1+a) \le a$, $a\ge 0$.  To complete the proof, it remains
to choose $\gamma < c_1$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{r01}
By \eqref{115}, any estimate of
\begin{equation}
\label{116}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
\sum_{x\in y+ B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \Big(\,
\tau_x h \, -
\, E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } \big[\,
\tau_x h \,\big]\, \Big)
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\end{equation}
uniform over $y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}}$ can be turned into an estimate of the
same quantity with the inner set $B^o_{{\mathtt k}}$ replaced by the full
set $B_{{\mathtt k}}$ at a cost given by the multiplicative constant equal
to $|B_{{\mathtt k}}|/|B^o_{{\mathtt k}}|$.  On the other hand, for a fixed
$y \in {\mathbb Z}^d$, the cylinder functions
$h_{y, {\mathtt k}} := \sum_{x\in y+ B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \tau_x h$,
${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}$, have disjoint support and the support of
$h_{y, {\mathtt k}}$ is contained in the cube $y+ B_{{\mathtt k}}$. This
property will be important in the proofs of this section and the next.

In view of this remark, in this section and in the next, we estimate
the sum \eqref{116} for $y=0$ and make sure that the arguments provide
the same bound if the expression is translated by $y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}}$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{r03}
The definition of the cubes $B_{{\mathtt k}}^o$ depends on the cylinder
function $h$. There is a finite number of such functions which appear
in the proofs. One could define an integer $\ell'$ as the maximum of
such integers $\ell_h$ and define $B_{{\mathtt k}}^o$ accordingly.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{s01}
Let $\rho\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to (0,1)$ be a density profile of class
$C^3({\mathbb T}^d)$ satisfying \eqref{83}.  For every cylinder function
$h$, and function $J\colon {\mathbb T}^d\to{\mathbb R}$ of class $C^1({\mathbb T}^d)$,
there exist constants ${\mathfrak a}_1$, ${\mathfrak a}_2 = {\mathfrak a}_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$,
${\mathfrak a}'_2 = {\mathfrak a}'_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,1}$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$
such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
\Big\{  \sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \overline{W}^h_{{\mathtt k}, x}  
\Big\}\, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\\
&\quad
\,\le\, \delta \, n^2\, I_n(f \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,1} \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \,
\Big[  \, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \ln(2) \,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {\ell_1}\Big)^d\, 
e^{- {\mathfrak a}_1 \ell_1^d}\,\Big]
\\
&\quad 
\,+\,  \Big\{\, {\mathfrak a}_2  \, \frac{1}{\delta} \,  
\Vert J\Vert^2_\infty\, +\,
{\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,\Big\}
\Big(\frac{\ell_1}{n}\Big)^2\, n^d
\,+\,
{\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,
\frac{1}{n\, \ell^d_1} \, n^d
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{2} \,  \Vert J\Vert_\infty
\Big( \frac{n}{\ell_1^{3}} \Big)^d
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
for all $\delta>0$, integers $\ell_1 \ge \ell_h$ such that
$\Vert h \Vert_\infty\,  \Vert J\Vert_\infty\,  \ell_1^{d+2} \le {\mathfrak a}'_2 \, \delta \,
n^2$, $L_2\ge 2$, and densities $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{r02b}
This estimate remains valid if we replace $J(\cdot)$ by
$-J(\cdot)$. In particular, the same bound holds for the absolute
value of the left-hand side.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{r02}
In dimension $d\ge 4$, for the term $n^d (\ell_1/n)^2$ to be of order
$n^{d/2}$, $\ell_1$ has to be bounded by a constant. This shows that, in
dimension $d\ge 4$, Theorem \ref{s01} does not allow us to replace
the average of a cylinder function over a large box by its expectation with
respect to the canonical measure with density given by the empirical
density ${\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
The condition
$\Vert h \Vert_\infty\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\, \ell_1^{d+2} \le {\mathfrak a}'_2 \,
\delta \, n^2$ is imposed by the use in the proof of the standard
perturbation theorem on the largest eigenvalue of a symmetric operator
\cite[Theorem A3.1.1]{kl} which requires a $L^\infty$ bound on the
perturbation.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{s46}
Let $\rho\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to (0,1)$ be a density profile of class
$C^3({\mathbb T}^d)$ satisfying \eqref{83}.  For every cylinder function
$h$, and function $J\colon {\mathbb T}^d\to{\mathbb R}$ of class $C^1({\mathbb T}^d)$,
there exist constants ${\mathfrak a}_1$, ${\mathfrak a}_2 = {\mathfrak a}_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$,
${\mathfrak a}'_2 = {\mathfrak a}'_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,1}$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$
such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
\Big\{  \sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \Big(\,
\tau_x h  \, -
\, E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } \big[\,
\tau_x h \,\big]\, \Big)
\,-\,   |B^o_{{\mathtt k}}| \,  J_{{\mathtt k}}  \, \Big(\, {\mathtt p}_h({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})
\,-\,  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } \big[\, {\mathtt p}_h ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})
\,\big] \,\Big) \, \Big\}\,
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\\
&\quad
\,\le\, \delta \, n^2\, I_n(f \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,1} \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \,
\Big[  \, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \ln(2) \,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {\ell_1}\Big)^d\, 
e^{- {\mathfrak a}_1 \ell_1^d}\,\Big]
\\
&\quad 
\,+\,  \Big\{\, {\mathfrak a}_2  \, \frac{1}{\delta} \,  
\Vert J\Vert^2_\infty\, +\,
{\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,\Big\}
\Big(\frac{\ell_1}{n}\Big)^2\, n^d
\,+\,
{\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,
\frac{1}{n\, \ell^d_1} \, n^d
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{2} \,  \Vert J\Vert_\infty
\Big( \frac{n}{\ell_1^2} \Big)^d
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
for all $\delta>0$, integer $\ell_1 \ge \ell_h$ such that
$\Vert h\Vert_\infty \,  \Vert J\Vert_\infty \,  \ell_1^{d+2} \le {\mathfrak a}'_2 \, \delta \,
n^2$, $L_2\ge 2$, and density $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{s32} with $\gamma^{-1} = \Vert J\Vert_\infty$,
$r_1=\ell_1$, there exists a finite constant ${\mathfrak a}_2$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\int \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  
J_{{\mathtt k}}  \, 
\big\{  \, {\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) 
\,-\,  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } \big[\, {\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,\big] \,\big\}\,
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\,\le\, \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\,
\Big\{\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}) \,+\,
\ln (2) \, \Big\} 
\,+\,  {\mathfrak a}_2\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \, \Big( \frac{n}{\ell_1^2}\Big)^d
\end{equation*}
for all integers $\ell_1\ge \ell_h$, $L_2\ge 2$, and densities $f$
with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$.  This estimate takes care of
the correction term
$|B^o_{{\mathtt k}}|\, J_{{\mathtt k}} \, \ell^{-d}_1\, {\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) $ appearing in the statement of Theorem \ref{s01}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We start with a sketch of
the proof of this result. Recall from \eqref{91} that we denote by
$\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} $, ${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}$,
$0\le {\textsf M}\le |B_{{\mathtt k}}|$, the canonical measure concentrated on
the configurations of $\Omega_{{\mathtt k}}$ with ${\textsf M}$ particles.  The
proof is divided into two main steps.  In the first one, stated in
Proposition \ref{s02}, we estimate
\begin{equation*}
\int
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \Big(\,
\tau_x \eta_A \, -
\, E_{\nu^{\rm  c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}_{{\mathtt k}}} } \big[\,
\tau_x \eta_A \,\big]\, \Big)
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}\,.
\end{equation*}
In the second one, stated in Proposition \ref{s36}, we replace the
canonical measure $\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}_{{\mathtt k}}}$ by the grand
canonical $\nu^{\rm gc}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}_{{\mathtt k}}}$, through the local
central limit theorem (LCLT). As the error is required to be small, we
need to consider the first three terms of the Edgeworth expansion in
the LCLT. This explains the presence of the term ${\mathtt q}_A(\cdot)$
in Theorem \ref{s01}.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{s01}]
The result is a consequence of Propositions \ref{s02} and \ref{s36}. 
\end{proof}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The result is a consequence of Propositions \ref{s02} and \ref{s36}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{s02}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{s01}, for each cylinder function
$h$ there exist constants ${\mathfrak a}_2 = {\mathfrak a}_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$,
${\mathfrak a}'_2 = {\mathfrak a}'_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
\Big\{  \sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\,  \big\{ \tau_x h
-  E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}_{{\mathtt k}}}} [\tau_x h] \,\big\}   \, \Big\}\,
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\\
&\quad 
\,\le\, \delta \, n^2\, I_n(f \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_2 \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty  \, \Big\{\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {\ell_1} \Big)^d\, 
e^{- {\mathfrak a}_1 \ell_1^d} \,\Big\}
\,+\,  {\mathfrak a}_2  \, \frac{1}{\delta} \,  
\Vert J\Vert^2_\infty\, \Big(\frac{\ell_1}{n}\Big)^2\, n^d
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
for all $\delta>0$, integers $\ell_1 \ge \ell_h$ such that
$\Vert h\Vert_\infty\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\, \ell_1^{d+2} \le {\mathfrak a}'_2
\, \delta \, n^2$, $L_2\ge 2$, and densities $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The proof is divided into several steps. We first discard small and
large densities. Let $\delta_1 = {\mathfrak r}/2$ and rewrite the left-hand
side of the statement of the proposition as
\begin{equation}
\label{109}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
{\mathtt 1} \{{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \not\in (\delta_1 , 1- \delta_1)\}
V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\,+\,
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
{\mathtt 1} \{{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \in (\delta_1 , 1- \delta_1)\}
V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} \,,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
\label{161}
{\color{blue} V_{{\mathtt k}} } \,  :=\, 
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\,  \big\{ \tau_x h
-  E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}_{{\mathtt k}}}} [\tau_x h] \,\big\} \,.
\end{equation}
Since
$|V_{{\mathtt k}} | \le \, 2\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\, \Vert h\Vert_\infty \,
\ell_1^d$, by Lemma \ref{s07b} (with $r_1=\ell_1$), the first term is
bounded above by
\begin{equation*}
{\mathfrak a}_2  \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty  \, \Big\{\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {\ell_1} \Big)^d\, 
e^{- {\mathfrak a}_1  \ell_1^d} \,\Big\}
\end{equation*}
where ${\mathfrak a}_1$ is the constant appearing in Lemma \ref{s07b} with
${\mathfrak a}_0 = {\mathfrak r}/2$.

We turn to the second term in \eqref{109}.  By Lemma \ref{s03}, for
each $\delta>0$ there exist constants ${\mathfrak a}_2 = {\mathfrak a}_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$,
${\mathfrak a}'_2 = {\mathfrak a}'_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$ such that this term is
bounded above by 
\begin{equation*}
\delta \, n^2\, I_n ( f  \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}) 
\, +\, {\mathfrak a}_2\, \frac{1}{\delta} \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty \,
\, \Big(\frac{\ell_1}{n}\Big)^2 \, n^d
\end{equation*}
provided $\ell_1$ satisfies the hypothesis of the proposition.
To complete the proof, it remains to recollect the previous estimates.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{s03}
Let $\delta_1={\mathfrak r}/2$.  Under the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{s01},
there exist constants ${\mathfrak a}_2 = {\mathfrak a}_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$,
${\mathfrak a}'_2 = {\mathfrak a}'_2({\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG})$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
{\mathtt 1}\{ {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \in (\delta_1, 1-\delta_1) \}
\, V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f \, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} \,\le\, 
\delta \, n^2\, I_n ( f  \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}) 
\, +\, {\mathfrak a}_2\, \frac{1}{\delta} \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty \,
\, \Big(\frac{\ell_1}{n}\Big)^2 \, n^d
\end{equation*}
for all $\delta>0$, integers $\ell_1\ge \ell_h$ such that
$\Vert h\Vert_\infty \,\Vert J\Vert_\infty \,\ell_1^{d+2} \le {\mathfrak a}'_2 \, \delta \, 
n^2$, $L_2\ge 2$, and densities $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$. Here, $V_{{\mathtt k}}$ has been introduced in
\eqref{161}.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Repeat steps 1 and 2 in
the proof of Lemma \ref{s23} up to equation \eqref{93} to project the
measure $f(\cdot) \, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}(\cdot)$ on the hyperplanes
$\Omega_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$. This yields that the sum on the left-hand
side of the statement of the lemma is equal to
\begin{gather}
\label{94}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2 }} 
\sum_{{\textsf M} = \delta_1 | B_{{\mathtt k}} | }^{ (1-\delta_1) | B_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)}  (\Omega_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}})\,
\< f_{{\mathtt k}}  \>_{{\mathtt k} , {\textsf M}} \,
\int V_{{\mathtt k}} 
\, f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \, d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \,.
\end{gather}
The sum over ${\textsf M}$ runs from $\delta_1 | B_{{\mathtt k}} |$ to
$(1-\delta_1) | B_{{\mathtt k}} |$ due to the indicator function appearing
inside the integral in the statement of the lemma.


\smallskip\noindent{\bf Step 3: Eigenvalue estimate.} Fix
$\delta_1 | B_{{\mathtt k}} | \le {\textsf M} \le (1-\delta_1) | B_{{\mathtt k}} |$.
Since $V_{{\mathtt k}}$ has zero-mean with respect to
$\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$, by the standard perturbation theorem
on the largest eigenvalue of a symmetric operator \cite[Theorem
A3.1.1]{kl},
\begin{equation}
\label{03}
\int V_{{\mathtt k}} \,  f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} 
\, d\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} 
\,\le\, \epsilon^{-1} \, I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} ( f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}  \,;\,
\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}) \, +\,\epsilon \,
\frac{ \< V_{{\mathtt k}} ,\, (-L_{{\mathtt k}})^{-1} V_{{\mathtt k}} \>_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}}
{1 - 2 \, \epsilon \, {\mathfrak s}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \, \Vert V_{{\mathtt k}} \Vert_{\infty}}
\end{equation}
for all
$0<\epsilon < [2 \, {\mathfrak s}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \, \Vert V_{{\mathtt k}}
\Vert_{\infty}]^{-1}$. In this formula,
$\< \,\cdot\, ,\, \cdot\,\>_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$ represents the scalar
product in $L^2(\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}})$, $L_{{\mathtt k}}$ stands
for the generator of the exclusion dynamics on $B_{{\mathtt k}}$ reversible
with respect to $\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$,
${\mathfrak s}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$ for the inverse of the spectral gap of the
operator $L_{{\mathtt k}}$ in $L^2(\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}})$, and
$I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} (\,\cdot\,;\, \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} )$ for the
Dirichlet form induced by the generator $L_{{\mathtt k}}$:
\begin{gather*}
(L_{{\mathtt k}} g) (\xi) \,=\, \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x: \{x,x+e_j\} \subset
B_{{\mathtt k}}} 
c_{x,x+e_j}(\xi ; \rho (\cdot))\, 
[\, g(T_{x,x+e_j} \xi) - g(\xi)\,] \,,
\\
c_{x,x+e_j}(\eta; \rho(\cdot)) \,=\, \exp \big\{ - (1/2) [\, H_{x+e_j} - H_x \,]\,
[\eta_{x+e_j} - \eta_x]\,\big\}\,, \quad H_z \,=\,
\ln \frac{ \rho(z/n)}{1-\rho(z/n)} \,, 
\\
I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} (g  \,;\, \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} )
\,=\, \frac{1}{2}\, \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x: \{x,x+e_j\} \subset
B_{{\mathtt k}}}  \int c_{x,x+e_j}(\xi; \rho(\cdot))\,
\Big[\, \sqrt{ g(T_{x,x+e_j} \xi) } - \sqrt{ \vphantom{T_{x,y} } g(\xi) }
\, \Big]^2
\, d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}  \,.
\end{gather*}
Note that our choice of $L_{{\mathtt k}}$ is different from $L_n$ in
\eqref{10}.

By definition, $\Vert V_{{\mathtt k}} \Vert_{\infty}$ is bounded by
$2\, \Vert h\Vert_\infty \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \, \ell_1^d$. By the
spectral gap, stated in Corollary \ref{s84}, there exists a finite
constant ${\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG}$ such that
${\mathfrak s}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \le {\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG} \, \ell_1^2$ for all
$\ell_1\ge 2$, $0\le {\textsf M}\le |B_{{\mathtt k}}|$,
${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}$. Therefore, if we choose
$0<\epsilon < [8 \, {\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG} \, \Vert h\Vert_\infty \, \Vert
J\Vert_\infty \, \ell_1^{d+2}]^{-1}$, since
$\< V_{{\mathtt k}} ,\, (-L_{{\mathtt k}})^{-1} V_{{\mathtt k}} \>_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}
\le {\mathfrak s}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \< V_{{\mathtt k}} ,\, V_{{\mathtt k}} \>_{{\mathtt k},
{\textsf M}} $,
\begin{gather*}
\int V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}  
\, d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}  
\,\le\, \epsilon^{-1} \, I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} ( f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}   \,;\,
\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} ) \, +\, 2\, \epsilon \,
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG} \, \ell_1^2 \,
\int V_{{\mathtt k}}^2  \, d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} \,.
\end{gather*}
By Corollary \ref{s42}, since
$\delta_1 | B_{{\mathtt k}} | \le {\textsf M} \le (1-\delta_1) | B_{{\mathtt k}} |$,
the variance term is less than or equal to
${\mathfrak a}_2 \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty\, \ell_1^d$. Thus,
\begin{gather*}
\int V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}  
\, d \nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}  
\,\le\, \epsilon^{-1} \, I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} ( f_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}  \,;\,
\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}} ) \, +\, {\mathfrak a}_2\, \epsilon \,
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG} \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty \, \ell_1^{d+2}  \,.
\end{gather*}

\smallskip\noindent{\bf Step 4: Conclusion.}  Inserting this bound into
equation \eqref{94} and summing over ${\textsf M}$ yields that
\begin{gather*}
\int {\mathtt 1} \{{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \in (\delta_1 , 1- \delta_1)\}\,
V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f_{{\mathtt k}} \, d\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)}
\,\le\, \epsilon^{-1} \, I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}}  ( f_{{\mathtt k}}  \,;\,
\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)}) \, +\, {\mathfrak a}_2\, \epsilon \,
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG} \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty \, \ell_1^{d+2} \,.
\end{gather*}
As $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$ is a product measure, by the definition of
$f_{{\mathtt k}}$ introduced in display \eqref{06c}, 
\begin{equation*}
f_{{\mathtt k}} (\xi) \,=\,
\frac{\sum_{\eta} f(\xi, \eta) \, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} (\xi, \eta)}
{\sum_{\eta} \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} (\xi, \eta) }
\,=\,
\frac{\sum_{\eta} f(\xi, \eta) \, \nu^{A_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho(\cdot)} (\eta)}
{\sum_{\eta} \nu^{A_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho(\cdot)} (\eta) }
\,=\,
\sum_{\eta} f(\xi, \eta) \, \nu^{A_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho(\cdot)} (\eta)
\,.
\end{equation*}
In this formula, $\xi$ belongs to $\{0,1\}^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}$ and
$\eta$ belongs to $\{0,1\}^{A_{{\mathtt k}}}$, where
$A_{{\mathtt k}} = {\mathbb T}_n^d \setminus B_{{\mathtt k}}$, and
$\nu^{A_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho(\cdot)} (\cdot)$ is the marginal of the
measure $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} (\cdot)$ on $\{0,1\}^{A_{{\mathtt k}}}$.

It follows from the previous displayed equation and Schwarz inequality
that
\begin{equation*}
I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} ( f_{{\mathtt k}}  \,;\,
\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)})  
\,\le\,
I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}}  (f\,;\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} )\,,
\end{equation*}
where
\begin{equation*}
I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}}  (f\,;\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} ) \,=\,
\frac{1}{2}\, 
\sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x: \{x,x+e_j\} \subset
B_{{\mathtt k}}}  \int c_{x,x+e_j}(\xi)\,
\Big[\, \sqrt{ f(T_{x,x+e_j} \xi) } - \sqrt{ \vphantom{T_{x,y} } f(\xi) }
\, \Big]^2
 \, d \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} (\xi) \,.
\end{equation*}
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
\int {\mathtt 1} \{{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \in (\delta_1 , 1- \delta_1)\}\,
V_{{\mathtt k}} \, f_{{\mathtt k}} \, d\nu^{B_{{\mathtt k}}}_{\rho (\cdot)}
\,\le\, \epsilon^{-1} \, I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} ( f  \,;\,
\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}) \, +\, 
{\mathfrak a}_2\, \epsilon \,
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG} \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty \,  \, \ell_1^{d+2}  \,.
\end{equation*}

Summing over ${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}$, as the cubes have length
$\ell_1$, we conclude that the sum appearing on the left-hand side of
the statement of the lemma is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{\epsilon} \,  \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
I_{B_{{\mathtt k}}} ( f  \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)})
\, +\, {\mathfrak a}_2\, \epsilon \,
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm SG} \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty \,
\Big(\frac{n}{\ell_1}\Big)^d \, \ell_1^{d+2}
\end{equation*}
for all $\epsilon$ satisfying the restrictions imposed in Step 3.  As
the sets $B_{{\mathtt k}}$ are disjoint, the sum is bounded by
$I_n ( f \,;\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)})$. To complete the proof of the
lemma, it remains to set $\epsilon^{-1} = \delta\, n^2$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rm7}
Here is an alternative proof of Proposition \ref{s02}.
Instead of using the standard perturbation theorem on the largest
eigenvalue of a symmetric operator, one could apply the entropy
inequality and then the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, as in the
proof of Lemma \ref{s23}.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rm3}
For the last term on the right-hand side of Proposition \ref{s02} to
be of order $o(n^{d/2})$, one needs $\ell_1 \ll n^{1-(d/4)}$. Thus, to
fulfill also the second condition of Lemma \ref{s03} which
requires $\ell_1^{d+2} \le c \, n^2$, in dimension $1$, set
$\ell_1 = \epsilon_n n^{2/3}$, in dimension $2$,
$\ell_1 = \epsilon_n n^{1/2}$, and in dimension $3$,
$\ell_1 = \epsilon_n n^{1/4}$ for some sequence $\epsilon_n\to 0$.
These are the side lengths of the cubes reached after this first step.
However, we will need lengths of order at least $k\, n^{1/2}$ for some
$1\ll k \ll n$. Thus, in dimensions $2$ and $3$ we need to increase the
length further. This is the goal of the next section.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rm1}
This estimate is analogous to the one presented in \cite[Proposition
5.2]{jl23} with $a_n=1$, whose proof follows the method introduced by
Jara and Menezes \cite{jm1, jm2}. In \cite[Proposition 5.2]{jl23}, the
constant term is of order $g_d(\ell) \, n^{d-2}$, while it is here
$\ell^2 \, n^{d-2}$, which is much larger since $g_d(\ell) \ll \ell^2$
in all dimensions. However, unlike the bound established in
Proposition \ref{s02}, the estimate in \cite[Proposition 5.2]{jl23}
includes on the right-hand side an entropy term multiplied by a
constant which diverges as $n\to\infty$. Also, the
structure of the function $V$ in \cite[Proposition 5.2]{jl23} is
different from $V_{{\mathtt k}}$ here.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{s36}
Let $\rho\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to (0,1)$ be a density profile of class
$C^3({\mathbb T}^d)$ satisfying \eqref{83}.  Assume that
$\sup_{n\ge 1} (\ell^d_1/n) <\infty$.  Fix a function $J$ in
$C^1({\mathbb T}^d)$, and a finite set $A$.  Then, there exist constants
${\mathfrak a}_1$, ${\mathfrak a}_2$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,1}$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
&  \int \Big|\, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \overline {W}_{x, A} \,
\Big |\, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\\
&\quad
\,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,1} \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \,
\Big[  \, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \ln(2) \,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {\ell_1}\Big)^d\, 
e^{- {\mathfrak a}_1 \ell_1^d}\,\Big] 
\\
&\quad
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,
\Big\{\, \frac{1}{n\, \ell^d_1}
\,+\, \Big( \frac{\ell_1} {n}\Big)^2\,\Big\} \, n^d
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{2} \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty
\Big( \frac{n}{\ell_1^{3}} \Big)^d 
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
for all densities $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$,
$\ell_1\ge \ell_A$, $L_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rm4}
We need the bound on the right-hand side of Theorem \ref{s01} and
Proposition \ref{s36} to be of order $o(n^{d/2})$. In view of the
definition of $\ell_1$ presented in Remark \ref{rm3}, in dimension $1$
we may end the expansion in equation \eqref{88} at the zero-order
term which is $1$. In dimension $2$, at the first-order term
($ 1 + \Gamma_{{\mathtt k}}^{-1} \, {\mathtt T}^{(1)}_{{\mathtt k}, x+A} )$.  It is
only in dimension $3$ that we need to deal with the second-order term.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{s33}
Let $\rho\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to (0,1)$ be a continuous density profile
satisfying \eqref{83}.  Fix a continuous function
$J\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to {\mathbb R}$, and a finite set $A$. Then, there exist
constants ${\mathfrak a}_1$, ${\mathfrak a}_2$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  \int
{\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}}   \Big | \, J(x/n)\,  
\Big\{   \, E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}_{{\mathtt k}}}} [\tau_x \eta_A] \,
-\, W^{\rm exp}_{x,A}  ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \, \Big\}
\, \Big|  \, 
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_2  \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\, \Big(\frac{n}{\ell_1^{3}} \Big)^d 
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
for all densities $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}$, $\ell_1\ge \ell_A$, $L_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{s68}
Let $\rho\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to (0,1)$ be a density profile of class
$C^3({\mathbb T}^d)$ satisfying \eqref{83}.  Fix a continuous function
$J\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to {\mathbb R}$, and a finite set $A$. Then, there exist
finite constants ${\mathfrak a}_1$, ${\mathfrak a}_2$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\int \Big| \, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  
{\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\,
\overline{W}^{\rm neg}_{x, A} \, \Big | \, f\,
d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\, &\le\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty
\Big\{\, {\mathfrak a}_{2} \, \Big( \frac{n}{\ell_1^{4}} \Big)^d
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,3} \, 
\frac{\ell_1} {n} \,  \Big(\frac{n}{\ell_1^{2}} \Big)^d\, 
\,\Big\} 
\\
& + \, {\mathfrak a}_2 \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\,
\Big\{   \, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \ln(2) \,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {\ell_1}\Big)^d\, 
e^{- {\mathfrak a}_1 \ell_1^d} \Big\}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
for all densities $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}$,
$\ell_1\ge \ell_A$, $L_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The proof is based on Lemmata \ref{s32}, \ref{s07b}, and \ref{s15}. By
definition,
\begin{align*}
W^{\rm neg}_{x, A}\,=\,
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}_{{\mathtt k}}}} [\, \tau_x \eta_A\,] \,
\Big( \, \frac{1} {\sum_{z\in B_{{\mathtt k}} } \chi (\varrho_{{\mathtt k}}  (z/n) ) } \,\Big)^2
\, \Big( \sum_{y\in A} \big[\, 1 - \varrho_{{\mathtt k}}  ([x+y]/n)\, \big] \, \Big)^2 \,,
\end{align*}
where $\varrho_{{\mathtt k}} (\cdot)$ has been introduced at the beginning
of this subsection. As $\delta_1 \le {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \le 1-\delta_1$,
${\mathfrak r} \le \rho ({\mathtt x}) \le 1-{\mathfrak r}$, and $\delta_1$ has been set to
be ${\mathfrak r}/2$, by \eqref{56b}, there exists $0<{\mathfrak a}_1 <1/2$ such that
${\mathfrak a}_1 \le \varrho_{{\mathtt k}} (x/n) \le 1-{\mathfrak a}_1$ for all
$x\in B_{{\mathtt k}}$.  Thus, by Lemma \ref{s15} with $s_1=1$,
$s_2=\ell_1$, $s_3=L_2$, $\delta = \delta_1$, on the set
$\{{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \in (\delta_1 , 1-\delta_1)\}$, 
\begin{align}
\label{176}
W^{\rm neg}_{x, A}\,=\,
\frac{1} {\ell_1^{2d}} \, F ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_{n} (x) \,, \quad
\text{where}\quad
\max_{{\mathtt k} \in \Sigma^+_{L_2}} \max_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} |{\mathfrak R}_{n}
(x)| \le {\mathfrak a}_{3, 3}\, \frac{1}{\ell_1^{2d}}  \, \frac{\ell_1}{n}\,, 
\end{align} 
and $F$ has been introduced in \eqref{167}. On the set ${\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})$, we may replace $F(\cdot)$ by $F_{{\mathfrak r}}(\cdot)$. Thus, by the previous estimate and the definition of
$\overline{W}^{\rm neg}_{x, A} $, 
\begin{align*}
& \int \Big | \, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
{\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \overline{W}^{\rm neg}_{x, A}  \, \Big |
\, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\\
& \quad \leq
\int \Big| \, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}  
{\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \, 
\frac{|B^o_{{\mathtt k}}|} {\ell_1^{2d}} \,  J_{{\mathtt k}} \, 
\Big\{\, F_{{\mathfrak r}} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,-\,
E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot) }  } \big [\, F_{{\mathfrak r}} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,\big]\,
\Big\}\, \Big | \, 
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n \,,
\end{align*}
where
$|{\mathfrak R}_{n}| \le {\mathfrak a}_{3, 3}\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\, \ell_1^{-2d} \,
(\ell_1/n) \, n^d$, and $J_{{\mathtt k}}$ is defined in \eqref{90}.

At this point, and since $\Vert F_{{\mathfrak r}}\Vert_\infty \le {\mathfrak a}_2$,
applying Lemma \ref{s07b}, we may remove the indicator function
${\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \, $ at a cost given by the
right-hand side of \eqref{170}.  The remaining term is estimated
applying Lemma \ref{s32}.  By Lemma \ref{s32} with $r_1=\ell_1$,
${\mathfrak a} (\cdot) = (|B^o_{{\mathtt k}}|/\ell_1^{2d} ) \, J_{\cdot}$,
$\gamma = 1/\Vert J\Vert_\infty$, the sum on the left-hand side
(without the indicator) is bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\Vert J\Vert_\infty  \,
\Big\{   \, H_n(f \,|\, \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)}  )
\,+\, \ln(2) \, \Big\} \,+\, {\mathfrak c}_2 \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty  \,
\frac{1} {\ell_1^{2d}} \,  \Big( \frac{n}{\ell_1^{2}} \Big)^d
\end{equation*}
for some finite constant ${\mathfrak c}_2$, depending only on
$\Vert F_{{\mathfrak r}}\Vert_{C^1}$. However, by definition, this last quantity
depends only on $A$ and ${\mathfrak r}$. Hence, by convention, ${\mathfrak c}_2$ can
be represented by ${\mathfrak a}_2$. This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{s69}
Let $\rho\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to (0,1)$ be a density profile of class
$C^3({\mathbb T}^d)$ satisfying \eqref{83}.  Assume that
$\sup_{n\ge 1} (\ell^d_1 /n)<\infty$.  Fix a function $J$ in
$C^1({\mathbb T}^d)$, and a finite set $A$. Then, there exist constants
${\mathfrak a}_1$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,1}$, ${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$ such that
\begin{align*}
& \int \Big|\, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
{\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}}  J(x/n)\, \overline{W}^{{\rm e}, a}_{x,A} \, 
\Big |\, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\nonumber
\\
&\quad 
\,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,1} \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \,
\Big[  \, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)})
\,+\, \ln(2) \,+\, \Big( \frac{n} {\ell_1}\Big)^d\, 
e^{- {\mathfrak a}_1 \ell_1^d}\,\Big] 
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,
\Big( \frac{\ell_1} {n}\Big)^2\, n^d
\end{align*}
for all densities $f$ with respect to $\nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} $,
$\ell_1 \ge \ell_A$, $L_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
As ${\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}$ belongs to the interval $(\delta_1, 1-\delta_1)$,
by Corollary \ref{s35}, with $s_1=1$, $s_2=\ell_1$, $\delta=\delta_1$,
\begin{align*}
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}}  J(x/n)\,
W^{{\rm e}, a}_{x,A} 
\,=\, W_J( {\mathtt k}) \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^{|A|-1}\,
\chi({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})\,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation*}
W_J( {\mathtt k}) \,=\,
|B_{{\mathtt k}}^o| \, J_{{\mathtt k}}\, 
\frac{1} {\chi(\bar\rho_{{\mathtt k}})}\,
\sum_{y\in A} \frac{y}{n}\cdot (\nabla \rho)(x_{{\mathtt k}}/n)\,,
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
\max_{{\mathtt k} \in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
\max_{\delta_1 \le {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}  \le 1- \delta_1 } 
|\, {\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})\, | \,\le\,  {\mathfrak a}_{3, 3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,
\, (\ell_1/n)^2\, \ell^d_1 \,.
\end{equation*}

We may also apply Corollary \ref{s35} to the expectation of the
previous sum multiplied by the indicator to get that
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}} \Big[ \,
{\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \, \sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}}
J(x/n)\, W^{{\rm e}, a}_{x,A}\,\Big]
\,=\, 
W_J( {\mathtt k}) \,
E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}} \big[ \,
{\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,
{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^{|A|-1}\, \chi({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})
\,\big] \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})\,,
\end{equation*}
where the remainder ${\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})$ satisfies the same bound. 

Clearly,
$\max_{{\mathtt k}} |\, W_J ({\mathtt k}) \,| \le \Vert J\Vert_\infty\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,1}\, (\ell^d_1/n)$ which is bounded by hypothesis.  Let $G$ be
the polynomial $G(\alpha) = \alpha^{|A|-1} \, \chi(\alpha)$. After
replacing the sum
$\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, \overline{W}^{{\rm e}, a}_{x, A}$
by
$W_J({\mathtt k}) \, \big \{ \, G({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \, - \,
E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}} [\, {\mathtt 1}_{\delta_1} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,
G({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) \,] \, \big\}$, a step which required
${\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}$ to be bounded away from $0$ and $1$, as $W_J$ is
uniformly bounded (cf. \eqref{56b}), we may apply Lemma \ref{s07b}, as
in \eqref{170}, to remove all the indicators of the set
$\{{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} \in (\delta_1, 1-\delta_1)\}$ at the cost which
appears on the right-hand side of \eqref{170} with ${\mathfrak a}_{3,1}$
