For a polynomial ${\mathfrak p}\colon [0,1]\to {\mathbb R}$, 
let
\begin{equation*}
\begin{gathered}
{\color{blue}  W^{(3)}_{{\mathfrak p}, {\mathtt i}} } \, :=\,
{\mathfrak p}({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}})  \,+\, \frac{1}{2} \, \frac{1}{(\ell_1\ell_2)^d} \,
{\mathfrak p}'' ({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}})\, \chi ({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}})
\, :=\,
{\mathfrak p} ({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}})  \,-\, \frac{1}{(\ell_1\ell_2)^d} \,
{\color{blue} {\mathtt q}_{{\mathfrak p}}} ({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}}) \,.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation*}

Recall that
$\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}J(B_{{\mathtt k}}) = \ell_2^d \, J(B_{2, {\mathtt j}})$, and that $\ell_3 = \kappa\, n^{1/10 + 2{\mathtt e}}$ for some
$\kappa\ge 1$
so that $\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3 = \kappa \,n^{1/2}$. Assume that
$\epsilon <1$. A direct calculation shows that there exists an integer
$n_2 = n_2(\kappa, \epsilon, \delta', {\mathfrak r}, \Vert \rho\Vert_{C^3},
{\mathfrak p})$ such that for all $n\ge n_2$, the conditions of Theorem
\ref{s26} with ${\mathtt t}_1 = \ell_1\ell_2$, ${\mathtt t}_2 =\ell_3$ are
satisfied with $K_1=\kappa^ 6$, $K_2=1$.  Thus, applying Theorem
\ref{s26} with these choices and $\delta = \delta'/8$, we obtain a
finite constant ${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$ such that
\begin{align*}
& \int
\sum_{{\mathtt i} \in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
\sum_{{\mathtt j} \in \Lambda_{3,{\mathtt i}}}  (\ell_1\ell_2)^d\, J(B_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \, \Big\{\,
{\mathtt p}_h({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})
\,-\, E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } \big[\,
{\mathtt p}_h({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \,\big]
\,-\, 
\big(\, W^{(3)}_{{\mathtt p}_h,{\mathtt i}}  
- E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } [\,  W^{(3)}_{{\mathtt p}_h,{\mathtt i}}  \, ] \,\big)
\, \Big\}\,
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\nonumber
\\
&  \le\, \frac{\delta'}{8} \, n^2 \,  I_n  ( f ; \nu^n_{\rho (\cdot)} )
\,+\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1}  \, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}) \,+\,
C({\mathfrak p})\, e^{({\mathfrak c}_{\rm LS}/\delta')\kappa^6\,
\, [1+{\mathfrak a}_{3,3}]\,[1 + \Vert J\Vert_{C^1}]}  \, \kappa^{1/2}\,
n^{5/4} 
\end{align*}
for all $n\ge n_2$.

Each time Theorem \ref{s01} or \ref{s26} is applied, a correction
term is produced. As we apply Theorem \ref{s01} once and Theorem
\ref{s26} twice there are at the end $8$ terms arising from
$h(\eta)$. We denote these terms by $T_{abc}$ where $a$, $b$,
$c\in \{0,1\}$. The index $a$ refers to Theorem \ref{s01}, and the
indices $b$, $c$ to the first and second application of Theorem
\ref{s26}, respectively.  For the main terms, we set the index $a$,
$b$ or $c$ to be $0$, and $1$ for the correction terms. Hence, the
term $T_{000}$ is the one obtained at the end of the three steps
described above, choosing at each step the main contribution, so that
\begin{equation*}
T_{000} \,=\, \int
\sum_{{\mathtt i} \in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
(\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3)^d\, J(B_{3,{\mathtt i}}) \, \Big\{\,
{\mathtt p}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}})
\,-\, E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } \big[\,
{\mathtt p}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}}) \,\big]  
\, \Big\}\,
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}
\end{equation*}
On the other hand, the term $T_{100}$ corresponds to the correction
produced in Theorem \ref{s01} and contains expressions of the form
$\ell_1^{-d} {\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}})$.

With the exception of $T_{100}$ and $T_{010}$, examined at the end of
this proof, the correction terms can be estimated with Lemma
\ref{s45}. We present the bound for $T_{001}$, the other ones being of
smaller order and easier to estimate. $T_{001}$ is given by
\begin{equation*}
-\, \int \sum_{{\mathtt i} \in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
\ell_3^d\, J(B_{3,{\mathtt i}}) \, \big\{\,
{\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}})
\,-\, E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)} } \big[\,
{\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}}) \,\big] \,\big\}
\, f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}\,.
\end{equation*}
By Lemma \ref{s45} with $r_1 = \ell_1 \ell_2 \ell_3$,
${\mathfrak a}({\mathtt i}) = \ell_3^d\, J(B_{3,{\mathtt i}})$, and
${\mathfrak c}_0=\Vert J \Vert_\infty$ [note that
$\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty \le \Vert J \Vert_\infty \, \ell_3^d \le
\Vert J \Vert_\infty\, (\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3)^{d/2}$ for all
$n\ge n_0(\kappa)$], this expression is less than or equal to
\begin{equation*}
C(h)\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \,\Big\{   \, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}) +
\Big(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_1\ell_2} \Big)^{d/2}\,
\frac{n^{d/2}}{\kappa^d} \, \Big\} 
\end{equation*}
for some finite constant $C(h)$ depending only on $h$. By the previous
choice of $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, $\ell_3$, the second term inside braces
is bounded by $n^{(21/20)+6{\mathtt e}} \le n^{(3/2) - 2{\mathtt e}}$ because
${\mathtt e}<1/30$, $\kappa\ge 1$.

We turn to $T_{100}$ and $T_{010}$. The first one appears as we apply
Theorem \ref{s01} and is given by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}} |}\, 
\sum_{y \in B_{{\mathtt 0}}}  \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}  \int
(\ell_2\ell_3)^d \,
J(B_{3, {\mathtt i}, y} ) \, \big\{ \, {\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}, y} ) 
\,-\,  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}  } \big[\,
{\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}, y} ) \,\big] 
\, \big\}\,
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}\,.
\end{equation*}
The second one, $T_{010}$, comes from Theorem \ref{s26}. By
\eqref{111} it is equal to the sum appearing in the previous displayed
equation but with a minus sign.  Hence $ T_{100} +T_{010} =0$ and we
do not need to estimate these expressions.  Recollecting all previous
estimates completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
\label{r06}
Along the proof of the replacement of a cylinder function $h$ by its
canonical expectation on a cube of width $n^{1/2}$, presented in
Sections \ref{sec4} and \ref{sec9}, two identical correction terms
appeared. The first one in Proposition \ref{s36} is due to the
equivalence of ensembles. As the width of the cube is small, we need
to take into consideration the first order term in the expansion of
$E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}} [h]$ as a function of the density
${\textsf M}/|B_{{\mathtt k}}|$. More precisely, the local central limit theorem
yields that
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}} [h] \,=\,
{\mathtt p}_h({\textsf M}/|B_{{\mathtt k}}|)
\,+\, \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt k}}|} \, {\mathtt q}_h({\textsf M}/|B_{{\mathtt k}}|)
\,+\, O\Big( \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt k}}|^2} \Big) \,\cdot
\end{equation*}
As $|B_{{\mathtt k}}| = \ell_1^d$ is not large enough in $d=3$, we need to
carry the polynomial ${\mathtt q}_h({\textsf M}/|B_{{\mathtt k}}|)$.

The second correction term, though identical to the first one up to
the sign, has a completely different origin. In Section \ref{sec9}, at
Proposition \ref{s44}, when we replace
$E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}} [{\mathtt p}_h ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})] $ by
${\mathtt p}_h ({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})$, we have to exchange
$E_{\nu^n_\rho} [{\mathtt p}_h ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})]$ by
${\mathtt p}_h ( E_{\nu^n_\rho} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}])$. This swap is based on
Corollary \ref{s30b}, which relies on Lemma \ref{s22}. In that lemma
it is shown that
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^n_\rho(\cdot)} [{\mathtt p}_h ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})] \,=\,
{\mathtt p}_h ( E_{\nu^n_\rho(\cdot)} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}]) \,-\,
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt k}}|} \,  {\mathtt q}_h ( E_{\nu^n_\rho(\cdot)} [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}])
\,+\, O\Big( \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt k}}|^2} \Big) \,\cdot 
\end{equation*}

As noted in Remark \ref{r09}, it is fortuitous that both terms are the
same with opposite signs, and therefore cancel. Without this
cancellation, we would have on the right-hand side of Lemma \ref{s49}
an extra term of the form
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}} |}\, 
\sum_{y \in B_{{\mathtt 0}}}  \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}  \int
(\ell_2\ell_3)^d \,
J(B_{3, {\mathtt i}, y} ) \, \big\{ \, {\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}, y} ) 
\,-\,  E_{\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}  } \big[\,
{\mathtt q}_h({\textsf m}_{3,{\mathtt i}, y} ) \,\big] 
\, \big\}\,
f\, d\nu^n_{\rho(\cdot)}\,.
\end{equation*}

This cancellation is however not crucial in the proof.  It is possible
to complete the proof of Proposition \ref{s88} with this extra term.
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Fix $0\le s\le t\le T$, $\kappa \ge 1$, $0<{\mathtt e}<1/30$, and $\delta_0>0$.
By Lemma \ref{s49} with $J(\cdot) = G(s, \cdot)$,
$\delta' = \delta_0$, and \eqref{135}, the expression appearing in the
statement of the proposition is bounded by
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}} |}\, 
\sum_{y \in B_{{\mathtt 0}}}  \int\,  \ell^d\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}  
G(s, B_{3, {\mathtt i}, y} )\,
{\mathtt E}( {\mathtt p}_{h} ,{\textsf m}_{3, {\mathtt i},y} ) \,  f\, d\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}
\\
& \quad
\,+\, \delta_0 \, n^2\, I_n(f ; \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}  )
\,+\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,3} \, \Vert G(s)\Vert_{C^2}\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}  )
\,+\,  {\mathtt K}_5 \, n^{3/2 - 2{\mathtt e}}
\end{align*}
for all integers $n \ge n_0$, and densities $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}$. In this formula,
${\mathtt K}_5 = {\mathfrak c}_{1,3} (\delta_0, h) \, \Vert G(s) \Vert_{C^1} \,+\,
{\mathtt K}_4(\kappa, G(s)) + {\mathfrak c}_{1,2} (h) \, \Vert G(s) \Vert_{C^2}
\kappa^4$, where ${\mathtt K}_4(\kappa, G(s))$ is defined in the statement
of the previous lemma, $\ell = \ell_1 \ell_2 \ell_3 = \kappa n^{1/2}$,
and, for a polynomial ${\mathfrak p}$,
\begin{equation*}
{\mathtt E}( {\mathfrak p} ,{\textsf m} )  \, =\,
{\mathfrak p}({\textsf m}) \,-\, E_{\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}} \big[\, {\mathfrak p}({\textsf m})  \,\big]
\,-\, {\mathfrak p}' \big(\, E_{\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}} [\, {\textsf m} \,]
\,\big) \,
\big \{\, {\textsf m} - E_{\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}} [\, {\textsf m} \,] \, \big\} \,.
\end{equation*}

By \eqref{120} with $r_1=\ell$, the expression in the penultimate
equation is less than or equal to
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}} |}\, 
\sum_{y \in B_{{\mathtt 0}}}
\int\,  \ell^d\, \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}  
G(s, B_{3, {\mathtt i},y} )\, 
{\mathtt E}_c( {\mathtt p}_{h} ,{\textsf m}_{3, {\mathtt i},y} ) \, 
f\, d\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}
\\
& \quad
\,+\, \delta_0 \, n^2\, I_n(f ; \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}  )
\,+\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,3} \, \Vert G(s)\Vert_{C^2}\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}  )
\,+\,  {\mathtt K}_5 \, n^{3/2 - 2{\mathtt e}}
\,+\, C_0\, \Vert G(s) \Vert_\infty\,  \frac{n^d}{\ell^d} \,,
\end{align*}
where ${\mathtt E}_c( {\mathfrak p} ,{\textsf m})$ is defined as
${\mathtt E}( {\mathfrak p} ,{\textsf m})$ replacing
$E_{\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}} [\, {\mathfrak p}({\textsf m}) \,]$ by
${\mathfrak p}( E_{\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}} [\, {\textsf m} \,])$. Since
$\ell = \kappa n^{1/2}$, the last term can be written as
$n^{3/2}/\kappa^3$.  Note that ${\mathtt E}_c( {\mathfrak p} ,{\textsf m}_{3, {\mathtt i}} )$
is a second-order Taylor expansion. Hence, by Lemma \ref{l02} with
$r_1=\ell$, which yields an extra term
$C_0\, \Vert G(s) \Vert_\infty\, [H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)} ) +
(n/\ell)^d]$, the previous expression is bounded by
\begin{align*}
\delta_0 \, n^2\, I_n(f ; \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}  )
\,+\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,3} \, \Vert G(s)\Vert_{C^2}\, H_n (f\,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}  )
\,+\,  {\mathtt K}_5 \, n^{3/2 - 2{\mathtt e}}
\,+\, C_0\, \Vert G(s) \Vert_\infty\,  
\frac{n^{3/2}}{\kappa^3}  \,.
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the proposition.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{t02b}
Assume the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{t02}. Fix $T>0$, a function $G$
in $C^{0,2}({\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb T}^d)$, and a cylinder function
$h\colon \{0,1\}^{{\mathbb Z}^d} \to {\mathbb R}$. In dimension $1$ fix also
$0<b<1/6$, and in dimension $3$ a constant $\kappa>1$.  Let $\mu_n$ be
a sequence of probability measures on $\Omega_n$ such that
$H_n(\mu_n \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)} ) =o(n^{d/2}) $. Then, there exist
a finite constant ${\mathfrak c}_{1,4} = {\mathfrak c}_{1,4} (h)$, and an integer
$n_0 = n_0 ({\mathfrak r}, h, \Vert u\Vert_{T,4})$ such that
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_s^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} G (r, x/n)\,
\Pi_{u(r, \cdot), h}(x, \eta^n(r) ) \, dr \, \Big| \, \Big] \;\le \;
{\mathtt A}^{(d)}_n (s) \,+\, \int_s^t {\mathtt B}^{(d)}_n(r)\, dr
\end{equation*}
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$, and $n\ge n_0$.  In this formula,
\begin{gather*}
{\mathtt A}^{(d)}_n (s) \, = \, \frac{d}{n^{d/2}}\,  \Vert G\Vert_{T,2}\, 
\big\{ \, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,,
\end{gather*}
 
\begin{align*}
{\mathtt B}^{(d)}_n(r) \,= \, {\mathfrak c}_{1,4}\, \Vert G\Vert_{T,2}\,
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\Big\{ n^2 \, I_n(f_r ;\, \nu^n_{u(r,\cdot)}) \, +\,
H_n(f_r\,|\,\nu^n_{u(r, \cdot)}) \,+\, \varkappa^{(d)}_n \, \Big\}\,,
\end{align*}
where $\varkappa^{(1)}_n = n^{(1/3) + b}$, $\varkappa^{(2)}_n =
n^{4/5}$, $\varkappa^{(3)}_n = n^{3/2}/\kappa^3$.
In dimension $1$, the constants ${\mathfrak c}_{1,4}$, $n_0$ may depend on $b$ as
well. In dimension $3$ the constant ${\mathfrak c}_{1,4}$ does not depend on
$\kappa$, and $n_0$ may depend on $\kappa$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{s94}
Assume the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{t02}.  Fix $T>0$.  Then, there
exists a finite constant ${\mathfrak c}_{1,4} $ such that
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_s^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} G (r, x/n)\,
\Pi_{u(r, \cdot), h}(x, \eta^n(r) ) \, dr \, \Big| \, \Big] \;\le \;
{\mathfrak c}_{1,4} (h_j) \, (1+T)\, \Vert G\Vert_{T, 2}\,
\big\{\, 1 + (t-s) \,\big\} \, {\mathtt h}_n
\end{equation*}
for all functions $G$ in $C^{0,2}({\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb T}^d)$,
$0\le s\le t\le T$, cylinder function $h=h_j$, $1\le j\le d$, and
$n\ge 1$.  In this formula,
\begin{equation}
\label{225}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt h}_n} \;:=\;
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\, \Big\{\,
\sup_{0\le r\le T} H_n\big(f_r \,\big|\,
\nu^n_{u(r, \cdot)}\big) \;+\; \int_0^T n^2\,
I_n\big(f_r ;  \nu^n_{u(r, \cdot)}\big) \, dr \, +\kappa_n \,\Big\} \,.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{s78}
For all $n\ge 1$,
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
\Pi^{(3)}_{y,{\mathtt k}, s} (\eta^n(s))  \, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big]
\\
& \le\,
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
|B^o_{{\mathtt k}} |\, G (s, y+B_{{\mathtt k}} )\,
F_{y,{\mathtt k}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, {\mathtt k}}(s)) \,
{\mathtt 1}_{{\mathfrak a}_0} \big({\textsf m}_{y,{\mathtt k}}(s) \big)  \, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big] \, + \,  {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78})}_n  \,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78})}_n} \,:=\,
{\mathfrak c}_{1,3}\, 
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\, 
\int_0^t \|G(s) \|_{C^1}\, \Big\{ \,  H_n(f_s|\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})\,
\,+ \, \ln (2)\,+\,
\Big[ \frac{1}{\ell^{3d}_1} + \frac{1}{n\, \ell^d_1}
+ \Big(\frac{\ell_1}{n}\Big)^2\Big]\, n^d\, \Big\}\, ds\,.
\end{gather*}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The proof relies on Proposition \ref{s36} and uses the notation
introduced in that result. The linear terms of
$\Pi^{(3)}_{y,{\mathtt k}, s} (\eta)$ and
$F_{y,{\mathtt k}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, {\mathtt k}})$ coincide.  We are left to estimate
the non-linear term of $\Pi^{(3)}_{y,{\mathtt k}, s}$, that is,
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
{\mathtt 1}_{{\mathfrak a}_0} ({\textsf m}_{y, {\mathtt k}}) \,
& \sum_{x\in y+B^o_{{\mathtt k}} } G (s, x/n)\,
\overline{W}_{y, x, A, s} \,.
\end{align*}
As above, we added the subscripts $s$ and $y$ to $\overline{W}_{x,A}$
because the expectation is taken here with respect to
$\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}$, and averages in the term $W_{{\mathtt k}, A}$ are
performed over the cubes $y+B_{{\mathtt k}}$ instead of $B_{{\mathtt k}}$.

This expression is equal to the one appearing in the statement of
Proposition \ref{s36}. We have to estimate the expectation of the
absolute value of the time integral of this quantity. We move the sum
over $y$ out of the expectation and estimate the expectation for each
fixed $y$. As the bounds are uniform in $y$, we set $y=0$.  By
Proposition \ref{s36},
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big|
\int_0^t \frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} G (s, x/n)\,
\overline{W}_{x,A,s}  \,
{\mathtt 1}_{{\mathfrak a}_0} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \, \Big]
\,\le \, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78})}_n \,,
\end{equation*}
where ${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78})}_n$ is introduced in the statement of the
lemma.  We do not have on the right-hand side the term
$(n/\ell_1)^d\, \exp\{-\ell^d_1/{\mathfrak a}_1\}$ which appears in
Proposition \ref{s36} due to the presence of the indicator
${\mathtt 1}_{{\mathfrak a}_0} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{s79}
Fix a finite subset $A$ of ${\mathbb Z}^d$, and a function $G$ in
$C^{0,2}({\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb T}^d)$. Let ${\mathfrak a}_0 = {\mathfrak r}/2$. Then,
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|}
\sum_{i\in \{1,3,4\}} \sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } 
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
\Pi^{(i)}_{y,{\mathtt k}, s}  (\eta^n(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \, \Big]
\\
&\quad \le \,
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|}  \sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} }
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
|B^o_{{\mathtt k}} |\, G (s, y+B_{{\mathtt k}} )\,
F_{y, {\mathtt k}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, {\mathtt k}}(s)) \,
\, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big] \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s79}) }_n \,,
\end{align*}
where ${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s79}) }_n \,=\,  {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s79}) }_n
(G,\eta_A)$ is given by
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s79}) }_n} \,=\,\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\int_0^t  {\mathtt S}^{\eqref{135}}_{n,\ell_1}
(G_s,{\mathtt p}'_A, u_s) \, ds \,+\, 2\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1, G} \,+\,
{\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78})}_n \,.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- remark-25: body_md -->
\label{r04}
Inspecting each term yields that
\begin{equation*}
{\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s79})}_n \,\le\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,3}\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\int_0^t \Vert G(s)\Vert_{C^2}\, \big[\,
H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})
+  {\mathtt e}^{(\ref{s79})}_{n,d} \,\big] \; ds  \,,
\end{equation*}
where ${\mathtt e}^{(\ref{s79})}_{n,1} = n^{(1/3)-2b}$ in dimension $1$,
${\mathtt e}^{(\ref{s79})}_{n,2} = n^{4/5}$ in dimension $2$, and
${\mathtt e}^{(\ref{s79})}_{n,3} = \upsilon_n^{2} \, n^{3/2}$ in dimension
$3$. Since $\upsilon_n\to 0$, by the a priori entropy bounds, the
remainder ${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s79})}_n$ vanishes as $n\to\infty$ in
dimension $d\le 3$.
<!-- end remark-25 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{s85}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s79},
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } 
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
\Pi^{(2)}_{y,{\mathtt k}, s}(\eta^n(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \, \Big]
\,\le \, \frac{1}{2\, n^{d/2}}  \, {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \int_0^t
\Psi_n(s)  \, ds \, \Big]
\,+\,   {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n\,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue}  {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n } \,:=\,
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\big\{ \, H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,
+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s03} )}_n\,,
\\
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s03} )}_n}\, =\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,0}\,
n^{d/2}\, \left(\frac{\ell_1}{n}\right)^2  \,
\int_0^t  \big\{\, \|G(s)\|_\infty^2
+ \sum_{D\in{\mathcal A}} \|H_D(s)\|_\infty^2\,\big\} \, ds\,.
\end{gather*}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
As before, we fix $y=0$ and make sure that all estimates are uniform
over $y$. Let
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} V_{s} }  \,:= \, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
\Pi^{(2)}_{{\mathtt k}, s}(\eta^n(s)) \,.
\end{align*}
Recall the definition of $\Psi_n(s)$ introduced just before \eqref{196}.
Write the expectation appearing in the statement of the lemma with
$y=0$ as
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \Big| \int_0^t \frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \, V_s \, ds
\, \Big| \, - \, \frac{1}{2}\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\int_0^t \, \Psi_n(s) \, ds \, \Big]
\, + \, {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \frac{1}{2}\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\int_0^t \, \Psi_n(s) \,ds\, \Big]\,.
\end{equation*}
The second term appears on the right-hand side of the statement of the
lemma. We turn to the first one. By the entropy inequality, this
expectation is bounded by
\begin{equation}
\label{197}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)})
\,+\, \frac{1}{ n^{d/2}}
\ln {\mathbb E}_{\nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}}\Big[\exp\Big\{ \, \Big|\, \int_0^t
V_{s} \, ds\, \Big|
\,-\, \int_0^t \frac{1}{2} \, \Psi_n(s) \, ds \, \Big\}\, \Big] \,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Since $e^{|x|} \leq  e^x + e^{-x}$, for any random variables $Y$, $Z$,
\begin{equation*}
\ln E[e^{|Z| + Y}] \, \le\, \ln \Big\{  E[e^{Z+Y}]  + E[e^{-Z+Y}] \Big\}
\, \le\, \ln \Big\{ \, 2 \max_{b=\pm 1}  E[e^{b Z+Y}]  \Big\}
\, =\, \ln 2 + \max_{b=\pm  1}  \ln E[e^{bZ+Y}]  \,.
\end{equation*}
Hence, invoking the inhomogeneous-in-time Feynman--Kac formula
\cite[Lemma A.2]{jm2}, the second term in \eqref{197} is bounded
by
\begin{align*}
\frac{\ln(2)}{n^{d/2}} \,+\, \max_{b=\pm 1}
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \, \int_0^t 
\sup_f \Big\{\, \int  \Big[ \, 
b V_s - \frac{1}{2} \,  \Psi_n(s) + \frac{1}{2} \, \big(L^*_{n,s} {\bf  1}
-\partial_s \ln \psi^n_s\big)\, \Big]
\, f\, d\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)} - n^2I_n(f ; \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}) \,
\Big\} \; ds \,,
\end{align*}
where the supremum is carried out over all densities $f$ with respect to
$\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}$. 

By \eqref{196}, the second term of this sum is equal to
\begin{gather}
\label{210}
\max_{b=\pm 1}
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \, \int_0^t 
\sup_f \Big\{\, \int  {\mathtt X}^b_n
\, f\, d\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)} - n^2I_n(f ;\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}) \, \Big\} \; ds \,,
\end{gather}
where
\begin{align*}
{\mathtt X}^b_n (\eta) \, & =\, b\,
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}} \, \Pi^{(2)}_{{\mathtt k}, s} (\eta)
\,+\, \frac{1}{2}\, 
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|} \sum_{D\in {\mathcal A}}
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}} \,
\Pi^{2,D}_{y, {\mathtt k}, s} (\eta) \,.
\end{align*}
By definition of $\Pi^{(2)}_{{\mathtt k}, s} (\eta)$,
$\Pi^{2,D}_{y, {\mathtt k}, s} (\eta) $, and by Lemma \ref{s03} with
$\delta = 1/(1+|{\mathcal A}|)$, the expression \eqref{210} is less than or
equal to ${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s03} )}_n$. To complete the proof, it remains
to recollect all previous estimates.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{s82}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s79},
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}  {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \int_0^t
\Psi_n(s)  \, ds \, \Big]
\, \le\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d}(\delta)
\end{align*}
for all $\delta>0$. In this formula,
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s82})}_{n,d} (\delta)} \,=\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s88} )}_{n,d} \,+\, 
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\, \int_0^t \Big\{ \delta\, n^2 \,
I_n(f_s ;\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}) \,+\, C_1 \,
H_n( f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)} ) \,+\,
{\mathfrak c}_{1,4}\, \frac{1}{\delta}\, \ell_1^2 \, n^{d-2}\, \Big\}\, ds\,,
\end{align*}
and ${\color{blue}  {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s88} )}_{n,d}}$ is the sum in $a$ and $j$ of the
expression appearing on the right-hand side of Proposition \ref{s88}
with $G=G_{a, j}$, $h=f_{a,j}$ divided by $n^{d/2}$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- remark-26: body_md -->
\label{r08}
A simple inspection provides a bound for the error terms
${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n$ and
${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d} (1/2)$:
\begin{gather*}
{\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n \, \le\,
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\big\{ \, H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,
+\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,4}\,  \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\, {\mathtt e}^{( \ref{s85} )}_{n,d}\,
\int_0^t \big\{ \,  1+ \Vert G(s) \Vert^2_\infty \big\}\, ds 
\\
{\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d} (1/2) \, \le\, \, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\, 
\int_0^t \Big\{ \, n^2I_n(f_s ;\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}) \, +\,
{\mathfrak c}_{1,3}\,  \big[\, (1 + {\mathtt K}_{d,1}(s)) \, H_n( f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)} )
\,+\, {\mathtt K}_{d,2} (s) \,\big]\, \Big\} \, ds \,.
\end{gather*}
In this equation, the variables ${\mathtt K}_{d,1} (s)$, ${\mathtt K}_{d,2} (s)$
are defined in Proposition \ref{s88}, and
${\mathtt e}^{( \ref{s85} )}_{n,1} = n^{(1/3)-2b}$,
${\mathtt e}^{( \ref{s85} )}_{n,2} = n^{4/5}$,
${\mathtt e}^{( \ref{s85} )}_{n,3} = \upsilon_n^{2} \, n^{3/2}$.  In
Proposition \ref{s88} we chose $\delta_0 = 1/(6d)$ and in Lemma
\ref{s82} $\delta=1/2$ to end up with
$n^2I_n(f ;\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})$ multiplied by $1$, a purely
cosmetic decision.
<!-- end remark-26 -->
<!-- conclusion-1: body_md -->
\label{s87}
In view of the decomposition \eqref{203}, Proposition \ref{s79} (and
Remark \ref{r04}), Lemmata \ref{s85}, \ref{s82} (and the previous
remark), to prove Theorem \ref{t02b}, it remains to estimate the
expressions involving $F_{y, {\mathtt k}, s}$. The argument is dimension
dependent.
<!-- end conclusion-1 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{s80}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s79},
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|}  \sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} }
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}}
|B^o_{{\mathtt k}} |\, G (s, y+B_{{\mathtt k}} )\,
F^o_{y, {\mathtt k}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, {\mathtt k}}(s)) \,
{\mathtt 1}_{{\mathfrak a}_0} \big({\textsf m}_{y, {\mathtt k}}(s) \big)  \, ds \, \Big|\,\Big]
\,\le\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s80})}_n\,,
\end{align*}
where
${\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s80})}_n} \,=\, {\mathtt S}^{(\ref{120})}_n \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_n$,
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt S}^{(\ref{120})}_n} \,:=\, C_1 \, \frac{n^{d/2}}{\ell_1^d}
\, \int_0^t \|G(s)\|_\infty\, ds\,,
\quad
{\color{blue}  {\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_n} \,:=\, 
\frac{C_1}{n^{d/2}}
\int_0^t \|G(s) \|_\infty \, \Big\{\, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})
+ \Big(\frac{n}{\ell_1}\Big)^d\, \Big\}\, ds \,.
\end{gather*}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
As before, we set $y=0$ and make sure that the estimates are uniform
over $y$.  By \eqref{120}, in the definition of $F^o_{{\mathtt k}, s}$ we may
replace $E_{\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}}\big[{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^{|A|}\big]$ by
$u(s, {\mathtt k})^{|A|}$ at a cost ${\mathtt S}^{(\ref{120})}_n$, defined in
the statement of the lemma.

At this point, and since ${\mathtt p}_A(\rho) = \rho^{|A|}$, to complete
the proof of the lemma, it remains to estimate
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt p}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt k}, s} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) } \,:=\,
{\mathtt p}_A({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) - {\mathtt p}_A(u(s,{\mathtt k}))-{\mathtt p}_A'(u(s,{\mathtt k}))\big[{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - u(s, {\mathtt k})\big] \,.
\end{align*}
By the Taylor estimate, the absolute value of this expression is less
than or equal to $C_1 \big[{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - u(s, {\mathtt k})\big]^2$.
Thus, by Lemma \ref{l02},
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n}\Big[ \,\Big| \int_0^t \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}} |B^o_{{\mathtt k}}|\, 
G(s, {\mathtt k}) \,  {\mathtt p}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt k}, s} ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})
\, ds\,\Big|\,\Big] \,\le\, {\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_n \,,
\end{align*}
where ${\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_n$ is defined in the statement of the
lemma. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Fix $T>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$.
Recall the definition of the norm
$\Vert G\Vert_{T,2}$ introduced just before the statement of the
theorem and let $\widehat G = G / \Vert G\Vert_{T,2} $, so that
$\sup_{0\le r\le T} \Vert \widehat G (r)\Vert_{C^2} \le 1$. Rewrite
the expectation appearing in the statement of the theorem as
\begin{align}
\label{235}
\Vert G \Vert_{T,2} \;
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n}\Big[\, \Big| \, \int_s^t \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} \widehat G(r, x/n) \, \Pi_{u(r,\cdot),h}(x, \eta^n(r))
\, dr\, \Big|\, \Big] \,.
\end{align}

By Proposition \ref{s79}, Lemmata \ref{s85}, \ref{s82}, the estimate
\eqref{208}, and Lemma \ref{s80},
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n}\Big[\, \Big| \, \int_s^t \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} \widehat G(r, x/n) \, \Pi_{u(r,\cdot),h}(x, \eta^n(r))
\, dr\, \Big|\, \Big]
\,\leq\,
{\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s79} )}_n \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n
\,+\, \frac{1}{2}\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d} (1/2)
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s32})}_{n, \ell_1} \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s80} )}_n \,. 
\end{align*}
In the formulae for the remainders we need to replace the
time-integrals between $0$ and $t$ by integrals between $s$ and $t$,
the entropy $H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)})$ by
$H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)})$, and $G$ by $\widehat G$.  The
term $\ell_1^{-d}\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1, G}$ does not
appear explicitly on the right-hand side because it is part of the
remainder ${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s79} )}_n$ (without the factor
$\ell_1^{-d}$).

By Remarks \ref{r04} and \ref{r08} and the explicit formula for
${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s80} )}_n$, the right-hand side is bounded by
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{n^{1/2}}\,
\big\{ \, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,
+\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,4}\,  \frac{1}{n^{(1/6) - b}}\, (t-s)
\\
\, &+\, \frac{1}{n^{1/2}}\, 
\int_s^t \Big\{ \, n^2I_n(f_r ;\, \nu^n_{u(r,\cdot)}) \, +\,
{\mathfrak c}_{1,3}\,  \big[\, H_n( f_r \,|\, \nu^n_{u(r, \cdot)} )
\,+\, n^{(1/3)+b} \,\big]\, \Big\} \, dr \,.
\end{align*}
This completes the proof in dimension $1$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{s78b}
For all $n\ge 1$,
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{L_3}}
\Pi^{2,3}_{y,{\mathtt j}, s} (\eta^n(s))  \, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big]
\\
& \le\,
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{L_3}}
|B_{2, {\mathtt j}} |\, G (s, y+B_{2, {\mathtt j}} )\,
F^{(2)}_{y,{\mathtt j}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, 2, {\mathtt j}}(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big] \, + \,  {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78b})}_n  \,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78b})}_n } \,:=\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\int_0^t {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s44})}_{\ell_1, \ell_2, 1, 1} (s)\, ds
\, +\, 2\,{\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2, G}
\,+ \, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s32})}_{n, \ell_1\ell_2, \ell_1}\,,
\end{equation*}
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s32})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2, \ell_1} }\, &:=\,
\frac{{\mathfrak c}_{1,0}}{n^{d/2}} \,
\Big(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\Big)^{d}\,
\Big(\frac{n}{(\ell_1\ell_2)^2}\Big)^d 
\int_0^t  \|G(s) \|_\infty \; ds
\\
& + \, 
\frac{{\mathfrak c}_{1,0}}{n^{d/2}}\, 
\Big(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\Big)^{d} \, 
\int_0^t  \Vert G(s)\Vert_\infty  
\big[\, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})
+ \ln (2)\,\big] \; ds  \,.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The proof follows closely the one of Lemma \ref{s78}, with two
modifications.  As before, we move the sum over $y$ out of the
expectation, fix $y=0$, and make sure that the estimates are uniform
over $y$.

First, instead of applying Proposition \ref{s36} we apply Proposition
\ref{s44} with ${\mathfrak p} = {\mathfrak p}_A$, ${\mathtt t}_1 = \ell_1$,
${\mathtt t}_2 = \ell_2$, ${\mathtt t}_3 = L_3$, $K_1 = K_2 = 1$.  This is
legitimate: as $\ell_1\ell_2 = n^{3/5}$ in $d=2$ and
$\ell_1\ell_2 = \upsilon_n^{2}\, n^{2/5}$ in $d=3$, the conditions
$(\ell_1\ell_2)^{d+3} \le n^3$, $(\ell_1\ell_2)^{1+(d/4)} \le n$ and
$\ell_2 \le \ell_1$ are satisfied for all $n$ large enough.
Proposition \ref{s44} replaces
$\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} |B_{{\mathtt k}}| G(s, B_{{\mathtt k}}) \{{\mathfrak p}_A({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}) - E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}} [{\mathfrak p}_A({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}})]\}$ by
$|B_{2,{\mathtt j}}|\, G(s, B_{2, {\mathtt j}})\, \{ {\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A({\textsf m}_{2,
{\mathtt j}}) - E_{\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}} [ {\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})
]\}$, at a cost bounded by
$n^{-d/2}\int_0^t {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s44})}_{\ell_1, \ell_2, 1, 1} (s)\,
ds$.

Second, by \eqref{212}, ${\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}) -
E_{\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}} [ {\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})]$ is the
sum of $F^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, s}$, of $\overline{W}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, A, s}$
and of the linear term of $\Lambda^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, s}$, which cancels
the one appearing in the definition of $\Pi^{2,3}_{{\mathtt j}, s}$.  It
remains to remove $\overline{W}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, A, s}$.  This is done
as in the proof of \eqref{208}: apply first Lemma \ref{s07b} to get
rid of the indicator, at a cost bounded by
${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2, G}$ (the extra factor
$\ell_1^{-2d}$ present in the definition of
$\overline{W}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, A, s}$ only improves this bound), and
then Lemma \ref{s32} with $r_1 = \ell_1\ell_2$, $r_2 = L_3$,
$F = {\mathtt q}^{(2)}_A$,
${\mathfrak a}({\mathtt j}) = (\ell_2/\ell_1)^{d}\, G(s, B_{2,{\mathtt j}})$ and
$\gamma = \gamma(s) = (\ell_1/\ell_2)^{d} / \|G(s)\|_\infty$.  Note
that
$|B_{2,{\mathtt j}}|\, \ell_1^{-2d} = (\ell_2/\ell_1)^{d}$, so that
$\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty \gamma \le 1$.  This yields
${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s32})}_{n, \ell_1\ell_2, \ell_1}$.

Finally, we remove the indicator
${\mathtt 1}_{{\mathfrak a}_0} \big({\textsf m}_{y, 2, {\mathtt j}}(s) \big)$ multiplying
$F^{(2)}_{y,{\mathtt j}, s}$, as in Proposition \ref{s79}, at the cost of a
second term ${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2, G}$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{s81b}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s79},
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } 
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{L_3}}
\Pi^{2,2}_{y,{\mathtt j}, s}(\eta^n(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \, \Big]
\,\le \, \frac{1}{2\, n^{d/2}}  \, {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \int_0^t
\Psi_n(s)  \, ds \, \Big]
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s81b} )}_n \,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue}  {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s81b} )}_n } \,:=\,
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\big\{ \, H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s03} )}_n
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s37} )}_n \,,
\end{equation*}
and ${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s03} )}_n$ is defined in Lemma \ref{s85}.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
As before, we fix $y=0$ and make sure that all estimates are uniform
over $y$.  Let
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} V^{(2)}_{s} }  \,:= \, \sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{L_3}}
\Pi^{2,2}_{{\mathtt j}, s}(\eta^n(s)) \,,
\end{align*}
and repeat the proof of Lemma \ref{s85} up to equation \eqref{210},
with $V^{(2)}_s$ in place of $V_s$.  We obtain the same bound with
\begin{align*}
{\mathtt X}^b_n (\eta) \, =\, b\,
\sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{L_3}} \, \Pi^{2,2}_{{\mathtt j}, s} (\eta)
\,+\, \frac{1}{2}\, 
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}^o|} \sum_{D\in {\mathcal A}}
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}} \,
\Pi^{2,D}_{y, {\mathtt k}, s} (\eta) \,.
\end{align*}
In the first sum we have cubes of width $\ell_1\ell_2$, and in the
second cubes of width $\ell_1$.  It remains to apply Proposition
\ref{s37} with ${\mathfrak p} = {\mathfrak p}_A$, ${\mathtt t}_1 = \ell_1$,
${\mathtt t}_2 = \ell_2$, $K_1=1$ and $\delta = 1/2$ to estimate the first
sum, and Lemma \ref{s03} with $\delta = 1/(2|{\mathcal A}|)$ to estimate the
second one.  The hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s37} are fulfilled for
all $n$ large enough by the choices of $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$ made at the
beginning of this subsection.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- conclusion-2: body_md -->
\label{s87b}
In view of the decomposition \eqref{213}, of the estimates
\eqref{192c}, \eqref{214}, and of Lemmata \ref{s78b}, \ref{s81b},
\ref{s82}, the expression \eqref{206} is bounded by
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{L_3}}
|B_{2, {\mathtt j}} |\, G (s, y+B_{2, {\mathtt j}} )\,
F^{(2)}_{y,{\mathtt j}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, 2, {\mathtt j}}(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big]
\,+\, \frac{1}{2}  \, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d}(\delta)
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s87b})}_n\,,
\end{align*}
for all $\delta>0$, where
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s87b})}_n} \,:=\,
\frac{2}{n^{d/2}} \, \int_0^t {\mathtt S}^{(\ref{135})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2}
(G_s,{\mathtt p}'_A, u_s)\, ds
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2, G}
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78b})}_n \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s81b} )}_n \,.
\end{equation*}
It therefore remains to estimate the first one.  The argument is
dimension dependent.
<!-- end conclusion-2 -->
<!-- remark-27: body_md -->
\label{r10}
At this stage, the expression left to estimate has the same form as
the one in Subsection \ref{ssec9.1}, with
the cubes $B_{{\mathtt k}}$ of width $\ell_1$ replaced by the cubes
$B_{2, {\mathtt j}}$ of width $\ell_1\ell_2$, and the polynomial ${\mathfrak p}_A$
replaced by ${\mathtt p}_A$.  In dimension $d=2$ the cubes are now large
enough for the argument of Lemma \ref{s80} to apply, and the proof is
complete.  In dimension $d=3$ one further scale is needed, and the
construction of this subsection is repeated once more.
<!-- end remark-27 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{s80b}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s79},
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{L_3}}
|B_{2, {\mathtt j}} |\, G (s, y+B_{2, {\mathtt j}} )\,
F^{(2)}_{y, {\mathtt j}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, 2, {\mathtt j}}(s)) \, ds \, \Big|\,\Big]
\,\le\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s80b})}_n\,,
\end{align*}
where
${\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s80b})}_n} \,=\, {\mathtt S}^{(\ref{120})}_{n, \ell_1\ell_2}
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_{n, \ell_1\ell_2}$,
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt S}^{(\ref{120})}_{n,r_1}} \,:=\, C_1 \, \frac{n^{d/2}}{r_1^d}
\, \int_0^t \|G(s)\|_\infty\, ds\,,
\quad
{\color{blue}  {\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_{n,r_1}} \,:=\, 
\frac{C_1}{n^{d/2}}
\int_0^t \|G(s) \|_\infty \, \Big\{\, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})
+ \Big(\frac{n}{r_1}\Big)^d\, \Big\}\, ds \,.
\end{gather*}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
As before, we set $y=0$ and make sure that the estimates are uniform
over $y$.  By \eqref{120} with $r_1 = \ell_1\ell_2$, in the definition
\eqref{195d} of $F^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, s}$ we may replace
$E_{\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}}\big[{\mathtt p}_A ({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})\big]$ by
${\mathtt p}_A ( u(s, B_{2, {\mathtt j}}))$ at a cost bounded by
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\int_0^t \|G(s)\|_\infty\,
\sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{L_3}} (\ell_1\ell_2)^d\,
\big|E_{\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}}\big[{\mathtt p}_A({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(s))\big]
- {\mathtt p}_A( u(s, B_{2, {\mathtt j}}))\big|\; ds
\ \leq \ {\mathtt S}^{(\ref{120})}_{n, \ell_1\ell_2}\, .
\end{align*}
At this point, it remains to estimate
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt p}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, s} ({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}) } \,:=\,
{\mathtt p}_A({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}) - {\mathtt p}_A(u(s, B_{2, {\mathtt j}}))-{\mathtt p}_A'(u(s, B_{2, {\mathtt j}}))\big[{\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}} - u(s, B_{2,{\mathtt j}})\big] \,.
\end{align*}
By a Taylor expansion, the absolute value of this expression is less
than or equal to
$C_1 \big[{\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}} - u(s, B_{2, {\mathtt j}})\big]^2$.  Thus, by
Lemma \ref{l02} with $r_1 = \ell_1\ell_2$, $r_2 = L_3$,
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n}\Big[ \,\Big| \int_0^t \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{L_3}} (\ell_1\ell_2)^d\, 
G(s, B_{2, {\mathtt j}}) \,  {\mathtt p}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, s} ({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(s))
\, ds\,\Big|\,\Big] \,\le\, {\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_{n, \ell_1\ell_2} \,,
\end{align*}
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Fix $T>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$. Repeat the proof of the theorem in
dimension $1$ up to equation \eqref{235}.  By the decomposition
\eqref{203}, Proposition \ref{s79}, Lemmata \ref{s85}, \ref{s82},
Conclusion \ref{s87b}, and Lemma \ref{s80b}, the expression appearing
in \eqref{235} is bounded by
\begin{align*}
\Vert G \Vert_{T,2} \; \big\{\, 
{\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s79} )}_n \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d} (1/2)
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s87b})}_n \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s80b} )}_n \,\big\}
\,.
\end{align*}
In the formulae for the remainders we replace the time-integrals
between $0$ and $t$ by integrals between $s$ and $t$, the entropy
$H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)})$ by
$H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)})$, and $G$ by $\widehat{G}$.

We estimate the previous displayed equation. Since
$\sup_{0\le r\le T} \Vert \widehat G (r)\Vert_{C^2} \le 1$, inspecting
all terms yields that the expression inside curly braces is bounded by
\begin{align*}
&\frac{2}{n^{d/2}}\,
\big\{ \, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,
+\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,3}\,  \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\, 
\int_s^t  \, H_n( f_r \,|\, \nu^n_{u(r, \cdot)} ) \, dr
\\
\, &+\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\, 
\int_s^t \Big\{ \, 2\, n^2 \, I_n(f_r ;\, \nu^n_{u(r,\cdot)}) \, +\,
{\mathfrak c}_{1,4}\,  n^{4/5} \,  \Big\} \, dr \,,
\end{align*}
as claimed.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{s78c}
For all $n\ge 1$,
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
\Pi^{3,3}_{y,{\mathtt i}, s} (\eta^n(s))  \, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big]
\\
& \le\,
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt i} \in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
|B_{3, {\mathtt i}} |\, G (s, y+B_{3, {\mathtt i}} )\,
F^{(3)}_{y,{\mathtt i}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, 3, {\mathtt i}}(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \,
\Big] \, + \,  {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78c})}_n  \,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78c})}_n } \,:=\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\int_0^t {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s44})}_{\ell_1\ell_2, \ell_3, \kappa^6, 1} (s)\, ds
\, +\, 2\,{\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3, G}
\,+ \, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s45})}_{n, \ell_1\ell_2\ell_3}\,,
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s45})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3} }\, :=\,
\frac{C_1}{n^{d/2}} \,
\int_0^t  \Vert G(s)\Vert_\infty  \,\Big\{ \,
H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})
\,+\, \ell_3^d\, \Big(\frac{n}{(\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3)^{3/2}}\Big)^d
\,\Big\} \; ds  \,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The proof repeats the one of Lemma \ref{s78b}.  We fix $y=0$ and make
sure that the estimates are uniform over $y$.

We apply Proposition \ref{s44} with ${\mathfrak p} = {\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A$,
${\mathtt t}_1 = \ell_1\ell_2$, ${\mathtt t}_2 = \ell_3$, ${\mathtt t}_3 = L_4$,
$K_1 = \kappa^6$, $K_2 = 1$.  An inspection shows that the hypotheses
of that result are fulfilled for all $n$ large enough. For instance,
$\ell_3 \le \ell_1\ell_2$ because
$\ell_3/(\ell_1\ell_2) = \kappa\, \upsilon_n^{-4}\, n^{-3/10}$, which
vanishes since $\upsilon_n^{-1}\le n^{3/100}$.  This
proposition allows us to replace
\begin{align*}
\sum_{{\mathtt j}\in \Lambda_{3, {\mathtt i}}} |B_{2, {\mathtt j}}| G(s, B_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \{{\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}) - E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{3,{\mathtt i},
{\textsf M}}} [{\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})]\}
\end{align*}
by
\begin{align*}
|B_{3,{\mathtt i}}|\, G(s, B_{3, {\mathtt i}})\, \{ {\mathfrak p}^{(3)}_A({\textsf m}_{3,
{\mathtt i}}) - E_{\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}} [ {\mathfrak p}^{(3)}_A({\textsf m}_{3, {\mathtt i}})
]\}
\end{align*}
at a cost bounded by
$n^{-d/2}\int_0^t {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s44})}_{\ell_1\ell_2, \ell_3,
\kappa^6, 1} (s)\, ds$.

By \eqref{216}, the resulting expression is the sum of
$F^{(3)}_{{\mathtt i}, s}$, of $\overline{W}^{(3)}_{{\mathtt i}, A, s}$ and of
the linear term, which cancels the one appearing in the definition of
$\Pi^{3,3}_{{\mathtt i}, s}$.  It remains to remove
$\overline{W}^{(3)}_{{\mathtt i}, A, s}$.  We first apply Lemma \ref{s07b}
to get rid of the indicator, at a cost bounded by
${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3, G}$.  We then estimate
each of the three correctors of \eqref{216} separately.  The dominant
one is $(\ell_1\ell_2)^{-d}\, {\mathtt q}_A$. Its contribution is given by
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \int_0^t \int \Big| \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
\ell_3^d\, G(s, B_{3,{\mathtt i}}) \,
\big\{\, {\mathtt q}_A ({\textsf m}_{3, {\mathtt i}}) -
E_{\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}} [ {\mathtt q}_A ({\textsf m}_{3, {\mathtt i}})]\, \big\}\,
\Big|\, f_s\, d\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}\, ds \,.
\end{equation*}
As ${\mathtt q}_A$ is a polynomial, Lemma \ref{s45} applies to each of its
monomials with $r_1 = \ell_1\ell_2\ell_3$, $r_2 = L_4$,
${\mathfrak a} ({\mathtt i}) = \ell_3^d\, G(s, B_{3,{\mathtt i}})$ and
${\mathfrak c}_0 = \Vert G(s)\Vert_\infty$.  The hypothesis
$\Vert {\mathfrak a}\Vert_\infty \le {\mathfrak c}_0\, r_1^{d/2}$ of that lemma reads
$\ell_3^d \le (\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3)^{d/2}$, that is,
$\ell_3 \le (\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3)^{1/2} = \kappa^{1/2} n^{1/4}$, which
holds for all $n$ large enough because
$\ell_3 = \kappa\, \upsilon_n^{-2}\, n^{1/10}$,
$\upsilon_n^{-1}\le n^{3/100}$.  This yields
${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s45})}_{n, \ell_1\ell_2\ell_3}$.  The two remaining
correctors of \eqref{216} carry the extra factor $\ell_1^{-2d}$ and
are estimated in the same way, at a smaller cost.

Finally, we remove the indicator
${\mathtt 1}_{{\mathfrak a}_0} \big({\textsf m}_{y, 3, {\mathtt i}}(s) \big)$ multiplying
$F^{(3)}_{y,{\mathtt i}, s}$ at the cost of a second factor
${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3, G}$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{s81c}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s79},
\begin{align*}
& \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } 
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
\Pi^{3,2}_{y,{\mathtt i}, s}(\eta^n(s)) \, ds \, \Big| \, \Big]
\,\le \, \frac{1}{2\, n^{d/2}}  \, {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \int_0^t
\Psi_n(s)  \, ds \, \Big]
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s81c} )}_n \,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue}  {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s81c} )}_n } \,:=\,
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\big\{ \, H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s03} )}_n
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s37} ), 3}_n \,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
The proof is the one of Lemma \ref{s81b}, applying Proposition
\ref{s37} with ${\mathfrak p} = {\mathfrak p}^{(2)}_A$, ${\mathtt t}_1 = \ell_1\ell_2$,
${\mathtt t}_2 = \ell_3$, $K_1 = \kappa^6$, $\delta = 1/2$ to estimate the
first sum, and Lemma \ref{s03} with $\delta = 1/(2|{\mathcal A}|)$ to
estimate the second one.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{s80c}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s79},
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,\Big| \int_0^t
\frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt 0}}|} 
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt 0}} } \sum_{{\mathtt i}\in \Sigma^+_{L_4}}
|B_{3, {\mathtt i}} |\, G (s, y+B_{3, {\mathtt i}} )\,
F^{(3)}_{y, {\mathtt i}, s} ({\textsf m}_{y, 3, {\mathtt i}}(s)) \, ds \, \Big|\,\Big]
\,\le\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s80c})}_n\,,
\end{align*}
where
${\color{blue} {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s80c})}_n} \,=\, {\mathtt S}^{(\ref{120})}_{n,
\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3} \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{ ( \ref{l02} ) }_{n,
\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3}$, these remainders being defined in the statement
of Lemma \ref{s80b}.  In particular, as
$\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3 = \kappa\, n^{1/2}$ and $d=3$,
\begin{equation*}
{\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s80c})}_n \,\le\,
\frac{C_1}{\kappa^{3}} \, \int_0^t \|G(s)\|_\infty\, ds
\,+\, \frac{C_1}{n^{d/2}}
\int_0^t \|G(s) \|_\infty \, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)})\, ds \,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
The proof is the one of Lemma \ref{s80b}, with $\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3$ in
place of $\ell_1\ell_2$ and $L_4$ in place of $L_3$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Fix $T>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$. Recall the definition of the norm
$\Vert G\Vert_{T,2}$ introduced just before the statement of the
theorem and let $\widehat G = G / \Vert G\Vert_{T,2} $, so that
$\sup_{0\le r\le T} \Vert \widehat G (r)\Vert_{C^2} \le 1$. Rewrite
the expectation appearing in the statement of the theorem as in
\eqref{235}. 

Collecting Proposition \ref{s79}, Lemmata \ref{s85}, \ref{s82},
Conclusion \ref{s87b}, the decomposition \eqref{217}, the estimates
\eqref{218} and Lemmata \ref{s78c}, \ref{s81c}, \ref{s80c} with $G$
replaced by $\widehat G$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n}\Big[\, \Big| \, \int_s^t \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}
\sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} \widehat G(r, x/n) \, \Pi_{u(r,\cdot),h}(x, \eta^n(r))
\, dr\, \Big|\, \Big]
\,\leq\,
{\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s79} )}_n \,+\,  {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n
\,+\, \frac{3}{2}\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d}(1/2)
\,+\,   {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s87b})}_n
\\
&\qquad
\,+\, \frac{2}{n^{d/2}} \, \int_s^t
{\mathtt S}^{(\ref{135})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3} (\widehat G_r,{\mathtt p}'_A, u_r)\, dr
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3, \widehat G}
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78c})}_n \,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s81c} )}_n
\,+\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s80c} )}_n \,,
\end{align*}
where, as in dimension $2$, in the formulae for the remainders the
time-integrals between $0$ and $t$ are replaced by integrals between
$s$ and $t$, and the entropy $H_n(f_0 \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)})$ by
$H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)})$.  Note that the third scale
produced one further term
$(1/2)\, n^{-d/2}\, {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n}[\int_s^t \Psi_n(r)\, dr]$, coming
from Lemma \ref{s81c}, so that the total contribution of the term
$\Psi_n$ is at most $(3/2)\, {\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,3}(1/2)$, by
Lemma \ref{s82}.  

It remains to examine each term on the right-hand side. Recall that
$\ell_1 = \upsilon_n n^{1/4}$,
$\ell_1\ell_2 = \upsilon_n^{2} n^{2/5}$,
$\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3 = \kappa\, n^{1/2}$, and that
$\upsilon_n^{-1}\le n^{3/100}$. 

The remainders ${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s79} )}_n$, ${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s85} )}_n$
and ${\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s82} )}_{n,d}(1/2)$ have been estimated in Remarks
\ref{r04} and \ref{r08}. The remainder
${\mathtt S}^{(\ref{135})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3} (\widehat G_r,{\mathtt p}'_A,
u_r)$ is easily bounded, as well as
${\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s07b})}_{n,\ell_1\ell_2\ell_3, \widehat G}$.

A meticulous inspection yields that
\begin{align*}
{\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s87b})}_n \,\le\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}} 
\Big\{ H_n(f_s\,|\,\nu^n_{u(s,\cdot)}) + \ln(2) \Big\}
\,+\, \frac{{\mathfrak c}_{1,3}}{n^{d/2}} \int_s^t
\big\{\, H_n(f_r\,|\,\nu^n_{u(r, \cdot)})\,+\,
\upsilon^{2}_n\, n^{3/2}\,\big\}\,
dr\,,
\end{align*}
since $\upsilon^{- 1}_n =  n^{3/100}$. Similarly,
\begin{gather*}
{\mathtt R}^{(\ref{s78c})}_n 
\,\le\, 
\frac{{\mathfrak c}_{1,3}}{n^{d/2}} \int_s^t
\big\{\, H_n(f_r\,|\,\nu^n_{u(r, \cdot)})\,+\,
\kappa^{1/2}\, n^{5/4}\,\big\}\,
dr\,,
\\
{\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s81c} )}_n
\,\le\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}}\,
\big\{ \, H_n(f_s \,|\, \nu^n_{u_s, \cdot)}) \,+\, \ln (2)\,\big\}\,
\,+\, {\mathfrak c}_{1,3} \, \int_s^t \big\{\, \upsilon_n^{2}
\,+\, \kappa^5 \, \upsilon_n^{-12}\, n^{-2/5}\,\big\} \, dr \,,
\\
{\mathtt R}^{( \ref{s80c} )}_n  \,\le\,
C_1\, 
\int_s^t  \big\{\, \frac{1}{n^{d/2}} \, H_n(f_r \,|\, \nu^n_{u(r,\cdot)})\,
\,+\, \frac{1}{\kappa^{3}} \, \big\} \, dr \,.
\end{gather*}
To complete the proof of the theorem, it remains to recollect all
previous estimates.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{s65}
Recall that $0<t\le T$ is fixed. Fix a non-integer, real number
$\beta>0$, $F\in H^{\beta+2}$. Assume that the solution $u$ of the
hydrodynamic equation \eqref{127} belongs to
$H^{\beta/2,\beta} ([0,t]\times {\mathbb T}^d)$ and is bounded away from $0$
and $1$: there exists $0<{\mathfrak r}<1/2$ such that
${\mathfrak r}\le u(s,x) \le 1-{\mathfrak r}$ for all $(s,x) \in [0,T]\times {\mathbb T}^d$.
Then, there exists a unique classical solution
${\mathfrak v} \colon [0,t] \times {\mathbb T}^d \to {\mathbb R}$ in
$H^{(\beta+2)/2,\beta+2}$ to the Cauchy problem
\eqref{159b}. Moreover, there exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak c}^{(\rm k)}_{1}$, depending only on $T$, $\beta$ and $u$ in
$[0,t]\times {\mathbb T}^d$, such that
\begin{equation*}
\| {\mathfrak v} \|_{(\beta +2)} \,\leq \, 
{\mathfrak c}^{(\rm k)}_{1}\, \| F \|_{(\beta +2)} \,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{s77}
Let $d\leq 3$.  Assume that $\mu_n$ is a sequence of probability
measures on $\Omega_n$ satisfying
$H_n(\mu_n \,|\, \nu^n_{u_0(\cdot)}) = o(n^{d/2})$. Suppose that there
exists ${\mathtt r}_0 > d/2$ such that the sequence of laws of $X^n_0$ is
tight in ${\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}_0}$. Suppose, finally, that the solution $u$
of \eqref{127} satisfies ${\mathfrak r} \le u \le 1 - {\mathfrak r}$ and belongs to
$H^{\beta/2,\beta}([0,T]\times {\mathbb T}^d)$ for some non-integer
$\beta > {\mathtt r}_0 + (d/2) + 4$. Then, the sequence of probability
measures ${\mathbb Q}_{\mu_n}$ is tight in $L^1(0,T;{\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}})$ for
${\mathtt r} \;>\; {\mathtt r}^\star $, where ${\mathtt r}^\star$ has been introduced
in \eqref{242b}.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
The proof follows from the previous estimates, from the decomposition
\eqref{145b} and from the fact that a finite sum of tight sequences of
random elements of a separable Banach space is tight.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- remark-28: body_md -->
\label{s91b}
The threshold ${\mathtt r} > 6 + (3d+1)/2$ comes from the terms
${\mathfrak J}^{3,n}$, ${\mathfrak J}^{4,n}$, and the requirement
${\mathtt r} > {\mathtt r}_0 + d+ 4$ appears in the proof of the tightness of
the process ${\mathfrak J}^{1,n}$.
<!-- end remark-28 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{s55}
Let $\mu_n$ be a sequence of probability measures on $\Omega_n$
satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{t1}.  Fix $p\ge 1$,
$0\le t_1\le t_2 \le \cdots \le t_p$ and functions
$F_j\in C^\infty({\mathbb T}^d)$, $1\le j\le p$. Under the measure
${\mathbb P}_{\mu_n}$, the random vector
$(X^{n}_{t_1}(F_1), \dots, X^{n}_{t_p}(F_p))$ converges in
distribution to
$(X_{0}(P_{0,t_1} F_1), \dots, X_{0}( P_{0,t_p} F_p)) + ({\textsf M}_{t_1}(F_1), \dots, {\textsf M}_{t_p}(F_p))$, where the two vectors are
independent, $X_0$ is the limit of the sequence of
${\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}_0}$-valued fields $X^n_0$, and
$({\textsf M}_{t_1}(F_1), \dots, {\textsf M}_{t_p}(F_p))$ is a zero-mean
Gaussian vector with covariances given by
\begin{equation}
\label{152}
{\mathbb E} \big[\, {\textsf M}_{t_i}(F_i) \, {\textsf M}_{t_j}(F_j) \,\big]
\,=\,
\int_0^{t_i\wedge t_j} \int_{{\mathbb T}^d} 2\, \chi(u(s,x))\,
(\nabla P_{s,t_i} F_i)(x) \cdot  D(u(s,x)) \, (\nabla P_{s,t_j}
F_j) (x) \; dx \; ds \,.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{s54}
Fix a cylinder function $f$. Then, there exists a finite constant $C_0
= C_0(f)$ such that
\begin{align*}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\int_0^t \,\Big|\, \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n} J(s,x) \,
\Big\{ \, f(\tau_x \eta^n(s)) -  E_{\nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)} } [ \tau_x f]  \,\Big\}
\,\Big| \,  \, ds \, \Big] \\
&\qquad \le\;
\int_0^t \Big\{ \, \frac{1}{\gamma}\, 
\big[\, H_n(f^n_s\,|\, \nu^n_{u(s, \cdot)}  ) \,+\, \ln (2) \,\big] \;+\;
C_0 \, \gamma\, n^d\, \Vert  J_s \Vert^2_\infty\,
e^{C_0 \, \gamma\,  \Vert  J_s \Vert_\infty} \,\Big\} \; ds
\end{align*}
for every function $J\colon {\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb T}^d_n \to {\mathbb R}$,
$t>0$, $n\ge 1$, $\gamma>0$. In this formula, $J_s$ is the function
which takes the value $J(s,x)$ at $x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{s62}
For each $F$, $G \in C^\infty({\mathbb T}^d)$, $t>0$, the random variables
$X^n_0(G)$ and $M^{n,t}_t(F)$ are asymptotically independent:
for every $\theta\in{\mathbb R}$,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
& \lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp i\, \theta\,  \big\{  M^{n,t}_t(F) + X^n_0 (G) \big\}
\,\Big]
\\
&\quad \,=\,
\lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp \big\{   i\, \theta\,  M^{n,t}_t(F) \big\}
\,\Big] \lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp \big\{   i\, \theta\,  X^n_0 (G) \big\}
\,\Big] \,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
As $M^{n,t}_t(F)=0$ for $t=0$, we may assume that $t>0$.
For $\theta\in {\mathbb R}$, $0\le s\le t$, consider the exponential
\begin{equation*}
e^{ i\, \theta\, M^{n,t}_s (F)} \,=\,
\exp\Big\{ i\,\theta\, X^n_s(H_s) \,-\, i\,\theta\, X^n_0(H_0)
\,-\, i\,\theta\, \int_0^s (\partial_r + L_n) X^n_r(H_r)\,
dr\Big\}\,, 
\end{equation*}
where ${\color{blue} H_r = P_{r,t} F}$. Let
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} W^n_s(H_\cdot) } \,:=\, e^{- i\,\theta\, X^n_s (H_s)  }
(\partial_s + L_n)  e^{i\,\theta\, X^n_s (H_s)  }
\,-\,  i\,\theta \, (\partial_s + L_n) X^n_s(H_s)\,,
\end{equation*}
and write the previous exponential as
\begin{equation}
\label{151}
{\mathbb M}^n_s (H_\cdot)\, \exp\Big\{ \int_0^s W^n_r (H_\cdot) \, dr \Big\}
\end{equation}
where ${\mathbb M}^n_s (H_\cdot)$ is the exponential martingale given by 
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue}  {\mathbb M}^n_s (H_\cdot)} \, :=\, 
\exp\Big\{ i\,\theta\, X^n_s(H_s) \,-\, i\,\theta\, X^n_0(H_0)
\,-\, \int_0^s e^{- i\,\theta\, X^n_r (H_r)  }
(\partial_r + L_n)  e^{i\,\theta\, X^n_r (H_r)  }\, dr\Big\}\,.
\end{equation*}
Note that ${\mathbb M}^n_s(H_\cdot)$ is equal to $1$ at time $0$.

In the definition of $W^n_s(H_\cdot)$, the time-derivatives
cancel. Perform a Taylor expansion in the first term. The first-order
term in the expansion cancels with the second term in the definition
of $W^n_s(H_\cdot)$ so that
\begin{equation*}
W^n_s (H_\cdot)\,=\, \frac{-\, \theta^2}{2}\, 
\frac{1}{n^d} \sum_{j=1}^d \sum_{x\in {\mathbb T}^d_n}
c_{0,e_j}  (\tau_x \eta^n(s)) \, [\eta^n_{x+e_j} (s) - \eta^n_x(s)]^2\,
[(\nabla^n_j H_s)(x/n)]^2 \,+\, O(n^{-(d/2)-1})\,.
\end{equation*}
By Lemma \ref{s54} with $J(s,x)$ replaced by
$n^{-d} \, [\nabla^n_j P_{s,t}F (x/n)]^2$, the time integral over the
interval $[0,s]$ of $W^n_r(H_\cdot)$ converges in $L^1({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$
to  $- (1/2) \,\theta^2\, {\textsf V}_s (H_\cdot)$, where
\begin{equation}
\label{153}
{\color{blue}  {\textsf V}_s (H_\cdot)}  \,:=\, 
\int_0^s \int_{{\mathbb T}^d} 2\, \chi(u(r,x))\,
(\nabla H_r)(x) \cdot  D(u(r,x)) \, (\nabla H_r) (x) \; dx \; dr \;.
\end{equation}
In conclusion, $\exp\{ i\, \theta\, M^{n,t}_s (F)\}$ is the product of
an exponential martingale with
$\exp \{ \int_0^s W^n_r (H_\cdot) \, dr \}$, where $W^n_r(H_\cdot)$ is
a uniformly bounded expression which converges in probability to the
deterministic value $- (1/2) \,\theta^2\, {\textsf V}_s (H_\cdot)$.

Fix $\theta\in {\mathbb R}$. By the previous considerations,
\begin{align*}
& \lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp i\, \theta\,  \big\{  M^{n,t}_t(F) + X^n_0 (G) \big\}
\,\Big]
\\
&\quad 
\,=\,
\lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp \big\{ i\, \theta\, X^n_0 (G) \big\}\, {\mathbb M}^n_t (H_\cdot)
\, \exp\Big\{ \int_0^t W^n_r (H_\cdot)\, dr \Big\} \,\Big]
\end{align*}
Since the time-integral of $W^n_r(H_\cdot)$ converges in probability to $-
(1/2) \,\theta^2\, {\textsf V}_t(H_\cdot)$ and ${\mathbb M}^n_t $ is a
martingale equal to $1$ at time $0$, the previous expression is equal
to
\begin{align*}
&\quad \lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp \big\{ i\, \theta\, X^n_0 (G) \big\}\, {\mathbb M}^n_t (H_\cdot)
\, \,\Big]\, \exp\big\{  - (1/2) \,\theta^2\, {\textsf V}_t(H_\cdot)
\big\}
\\
&\quad  \,=\,
\lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp \big\{ i\, \theta\, X^n_0 (G) \big\} \,\Big]\,
\exp\big\{  - (1/2) \,\theta^2\, {\textsf V}_t(H_\cdot) \big\}
\end{align*}
The same computation shows that the second term is equal to
$\lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} [\, \exp \{i\, \theta\,
M^{n,t}_t(F)\} \,]$. This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
\label{s60}
The previous proof yields also that $M^{n,t}_t(F)$ converges in
distribution to a Gaussian random variable with zero mean and variance
equal to ${\textsf V}_t(H_\cdot) = {\textsf V}_t(P_{\cdot, t}F)$.
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{s59}
For each $p\ge 1$, $0\le  t_1\le \cdots \le t_p$, $F_1, \dots, F_p$,
$G \in C^\infty({\mathbb T}^d)$, the random variables $X^n_0(G)$ and
$\sum_{1\le j\le p} M^{n,t_j}_{t_j}(F_j)$ are asymptotically
independent: for every $\theta\in{\mathbb R}$,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
& \lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp i \theta\,  \Big\{ X^n_0 (G) + \sum_{j=1}^p 
M^{n,t_j}_{t_j}(F_j) \Big\} \,\Big]
\\
&\quad \,=\,
\lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp \big\{   i\, \theta\,  X^n_0 (G) \big\}
\,\Big] 
\lim_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\,
\exp i \theta\, \sum_{j=1}^p 
M^{n,t_j}_{t_j}(F_j)  \,\Big]
\,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The proof is similar to the previous one. We may also assume here that
$t_1>0$.  Write the expression inside braces on the left-hand side as
\begin{align*}
X^n_0 ( G) 
\,+\, \sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \Big\{ \, {\textsf M}^{n} _{t_{k+1}}
( \sum_{j=k+1}^p P_{\cdot, t_j} F_j) - {\textsf M}^{n}_{t_{k}}
( \sum_{j=k+1}^p P_{\cdot,t_j} F_j)\, \Big\}\,,
\end{align*}
where $t_0=0$. Recall the definitions of the exponential martingale
${\mathbb M}^n_s(H_\cdot)$, and the process $W^n_s (H_\cdot)$ introduced in
\eqref{151}. In view of the previous displayed equation rewrite the
expectation appearing in the statement of the lemma as
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \exp \big\{ i  \theta\,  X^n_0 (G) \big\} \,
\prod_{k=0}^{p-1} \,
\frac{{\mathbb M}^n_{t_{k+1}} (G^{(k)}_\cdot) } {{\mathbb M}^n_{t_k}(G^{(k)}_\cdot)}
\, \exp\Big\{ \int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}} W^n_r  (G^{(k)}_\cdot) \, dr \Big\} \,
\Big]\,, 
\end{equation*}
where $G^{(k)} = \sum_{j=k+1}^p P_{\cdot, t_j} F_j$.

As in the previous lemma, $\int_{[t_k, t_{k+1}]} W^n_r
(G^{(k)}_\cdot) \, dr$ converges in $L^1({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$ to the
deterministic value
\begin{equation*}
-\, \theta^2\,
\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}   \int_{{\mathbb T}^d} \chi(u(r,x))\,
(\nabla G^{(k)}_r)(x) \cdot  D(u(r,x)) \, (\nabla G^{(k)}_r) (x) \; dx \; dr \;.
\end{equation*}
In the penultimate displayed equation, we may, therefore, replace
$\int_{[t_k, t_{k+1}]} W^n_r (G^{(k)}_\cdot) \, dr$ by the previous
quantity paying a cost which vanishes as $n\to\infty$. After this
replacement, taking successive conditional expectations we show that
the remaining expectation is equal to
${\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} [\, \exp \{ i \theta\, X^n_0 (G) \} \,]$. This proves
the asymptotic independence claimed.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
\label{s61}
The previous proof yields that the sequence of random variables
$\sum_{1\le j\le p} M^{n,t_j}_{t_j}(F_j)$ converges in distribution to
a zero-mean Gaussian variable with variance equal to
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}   \int_{{\mathbb T}^d} 2\, \chi(u(r,x))\,
(\nabla G^{(k)}_r)(x) \cdot  D(u(r,x)) \, (\nabla G^{(k)}_r) (x) \; dx \; dr \;.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Let $\mu_n$ be a sequence of probability measures on $\Omega_n$
satisfying the hypotheses of the proposition.  Fix $p\ge 1$,
$0 \le  t_1\le t_2 \le  \cdots \le t_p$, functions $F_j\in C^\infty({\mathbb T}^d)$,
$1\le j\le p$, and $T>t_p$.

Since $M^{n,t}_t (F)=0$ if $t=0$, we may assume that $t_1>0$. 
We first prove the proposition for $p=1$. By Lemma \ref{s56},
$X^n_{t_1}(F_1) - X^n_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1) -M^{n,t_1}_{t_1}(F_1)$ converges
to $0$ in $L^1({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$. By hypothesis, $X^n_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1)$
converges in law to $X_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1)$, and by Remark \ref{s60},
$M^{n,t_1}_{t_1}(F_1)$ converges in law to ${\textsf M}_{t_1}(F_1)$. By
Lemma \ref{s62}, $X^n_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1)$, $M^{n,t_1}_{t_1}(F_1)$ are
asymptotically independent. Thus,
$X^n_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1) +M^{n,t_1}_{t_1}(F_1)$ converges in law to the sum of
two independent random variables which are distributed as
$X_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1)$ and ${\textsf M}_{t_1}(F_1)$. This completes the proof of
the proposition for $p=1$.

The proof for the general case is similar. By Lemma \ref{s56}, it is
enough to consider the limit of the vector
$(X^n_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1) +M^{n,t_1}_{t_1}(F_1), \dots, X^n_0(P_{0,t_p}F_p)
+M^{n,t_p}_{t_p}(F_p))$. By Lemma \ref{s59}, the vectors
$(X^n_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1) , \dots, X^n_0(P_{0,t_p}F_p))$,
$(M^{n,t_1}_{t_1}(F_1), \dots, M^{n,t_p}_{t_p}(F_p))$ are
asymptotically independent [By Fourier transform two vectors are
independent, or asymptotically independent, if all linear combinations
of the coordinates are independent]. By hypothesis,
$(X^n_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1) , \dots, X^n_0(P_{0,t_p}F_p))$ converges in
distribution to $(X_0(P_{0,t_1}F_1) , \dots, X_0(P_{0,t_p}F_p))$. By
Remark \ref{s61}, and a straightforward computation, the vector
$(M^{n,t_1}_{t_1}(F_1), \dots, M^{n,t_p}_{t_p}(F_p))$ converges in
distribution to a zero-mean Gaussian vector with covariances given by
\eqref{152}. This completes the proof of the proposition.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{s95}
Fix ${\mathtt r} > {\mathtt r}^\star$, where ${\mathtt r}^\star$ has been introduced
in \eqref{242b}.  Fix $G\in {\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}$ and $0\le s<t\le T$.  Then,
$\Gamma^{s,t}_0 G$ belongs to ${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{247}
\Vert \Gamma^{s,t}_0 G \Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}} \;\le\;
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \, T\, \Vert G \Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}}\;,
\qquad
\sup_{0\le r\le t} \Vert \Gamma^{s,t}_r G \Vert_{C^{2}} \;\le\;
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \, T\, \Vert G \Vert_{C^{3}} \;.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for all $0\le r\le t$ and $0\le a\le b\le t$,
\begin{equation}
\label{248}
\Big\Vert \, \Gamma^{s,t}_r G \,-\, \int_{a}^{b} P_{r,r'}\, G \; dr'\,
\Big\Vert_{C^{2}} \;\le\; {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \, 
\Vert G \Vert_{C^{4}} \, \big\{\, |a - (r\vee s)| \,+\, |b-t| \,\big\}\;.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Let $p$ be the smallest even integer larger than ${\mathtt r}_0 + (d/2)$,
so that $p\le {\mathtt r}_0 + (d/2) + 2$ and, by \eqref{242b},
${\mathtt r} > p + 2 + (d/2)$.  By \eqref{220b} with $q=p$,
$\Vert P_{0,r'} G\Vert_{C^p} \le {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \Vert G
\Vert_{C^{p+1}}$. Thus, since $p> {\mathtt r}_0 + (d/2)$ and
${\mathtt r}> p+1+ (d/2)$, by \eqref{243},
$\Vert P_{0,r'} G\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}} \le {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \Vert G
\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}}$ for all $0\le r'\le T$.

The same argument, with \eqref{221} in place of \eqref{220b}, yields
that the map $r'\mapsto P_{0,r'} G$ is Lipschitz-continuous with
values in ${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}$. Hence, the integral in \eqref{246} is a
Bochner integral in ${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}$, and the first bound in
\eqref{247} follows.  The second one is proved in the same way.  By
\eqref{220d} with $0<\beta<1$,
$\Vert P_{r,r'} G\Vert_{C^2} \le \Vert P_{r,r'} G\Vert_{(2+\beta)} \le
{\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \Vert G\Vert_{(2+\beta)} \le {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \Vert
G\Vert_{C^3}$.

We turn to \eqref{248}.  By \eqref{221} with $p'=2$,
\begin{equation}
\label{254}
\sup_{0\le r\le a\wedge b} \Vert P_{r,b}\, G - P_{r,a}\, G
\Vert_{C^{2}} \;\le\; {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f}\, \Vert G\Vert_{C^4}\, |b-a| \;,
\end{equation}
so that $r'\mapsto P_{r,r'} G$ is Lipschitz continuous in $C^2$,
uniformly in $r$, with Lipschitz constant ${\mathfrak c}_{\rm f}\, \Vert
G\Vert_{C^4}$.  As the two integrals in \eqref{248} are carried over
the intervals $[r\vee s, t]$ and $[a,b]$, whose symmetric difference
has Lebesgue measure bounded by $|a-(r\vee s)| + |b-t|$, and as the
integrand is bounded by ${\mathfrak c}_{\rm f}\Vert G\Vert_{C^3}$ in $C^2$,
the assertion follows.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- remark-31: body_md -->
\label{s96}
The first bound in \eqref{247} is the only place where the
condition ${\mathtt r} > {\mathtt r}_0+d+4$ of \eqref{242b} is needed in this
subsection; it ensures that $P_{0,r}$ maps ${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}$ into
${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}$.  It may be replaced by ${\mathtt r}\ge {\mathtt r}_0$ if one
disposes of the ${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}$-boundedness of the semigroup, which
follows from an elementary energy estimate.

This proof requires the same regularity of $u$ as in Proposition
\ref{s77} as it uses \eqref{221} with the same exponents.
<!-- end remark-31 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{s75}
Fix $H\in {\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}$, $0\le s < t \le T$. Then, the random
variable $\int_{s}^{t} X^n_r (H) \, dr$ converges in law to
$X_0 ( \Gamma^{s,t}_0 H) + {\mathfrak G}$, where $X_0$ and ${\mathfrak G}$ are
independent, and ${\mathfrak G}$ is a centered Gaussian random variable with
variance $\sigma^2(H;s,t)$.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Fix $H\in {\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}$, $0\le s < t \le T$, and let
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} \varepsilon^n_r} \,:= \, X^n_r (H) - X^n_0 (P_{0,r}\, H) - M^{n,r}_r
(H)\,, \quad 0\le r\le T\,.
\end{equation*}
By Fubini's theorem,
\begin{equation}
\label{250}
\int_{s}^{t} X^n_r (H) \, dr \,=\,
X^n_0\big( \Gamma^{s,t}_0 H \big) \;+\;
\int_{s}^{t} M^{n,r}_r (H) \, dr \;+\;
\int_{s}^{t} \varepsilon^n_r \, dr \,.
\end{equation}
By Lemma \ref{s56}, for each $r>0$, $\varepsilon^n_r$ converges
to $0$ in $L^1 ({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$. The same proof yields that the time
integral also converges to $0$ in $L^1 ({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$.

It remains to examine the first two terms on the right-hand side.  Fix
an integer $m\ge 1$, and let $t_i = s + (i /m)\, (t-s)$,
$0\le i\le m$. By linearity, we may rewrite these terms as
\begin{align}
\label{187}
X^n_0 \Big(\, \int_{s}^{t} P_{0,r} H\, dr\, \Big)
+ \frac{1}{m}\, (t-s)\, \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} M^{n, t_i}_{t_i} (H) 
\, +\, \sum_{i=0}^{m-1} \int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}} 
\big[\, M^{n,r}_{r} (H) - M^{n,t_i}_{t_i} (H)\,\big] \, dr \,.
\end{align}
Denote by ${\textsf S}^n_m$ the second term of \eqref{187} and by
${\textsf E}^n_m$ the third one, and recall that the first one is
$X^n_0(\Gamma^{s,t}_0H)$.

\smallskip\noindent {\it Step 1: The main term.}  Fix $m\ge 1$, and
apply Lemma \ref{s59} and Remark \ref{s61} with $p=m$, with the test
functions $F_j := [(t-s)/m]\, H$, and with $G := \Gamma^{s,t}_0H$.
Mind that $t_0 = s$, while, in Lemma \ref{s59}, $t_0=0$.  Mind also
that the proof of Lemma \ref{s59} uses the function $G$ only through
the random variable $X^n_0(G)$, and never differentiates it: the lemma
therefore holds for every $G$ in ${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}$, and
$\Gamma^{s,t}_0G$ belongs to this space by Lemma \ref{s95}.
Similarly, only finitely many derivatives of the functions $F_j$ are
used, so that $F_j\in C^5({\mathbb T}^d)$ suffices, which holds by
\eqref{243} since ${\mathtt r} > 5 + (d/2)$.

By hypothesis {\rm (H)}, since $\Gamma^{s,t}_0 H \in {\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}_0}$ and since the map ${\mathtt x} \mapsto {\mathtt x}(\Gamma^{s,t}_0 H)$ is
continuous from ${\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}_0}$ to ${\mathbb R}$,
$X^n_0(\Gamma^{s,t}_0H)$ converges in law to $X_0(\Gamma^{s,t}_0H)$.
Hence, by Lemma \ref{s59}, Remark \ref{s61} and the Cram\'er--Wold
device, as $n\to\infty$, the sum of the first two terms of \eqref{187}
converges in law to $X_0 ( \Gamma^{s,t}_0H ) + {\mathfrak G}_m$, where
$X_0 ( \Gamma^{s,t}_0 H)$ and ${\mathfrak G}_m$ are independent and ${\mathfrak G}_m$
is a centered Gaussian random variable with variance
\begin{gather*}
\sigma^2_m \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} \int_{\tau_k}^{\tau_{k+1}}
\int_{{\mathbb T}^d} 2\, \chi(u(r,x))\,
(\nabla H^{(k)}_r)(x) \cdot  D(u(r,x)) \, (\nabla H^{(k)}_r) (x) \; dx \; dr \;.
\end{gather*}
In this formula, $\tau_0=0$, $\tau_j = t_{j-1}$ for $1\le j\le m$, and 
$H^{(k)}_r= (1/m) (t-s) \sum_{i=k}^{m-1} P_{r, t_i} H$,
$\tau_k \le r\le \tau_{k+1}$.

\smallskip\noindent{\it Step 2: $\sigma^2_m\to\sigma^2(H;s,t)$.}  By
\eqref{248} and the Lipschitz continuity of $r'\mapsto P_{r,r'} G$ in
$C^2$, established in \eqref{254}, we obtain that
\begin{equation*}
\sup_{0\le k<m} \; \sup_{\tau_k\le r\le \tau_{k+1}}
\big\Vert \, H^{(k)}_r \,-\, \Gamma^{s,t}_r H \, \big\Vert_{C^2}
\;\le\; {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f}\,  \Vert H\Vert_{C^4}\,
\frac{t-s}{m}\;\cdot
\end{equation*}
Since $\tau_m = t_{m-1} = t - [(t-s)/m] \to t$, and since the
integrand in \eqref{249} is bounded, replacing $H^{(k)}_r$ by
$\Gamma^{s,t}_rH$ in the previous displayed formula for $\sigma^2_m$,
and $[0,\tau_m]$ by $[0,t]$, shows that $\sigma^2_m$ converges to
$\sigma^2(H;s,t)$ as $m\to\infty$.

Thus, as $m\to\infty$, the sequence of random variables
${\mathfrak G}_{m}$ converges in distribution to a centered Gaussian
random variable ${\mathfrak G}$ with variance $\sigma^2(H;s,t)$,
independent of $X_0$.

\smallskip\noindent{\it Step 3: The remainder ${\textsf E}^n_m$.}
It remains to show that the third term in \eqref{187} converges to $0$
in $L^1({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$ as $n\to\infty$ and then $m\to\infty$.  We
first obtain a bound for $r$ fixed. We affirm that there exists a
finite constant $C_0$, which depends only on the cylinder functions
$h_j$, such that  
\begin{equation}
\label{186}
\begin{aligned}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \big[\, \big|\, M^{n,r}_{r} (H) - M^{n,t_i}_{t_i}
(H)\,\big|\, \big] \,\le\,
C_0\, \Vert H \Vert_{C^1}\, (r-t_i)^{1/2}
\\
&\quad \, +\,
C_0 \, T\, \int_0^{t_i}\,
\Vert {\mathcal A}_u \,  P_{u,r}\,H - {\mathcal A}_u \,  P_{u,t_i} \,H \Vert_{C^1}
\, du \, +\,
C_0\, T\, \sup_{0\le u\le r}
\Vert {\mathcal A}_u \,  P_{u,r}\,H \Vert_{C^1}\, (r-t_i)
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
for all $t_i \le r\le t_{i+1}$, $0\le i<m$.  To prove this estimate,
recall from \eqref{56} the formula for $M^{n,r}_{r} (H)$. By the
triangle inequality, the expectation on the left-hand side is
bounded by
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
& {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \big[\, \big|\, M^{n}_{r} (H) - M^{n}_{t_i}
(H)\,\big|\, \big] \,+\,
\int_0^{t_i} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \Big[\, \big|\,  M^{n}_{u} \big( {\mathcal A}_u \, P_{u,r}
\,H - {\mathcal A}_u \,  P_{u,t_i} \,H \big) \,\big|\, \Big] \, du 
\\
&\quad \,+\, \int_{t_i}^r
{\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \big[\, \big|\, M^{n}_{u} ( \, {\mathcal A}_u \,  P_{u,r} \, H
\,)
\,\big|\, \big] \, du \,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
To complete the proof of the claim \eqref{186}, it remains to bound
the $L^1({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$ norm by the $L^2({\mathbb P}_{\mu_n})$ norm, to recall
from \eqref{143} the explicit formula for the quadratic variation of
the martingale $M^n_r(F)$, and the bound \eqref{134}.

The $C^1$-norm appearing in the second term of \eqref{186} is bounded
by ${\mathfrak c}_{\rm f}\, \Vert P_{u,r} H - P_{u,t_i} H\Vert_{C^{4}}$.  By
\eqref{221} with $p'=4$, this expression is less than or equal to
${\mathfrak c}_{\rm f}\, \Vert H\Vert_{C^{6}}\, (r-t_i)$. On the other hand,
by \eqref{220b} with $q=4$, the supremum in the third one is bounded
by
${\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \sup_u \Vert P_{u,r} H \Vert_{C^{4}} \le {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f}
\Vert H \Vert_{C^{5}}$.  Since $r-t_i\le (t-s)/m$ and, by \eqref{243},
$\Vert H \Vert_{C^6}\le {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \Vert H\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}}$
because ${\mathtt r} > 6 + (d/2)$, we conclude that
\begin{equation}
\label{251}
\sup_{n\ge 1} {\mathbb E}_{\mu_n} \big[ \, \big| {\textsf E}^n_m \big|\,
\big] \;\le\; {\mathfrak c}_{\rm f} \, (1+T)^2\, \Vert H \Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}}\, \Big( \frac{t-s}{m} \Big)^{1/2}\;\cdot
\end{equation}

\smallskip\noindent{\it Step 4: Conclusion.}
It remains to recollect all previous estimates to complete the proof
of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{s76}
Fix $p\ge 2$, elements $H_1, \dots, H_p$ of ${\mathcal H}_{{\mathtt r}}$, and
$0\le s_1 < t_1 \le s_2 < \cdots < t_{p-1} \le s_p <t_p\le T$. As
$n\to\infty$, the random vector \eqref{188} converges in law to the
sum of the random vector
$( X_0(\Gamma^{s_1,t_1}_0 H_1), \dots, X_0(\Gamma^{s_p,t_p}_0H_p))$ and of a
centered Gaussian random vector ${\mathfrak G}$ in ${\mathbb R}^p$, independent of
$X_0$, whose covariances are given by
\begin{equation}
\label{252}
{\mathbb E}\big[\, {\mathfrak G}_i \, {\mathfrak G}_j\,\big] \;=\;
\int_{0}^{t_i\wedge t_j} \int_{{\mathbb T}^d} 2\, \chi(u(r,x))\,
\big(\nabla \Gamma^{s_i,t_i}_r H_i\big)(x) \cdot  D(u(r,x)) \,
\big(\nabla \Gamma^{s_j,t_j}_r H_j\big)(x) \; dx \; dr \;.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
By the Cram\'er--Wold device, it is enough to prove the convergence in
law of $\sum_{i=1}^p \theta_i \int_{s_i}^{t_i} X^n_r(H_i)\, dr$ for
every $\theta\in{\mathbb R}^p$.  The proof of Lemma \ref{s75} applies
with minor modifications.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- remark-32: body_md -->
\label{s97}
In contrast with what happens at a fixed time, the components of
${\mathfrak G}$ are not independent, even when the intervals $[s_i,t_i]$ are
disjoint: they are all driven by the same space-time white noise on
$[0,t_p]\times {\mathbb T}^d$, and the covariance \eqref{252} does not
vanish for $i\neq j$.
<!-- end remark-32 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{s98}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition \ref{s77} and {\rm (H)}, the
sequence ${\mathbb Q}_{\mu_n}$ converges weakly, in
$L^1(0,T;{\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}})$, to ${\mathbb Q}$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{s77}, the sequence ${\mathbb Q}_{\mu_n}$ is tight.
By Corollary \ref{s74}, a probability measure on
$L^1(0,T;{\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}})$ is determined by the laws of the
$p$-tuples \eqref{188}.  By Lemma \ref{s76}, these laws are the same
for all the limit points of the sequence ${\mathbb Q}_{\mu_n}$, so that this
sequence converges.

It remains to identify the limit with ${\mathbb Q}$.  Let $Y$ be the
process \eqref{253}.  By \eqref{152}, ${\textsf M}_r(H)$ may be represented
as
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{j=1}^d \int_0^r \int_{{\mathbb T}^d} \sqrt{2\, \chi(u(v,x))\,
D_j(u(v,x))}\, (\partial_{x_j} P_{v,r} H)(x)\, \xi^j(dv,dx)\,,
\end{equation*}
where
$\xi = (\xi^1,\dots,\xi^d)$ is the space-time white noise which
appears in \eqref{58}.  Hence, by the stochastic Fubini theorem and
since
$\int_{v\vee s}^t \partial_{x_j} P_{v,r}\, H\, dr = \partial_{x_j}
\Gamma^{s,t}_v H$,
\begin{equation*}
\int_s^t {\textsf M}_r(H)\, dr \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^d \int_0^t
\int_{{\mathbb T}^d} \sqrt{2\, \chi(u(v,x))\, D_j(u(v,x))}\,
\big(\partial_{x_j} \Gamma^{s,t}_v H \big)(x)\, \xi^j(dv,dx)\;,
\end{equation*}
a centered Gaussian random variable with variance
$\sigma^2(H;s,t)$.  On the other hand,
$\int_s^t \< P^*_{0,r}X_0 , H\>\, dr = X_0(\Gamma^{s,t}_0H)$.  Hence,
under ${\mathbb Q}$, the $p$-tuple \eqref{188} has exactly the law described
in Lemma \ref{s76}, which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{s05}
For each finite subset $A$ of $\Sigma^+_r$,
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu_{r,{\textsf M}}} [ \eta_A ] \,=\, 
\sum_{k=0}^{|A|-1} \Big(\frac{-1}{N}\Big)^k\,
\rho^{|A|-k} \, (1-\rho)^k\, \sum_{|B|=k}
\prod_{j\in B} j \, \Big(  1 + \frac{j} {N-j} \Big) \,.
\end{equation*}
In this formula, $\rho = {\textsf M}/N$ and the sum over $B$ is carried out
over all subsets $B$ of $\{1, \dots, |A|-1\}$ with $k$ elements. In
particular,
\begin{align*}
E_{\nu_{r,{\textsf M}}} [ \eta_A ] \,=\,  \rho^{|A|}\,
+\, \frac{1}{N} \, {\mathtt p}_1(\rho) \,
+\, \frac{1}{N^2} \, {\mathtt p}_2\, (\rho)
+{\mathfrak R}_N
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation*}
