\begin{gathered}
{\mathtt p}_1(\rho) \,=\,  -\, 
\frac{1}{2}\, |A|\, (|A|-1) \, \rho^{|A|-1}\, (1-\rho)\,
\\
{\mathtt p}_2(\rho) \,=\,  \frac{1}{2}\, \chi(\rho)\, \rho^{|A|-3}\,
\big\{ \, {\mathfrak n}^2_{1} \, (1-\rho) - {\mathfrak n}_{2} \,(1+\rho)\,
\big\} \,,
\end{gathered}
\quad\text{and}\quad 
|{\mathfrak R}_N| \, \le \, C_A \, \frac{1}{N^3} 
\end{equation*}
for some finite constant $C_A$.
In this formula, ${\mathfrak n}_{k} = 1^k + \cdots + (|A|-1)^k$.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Since $\nu_{r,{\textsf M}}$ is the uniform measure,
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu_{r, {\textsf M}}} [ \eta_A] \,=\, \frac{{\textsf M}}{N}  \cdots  \frac{{\textsf M}-|A|+1}
{N-|A|+1}\,\cdot
\end{equation*}
Rewrite $({\textsf M}-j)/(N-j)$ as $({\textsf M}/N) + \epsilon_j$, where
$\epsilon_j = -\, (1-\rho) \, (j/N)  [ 1 + j/(N-j)]$ to conclude that
\begin{align*}
E_{\nu_{r, {\textsf M}}} [ \eta_A] \, & =\, \rho\, \prod_{j=1}^{|A|-1}
\Big\{ \rho -  (1-\rho) \, \frac{j}{N}\,  \Big(  1 + \frac{j} {N-j}
\Big)\, \Big\}\,.
\end{align*}
A straightforward computation yields the first assertion of the lemma.

We may now compute the first three terms in the expansion of
$E_{\nu_{r, {\textsf M}}} [ \eta_A]$. The first two terms are easy to
compute and correspond to the first two terms in the sum appearing in
the statement of the lemma. The third one, which has order $1/N^2$, is
obtained considering the term $k=2$ in the sum and the term $k=1$ of
order $1/N^2$. It is given by
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{N^2} \, \Big\{
\rho^{|A|-2} \, (1-\rho)^2\, \frac{1}{2}\,
\Big[ \, \Big( \sum_{j=1}^{|A|-1} j \Big)^2
\,-\, \sum_{j=1}^{|A|-1} j^2 \,\Big]
\,-\, \rho^{|A|-1} \, (1-\rho)
\sum_{j=1}^{|A|-1} j^2
\Big\}\,.
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{s29}
For each $p\ge 2$, finite subset $A$ of $\Sigma^+_r$, and bounded
interval $I \subset {\mathbb R}$, there exist a finite constant
${\mathfrak c}_{_{\rm CLT}} = {\mathfrak c}_{_{\rm CLT}}(\varrho(\cdot) , p, I)$
and a finite integer $r_0=r_0(\varrho(\cdot) , p, I, |A|)$
such that
\begin{equation*}
\sup_{\varphi \in I} \, \sup_{0\le M\le |\Sigma^+_r \setminus A|} \,
\Big\vert
\, \sqrt{ \Gamma_{N, A, \varphi} }  \;
\nu^{n, r}_{\varrho_\varphi(\cdot)} \big\{
\sum_{x\in \Sigma^+_{r} \setminus A} \eta_x = M  \, \big\}
\; -\;
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, e^{-z^2/2} \,-\, 
\sum_{j=1}^{p-2} \frac{1}{N_A ^{j/2}} q_{j, N,  A} (z) \, \Big\vert
\; \le\;
\frac{ {\mathfrak c}_{_{\rm CLT}} }{ N^{(p-1)/2}}
\end{equation*}
for all $r \ge r_0$. In this formula, 
\begin{equation}
\label{74}
z \,=\, \frac{ M -  \sum_{x\in \Sigma^+_{r} \setminus A}
\varrho_\varphi (x/n)}
{\sqrt{ \Gamma_{N,  A, \varphi} } } \,.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
For a fixed $\varphi\in {\mathbb R}$, this result is the local central limit
theorem presented in \cite[Theorem VII.12]{pet}. Going through the
proof, it is easily seen that the estimates are uniform for $\varphi$
in bounded sets. For $\varrho(\cdot)$ constant, this is \cite[Theorem
A2.1.3]{kl}, see \cite[Remark A2.1.2]{kl}.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{s12b}
For each $q\ge 1$, $0<\delta<1/2$, there exists a finite constant
$C_1 = C_1(\delta, {\mathfrak r}, q)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\sup_{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta}\, 
\Big|\, E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{r,{\textsf M}}  } [\, \eta_A \,]
\,-\,
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}}  } [\, \eta_A \,]
\, \Big( 1 \,+\, \frac{1}{\Gamma_N} \, {\mathtt T}_{1,A}
\,+\, \frac{1}{\Gamma^2_N}\, {\mathtt T}_{2,A} \,\Big)
\,\Big| \,\le\, \frac{C_1}{N^3}
\end{align*}
for all finite subsets $A$ of ${\mathbb Z}^d$ and $r \ge 1 $ such that
$A\subset \Sigma^+_r$, $|A|\le q$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Fix $ \delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta$, and recall that $\varphi$ was
selected to get \eqref{50c}.  By definition of the canonical measure,
\begin{equation}
\label{22c}
E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\, \eta_A\,\big]
\,=\,  
\frac{E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}}  } 
\big[\,  \eta_A \,  {\mathtt 1}\{
\sum_{y\in\Sigma^+_r}  \eta_y = {\textsf M}\}\, \big]}
{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} \big[\, \sum_{y\in\Sigma^+_r}   \eta_y =
{\textsf M} \,\big]} \,\cdot 
\end{equation}
As $\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}}$ is a product measure, and $\eta_A =1$
means $\eta_y=1$ for $y\in A$, the previous expression is equal to
\begin{equation}
\label{23b}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\, \eta_A \, \big]\;
\frac{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}}  
\big[\, \sum_{y\in\Sigma^+_r \setminus A}  \eta_y = {\textsf M} - |A|\big]}
{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}}  \big[\, \sum_{y\in\Sigma^+_r}   \eta_y =
{\textsf M} \,\big]}  \,. 
\end{equation}

Consider the denominator of the previous expression.  In Theorem
\ref{s29}, set $p=7$ so that the error in the expansion is of order
$N^{-3}$. By the choice of $\varphi$, the variable $z$ introduced in
\eqref{74} is equal to $0$.  Thus, as $q_{{2j+1}, N} (0) = 0$ for
$j\ge 0$, by Theorem \ref{s29} with $p=7$,
\begin{equation}
\label{24b}
\sqrt{2\pi \, \Gamma_{N}} \,
\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} \big[\,
\sum_{y\in\Sigma^+_r}   \eta_y = {\textsf M} \,\big]
\,=\, 1 \, +\, \frac{\sqrt{2\pi} }{N} \, q_{2, N} (0)
\, +\, \frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{N^2} \, q_{4, N} (0)
\,+\,   R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m})  \,,
\end{equation}
where 
\begin{equation}
\label{75}
\sup_{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta}\,
\big|\, R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m}) \, \big| \,\le\, 
{\mathfrak a}_1 \, \frac{1}{N^{3}}\,\cdot
\end{equation}
Here and below, we adopt the convention established in Section
\ref{sec4}: ${\mathfrak a}_1 = {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)$ represents a finite constant,
depending only on ${\mathfrak r}$ and $\delta$, whose value may change from
line to line. The same convention is used for the remainder
$R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m})$, which stands for a generic term satisfying
\eqref{75}.

We turn to the numerator of \eqref{23b}. Let
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} {\mathfrak q}_{j, N,A} (z) }\, :=\,  \sqrt{2\pi}\, e^{z^2/2}\,
q_{j, N,A} (z)\,,\quad
{\color{blue} {\mathfrak q}_{j, N} (z) }\, :=\,  \sqrt{2\pi}\, e^{z^2/2}\,
q_{j, N,\varnothing}  (z)\,,\quad
j \ge 1\,,\, z\in {\mathbb R}\,,
\end{equation*}
which cancels the factor $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$ in the expression
\eqref{78}.  Note that the functions ${\mathfrak q}_{j, N, A} (\cdot)$ are
polynomials. Moreover, ${\mathfrak q}_{2j ,N, A}(\cdot)$, $j\ge 1$, are sums
of monomials of even degree, while ${\mathfrak q}_{2j -1,N, A}(\cdot)$,
$j\ge 1$, are sums of monomials of odd degree.

Since by \eqref{50c}
${\textsf M} = \sum_{x\in \Sigma^+_r} \varrho_\varphi(x/n)$, by Theorem
\ref{s29} with $p=7$,
\begin{equation}
\label{25b}
\sqrt{ \Gamma_{N,A}}\; \nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}}  
\Big\{\, \sum_{y\in\Sigma^+_r \setminus A}  \eta_y = {\textsf M} -
|A|\, \Big\}
\,=\,
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \, e^{-{\mathtt x}^2/2} \Big\{ \, 1
\,+\, \sum_{j=1}^4 \frac{1}{N^{j/2}_A} \, {\mathfrak q}_{j, N,A} ({\mathtt x})\, 
\,+\,   R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m})   \, \Big\} \,,
\end{equation}
where $R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m}) $ satisfies \eqref{75}, $\Gamma_{N,A}$ is
defined in \eqref{79}, 
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue}  {\mathtt x} } \, :=\, \frac{{\mathtt s}_A}{\sqrt{\Gamma_{N,A}}}\, \,,
\end{equation*}
and ${\mathtt s}_A$ has been introduced in \eqref{77}.  In \eqref{25b}, we
estimated $\exp\{ {\mathtt x}^2/2\} \, R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m})$ by
$R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m}) $.  This is possible because,
$\varrho_\varphi(\cdot)$ being bounded away from $0$ and $1$ uniformly
for $\delta \le {\textsf m}\le 1-\delta$ (see \eqref{56b} for a proof of
this claim in a similar context), ${\mathtt x}$ is uniformly bounded in
$A$, with $|A|\le q$, $N$, and $\delta \le {\textsf m}\le 1-\delta$.
Actually, $|{\mathtt x}| \le {\mathfrak a}_1 (\delta, q)\, N^{-1/2}$. We also
incorporated in $R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m})$ the term $j=5$ of the expansion
provided by Theorem \ref{s29}: as ${\mathfrak q}_{5, N, A}(\cdot)$ is a sum of
monomials of odd degree, this term is bounded by
${\mathfrak a}_1 N^{-5/2}\, |{\mathtt x}| \le {\mathfrak a}_1 N^{-3}$.

Combining identities \eqref{22c}, \eqref{23b}, \eqref{24b}, \eqref{25b}
yields that
\begin{equation}
\label{33b}
\begin{aligned}
E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\, \eta_A\,\big]
\,=\,  & E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\, \eta_A\,\big]  \; 
\frac{\sqrt{\Gamma_{N}}} {\sqrt{\Gamma_{N,A}}} \, e^{-{\mathtt x}^2/2}\, 
\Big\{ \,  1 \,+\, \sum_{j=1}^4 \frac{1} {N^{j/2}_A} \,
{\mathfrak q}_{j, N,A} ({\mathtt x})\, 
\,+\,  R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m})  \, \Big\}
\\
&\times\, 
\Big\{ \, 1
\,-\,  \frac{1}{N} \, {\mathfrak q}_{2, N} (0)\,
\,-\,  \frac{1 }{N^2} \, {\mathfrak q}_{4, N} (0)\,
\,+\,  \frac{1}{N^2} \, {\mathfrak q}_{2, N} (0)^2\, 
\,+\,  R^{(1)}_N({\textsf m})  \, \Big\}
\,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We may further expand this expression by noting that
\begin{equation}
\label{35b}
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\sqrt{\Gamma_{N}}} {\sqrt{\Gamma_{N,A}}}  \,=\,
1\,+\, \frac{1}{2}\, \frac{{\mathtt t}_{2,A}}{\Gamma_{N}}
\,+\, \frac{3}{8}\, \frac{{\mathtt t}^2_{2,A}}{\Gamma^2_{N}}
\,+\,  O \Big( \frac{1}{N^{3}}\Big)\,, 
\\
e^{-{\mathtt x}^2/2}
\,=\, 1\,-\, \frac{1}{2}\, {\mathtt x}^2 \,+\, \frac{1}{8}\, {\mathtt x}^4
\,+\,  O \Big( \frac{1}{N^{3}}\Big)\,,
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
where ${\mathtt t}_{2,A}$ has been introduced in \eqref{77}.  Rewrite
${\mathtt x}$ as $({\mathtt s}_A /\sqrt{\Gamma_{N}}) \sqrt{\Gamma_{N} /\Gamma_{N,A}}$ and
recall the first expansion in \eqref{35b} to conclude that
\begin{equation}
\label{44b}
e^{-{\mathtt x} ^2/2}
\,=\, 1 \,-\, \frac{1}{2}\, \frac{{\mathtt s}_A^2} {\Gamma_{N}}
\,+\, \frac{1}{2}\, \Big(\, \frac{{\mathtt s}_A^4} {4}
- {\mathtt s}_A^2\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}\,\Big) \, \frac{1} {\Gamma^2_{N}}
\,+\,  O \Big( \frac{1}{N^{3}}\Big)\,.
\end{equation}

To estimate the right-hand side in \eqref{33b}, we collect all terms
of the same order in $ N$ in the previous equation.

\smallskip\noindent{\bf (A0) Zeroth order term.}  We start with the
terms of zero-order in \eqref{33b}. By \eqref{35b}, \eqref{44b}, and
the definition of the polynomials ${\mathfrak q}_{j,N,A} $, the zero-order
term is given by $E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\, 
\eta_A\,\big]  $. 

\smallskip\noindent{\bf (A1) First order term.}  Denote by
${\color{blue} {\mathfrak q}^{(k)}_{j, N, A}} (\cdot)$ the degree $k$ component of the
polynomial ${\mathfrak q}_{j, N, A} (\cdot)$. We adopt the same notation for
the polynomials ${\mathfrak q}^{(k)}_{j,N} (\cdot)$.

By \eqref{35b}, \eqref{44b}, and the definition of the polynomials
${\mathfrak q}_{j,N, A} $, the term of order $N^{-1}$ in \eqref{33b} is given by
\begin{equation}
\label{45b}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\, \eta_A\,\big] \,  \Big\{ 
\frac{1}{2\, \Gamma_N} \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}\, -\, \frac{1}{2\, \Gamma_N}\, {\mathtt s}_A^2
\,+\, \frac{1} {N^{1/2}_A} \,
{\mathfrak q}^{(1)}_{1, N, A} ({\mathtt x})\,
\,+\, \frac{1} {N_A} \, {\mathfrak q}^{(0)}_{2, N, A} ({\mathtt x})\, 
\,-\, \frac{1} {N} \, {\mathfrak q} ^{(0)}_{2, N} (0) \Big\} \,.
\end{equation}
The first term comes from the expansion of
$\sqrt{\Gamma_N}/\sqrt{\Gamma_{N,A}}$, the second one from
\eqref{44b}. The next two from the sum inside braces in \eqref{25b}
and the last one from \eqref{24b}.

The difference of the last two terms may be seen to be of order
$N^{-2}$ and should be examined in the next step where we
consider the terms of this order. Therefore, by definition of the
polynomial ${\mathfrak q}_{1, N, A} (\cdot)$, the expression inside braces
(omitting the difference of the last two terms) in the previous
displayed equation is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2\, \Gamma_N}\,  ({\mathtt t}_{2,A} - {\mathtt s}_A^2) 
-\, 
\frac{{\mathtt T}_3 - {\mathtt t}_{3,A}  }{2\, \Gamma^2_{N,A}}\, {\mathtt s}_A\,,
\end{equation*}
where ${\mathtt T}_k$, ${\mathtt t}_{k,A} $ have been introduced in equations
\eqref{43b} and \eqref{77}, respectively.

A Taylor
expansion similar to the previous ones yields that
\begin{equation}
\label{40b}
-\, \frac{1}{2}\, 
\frac{{\mathtt T}_3 - {\mathtt t}_{3,A} } {\Gamma^2_{N,A}}\, {\mathtt s}_A
\,=\, -\, \frac{1}{2}\, \frac{{\mathtt r}_{3} \, {\mathtt s}_A} {\Gamma_N}
\,-\,  \frac{1}{2}\,  \frac{1}{\Gamma^2_{N}} \, \big\{ 2 \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A} \,
{\mathtt r}_{3} \,-\, {\mathtt t}_{3,A}\,\big\} \, {\mathtt s}_A
\,+\, O \Big( \frac{1}{N^{3}}\Big)\,,
\end{equation}
where ${\mathtt r}_k$, $k\ge 3$,  has been introduced in \eqref{43b}.

The terms of order $N^{-2}$ in \eqref{40b} are kept for the next step
in the expansion, while the terms of order $N^{-1}$ are combined with
the previous terms of this order. After this operation one concludes
that the term of order $N^{-1}$ in \eqref{33b} is given by
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\,  \eta_A\,\big] \,   
\frac{1}{2\, \Gamma_{N}} \, \big\{ \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A} - {\mathtt s}_A^2
\,-\,  {\mathtt r}_{3} \, {\mathtt s}_A\,\big\} \,.
\end{equation*}

\smallskip\noindent{\bf (A2) Second order term.} We first collect all
terms of order $N^{-2}$ which appeared in (A1). By \eqref{45b} and
\eqref{40b}, they are
\begin{equation}
\label{76}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\,  \eta_A\,\big] \,
\Big\{ \, \frac{1} {N_A}
\, {\mathfrak q}^{(0)}_{2, N,A} ({\mathtt x})\, 
\,-\, \frac{1} {N} \, {\mathfrak q}^{(0)}_{2, N} (0) \,-\,
\frac{1}{2}\, \frac{1}{\Gamma^2_{N} } \, \big\{ 2 \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A} \,
{\mathtt r}_{3} \,-\, {\mathtt t}_{3,A}\,\big\} \, {\mathtt s}_A  \,\Big\} \,.
\end{equation}
Since the zero-order term of the polynomial corresponds to the
constants, ${\mathfrak q}^{(0)}_{2, N,A} ({\mathtt x})
= {\mathfrak q}^{(0)}_{2, N, A} (0)$. 
By the explicit formula for $N^{-1}_A{\mathfrak q}_{2, N, A}$,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
&  \frac{1} {N_A}
\, {\mathfrak q}^{(0)}_{2, N, A} (0)\, 
\,-\, \frac{1} {N} \, {\mathfrak q}^{(0)}_{2, N} (0)
\\
& \quad =\,
\frac{1}{\Gamma^2_{N}}\, \Big\{\, 
\frac{H_4(0)}{4!}\, \big[ \, 2\, {\mathtt r}_{4}\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A} 
\,-\, {\mathtt t}_{4,A}\, \big] 
\,+\, \frac{H_6(0)  }{ 2\, (3!)^2}\, \, \big[\, 3\, {\mathtt r}^2_{3}
\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}\, \,-\, 2 \, \, {\mathtt r}_{3} \,
{\mathtt t}_{3,A}\,\big] \Big\}
\, +\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^3}\Big) 
\\
& \quad =\,
\frac{1}{\Gamma^2_{N}}\, \Big\{\, 
\frac{1}{4}\, {\mathtt r}_{4}\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A} 
\,-\, \frac{1}{8}\, {\mathtt t}_{4, A} 
\,+\, \frac{5 }{ 12}\, {\mathtt r}_{3} \, {\mathtt t}_{3,A}
\,-\, \frac{5 }{8}\,  {\mathtt r}^2_{3} \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}  \Big\}
\, +\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^3}\Big) \,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
In this formula, $H_p(\cdot)$ is the Hermite polynomial of degree $p$,
and ${\mathtt t}_{p,A}$, ${\mathtt r}_{p}$ were introduced in \eqref{77},
\eqref{43b}. Therefore, the expression in \eqref{76} is equal to
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\,  \eta_A\,\big] \,
\frac{1}{\Gamma^2_{N}}\, {\mathtt a}_N
\, +\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^3}\Big) \,,
\end{equation*}
where ${\mathtt a}_N$ is defined just before the statement of the
proposition. 

On the other hand, by \eqref{33b}, \eqref{35b}, \eqref{44b}, and the
definition of the polynomials ${\mathfrak q}_{j,N, A} $, the remaining terms
of order $N^{-2}$ in \eqref{33b} are given by
${\mathtt B}_N\, E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r,{\textsf M}} } \big[\, \eta_A\,\big] $,
where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
{\mathtt B}_N   \, & =\,
\frac{1}{8\, \Gamma^2_{N}}\, \Big\{
3\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}^2
\,+\, {\mathtt s}^4_{A}
\,-\, 6\, {\mathtt s}^2_{A} \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}\, \Big\}
\,+\, \frac{1}{2\, \Gamma_{N}}\, \big\{\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A} - {\mathtt s}^2_{A}\, \big\}\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\, {\mathfrak q}_{1,N}^{(1)}({\mathtt x}) 
\\
& \,+\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\, {\mathfrak q}_{1,N}^{(3)}({\mathtt x})
\,+\, \frac{1}{N}\, {\mathfrak q}_{2,N}^{(2)}({\mathtt x}) 
\,+\, \frac{1}{N^{3/2}}\, {\mathfrak q}_{3,N}^{(1)}({\mathtt x}) 
\,-\, \frac{1}{N^{3/2}}\, {\mathfrak q}_{2,N}^{(0)}(0) \,
{\mathfrak q}_{1,N}^{(1)}({\mathtt x})
\, +\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^3}\Big)\,. 
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
To obtain this identity we observed that
\begin{gather*}
\frac{1} {N_A} \, {\mathfrak q}_{2,N,A}^{(0)}({\mathtt x})
\,-\, \frac{1} {N}  \, {\mathfrak q}_{2,N}^{(0)}(0)
\,=\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^2}\Big)\,,
\quad
\frac{1} {N^{2}_A} \, {\mathfrak q}_{4,N,A}^{(0)}({\mathtt x})
\,-\, \frac{1} {N^{2}} \, {\mathfrak q}_{4,N}^{(0)}(0)
\,=\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^3}\Big)\,,
\\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{ N_A} }\,  {\mathfrak q}_{1,N,A}^{(1)}({\mathtt x})
\,-\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}  }\,  {\mathfrak q}_{1,N}^{(1)}({\mathtt x})
\,=\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^2}\Big)\,,
\quad
\frac{1}{N^{j/2}_A}\,  {\mathfrak q}_{j,N,A}^{(4-j)}({\mathtt x})
\,-\, \frac{1}{N^{j/2} }\,  {\mathfrak q}_{j,N}^{(4-j)}({\mathtt x})
\,=\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^3}\Big)\,.
\end{gather*}
By the explicit formulae for the polynomials
${\mathfrak q}_{j,N}(\cdot)$,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
{\mathtt B}_N  \, & =\,
\frac{1}{8\, \Gamma^2_{N}}\, \Big\{
3\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}^2
\,+\, {\mathtt s}^4_{A}
\,-\, 6\, {\mathtt s}^2_{A} \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}\, \Big\}
\,-\, \frac{1}{4\, \Gamma^2_{N}}\, \big\{\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A} - {\mathtt s}^2_{A}\, \big\}\, {\mathtt r}_{3}\, {\mathtt s}_A
\\
& \,+\, \frac{1}{\Gamma^2_{N}} \,\Big\{\,
\frac{1}{6} \, {\mathtt r}_{3}\, {\mathtt s}^3_A
\,-\, \frac{1}{4} \,  {\mathtt r}_{4}\, {\mathtt s}^2_A
\,+\, \frac{5}{8} \,  {\mathtt r}^2_{3}\, {\mathtt s}^2_A
\,+\,  \frac{1}{8} \,  {\mathtt r}_{5}\, {\mathtt s}_A
\,-\,  \frac{35}{48} \,  {\mathtt r}_{3}\, {\mathtt r}_{4}\,
{\mathtt s}_A
\\
& \qquad\qquad 
\,+\,  \frac{35}{48} \,  {\mathtt r}^3_{3}\, {\mathtt s}_A
\,+\,  \frac{1}{16} \,  {\mathtt r}_{4}\, {\mathtt r}_{3}\, {\mathtt s}_A
\,-\,  \frac{5}{48} \,  {\mathtt r}^3_{3}\, {\mathtt s}_A \,\Big\}
\, +\, O\Big( \frac{1}{N^3}\Big)\,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
That is, up to an error of order $N^{-3}$, 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
{\mathtt B}_N  \, & =\,
\frac{1}{8\, \Gamma^2_{N}}\, \Big\{
3\, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}^2
\,+\, {\mathtt s}^4_{A}
\,-\, 6\, {\mathtt s}^2_{A} \, {\mathtt t}_{2,A}
\,-\,  2 \,  {\mathtt t}_{2,A} \, {\mathtt r}_{3}\, {\mathtt s}_A \, \Big\}
\\
& \,+\, \frac{1}{\Gamma^2_{N}} \,\Big\{\,
\frac{5}{12} \, {\mathtt r}_{3}\, {\mathtt s}^3_A
\,-\, \frac{1}{4} \,  {\mathtt r}_{4}\, {\mathtt s}^2_A
\,+\, \frac{5}{8} \,  {\mathtt r}^2_{3}\, {\mathtt s}^2_A
\,+\,  \frac{1}{8} \,  {\mathtt r}_{5}\, {\mathtt s}_A
\,-\,  \frac{2}{3} \,  {\mathtt r}_{3}\, {\mathtt r}_{4}\,
{\mathtt s}_A \,+\,  \frac{5}{8} \,  {\mathtt r}^3_{3}\, {\mathtt s}_A\,\Big\} \,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
With the notation introduced before the statement of the proposition,
${\mathtt B}_N = (1/\Gamma^2_{N})\, ({\mathtt b}^{(1)}_N + {\mathtt b}^{(2)}_N)$. To
complete the proof of the proposition for
$r\ge r_0 (\delta, {\mathfrak r},q)$, it remains to collect the previous
estimates. The result holds for $1\le r\le r_0$ by adjusting the
constant $C_1$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- remark-33: body_md -->
\label{s70}
If the density profile $\varrho(\cdot)$ is constant equal to $\rho$,
then a simple calculation yields that the first order term is equal to
$-\, (1/2N) \, {\mathtt p}_A '' (\rho)\, \chi(\rho) = (1/N) \, {\mathtt q}_A(\rho)$:
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r, {\textsf M}}  } [\, \eta_A \,]
\frac{1}{\Gamma_N} \, {\mathtt T}_{1,A} \,=\,
\frac{1}{N}\, {\mathtt q}_A(\rho) \,.
\end{equation*}
The first order term can also be represented as $(1/N)\, {\mathtt p}_1
(\rho)$, where 
\begin{equation*}
{\mathtt p}_1(\rho)  \,:=\,  \frac{1}{2}\, \Big\{\,
\frac{\gamma_3}{\gamma_2^{2}}\, 
E_{\nu_\rho} \Big[\, \eta_A\,;\, {\mathcal S}_A \,\Big] 
\,-\,  \frac{1}{\gamma_2}\, 
E_{\nu_\rho} \Big[\, \eta_A\,;\, {\mathcal S}_A^2\,\Big]
\, \Big\} \,,
\end{equation*}
where ${\color{blue} {\mathcal S}_A}: = \sum_{x\in A} (\eta_x - \rho)$, and we recover the
formula for the first order correction \eqref{37b} obtained in Lemma
\ref{s05}.

A similar formula can be derived for the second term in the expansion,
which is equal to $(1/N)^2\, {\mathtt p}_2 (\rho)$, where
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
{\mathtt p}_2(\rho) \;=& \; \frac{3|A|}{2}\, {\mathtt p}_1(\rho)
\;+\;\Big[\frac{2\gamma_3\gamma_4}{3\gamma_2^{4}}
-\frac{5\gamma_3^{3}}{8\gamma_2^{5}}
-\frac{\gamma_5}{8\gamma_2^{3}}\Big]\, E_{\nu_\rho}\big[\eta_A \,;\, {\mathcal S}_A\big]
\\
+&
\;\Big[\frac{5\gamma_3^{2}}{8\gamma_2^{4}}
-\frac{\gamma_4}{4\gamma_2^{3}}\Big]\,
E_{\nu_\rho}\big[\eta_A \,;\, {\mathcal S}_A^{2}\big]
\;-\;\frac{5\gamma_3}{12\gamma_2^{3}}\, E_{\nu_\rho}\big[\eta_A \,;\, {\mathcal S}_A^{3}\big] \;+\;\frac{1}{8\gamma_2^{2}}\,
E_{\nu_\rho}\big[\eta_A \,;\, {\mathcal S}_A^{4}\big]\,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
These representations have the advantage that they easily extend to
cylinder functions $h$.

In the inhomogeneous case, the first order term is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2}\, \frac{1}{\Gamma_{N}} \,  \Big\{\,
\frac{{\mathtt T}_{3} }{\Gamma_{N}} \, 
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r, {\textsf M}}  } \Big[\, \eta_A\,;\, \sum_{x\in A}
[\, \eta_x - \varrho_\varphi (x/n) \,]\, \,\Big] 
\,-\,  
E_{\nu^{\rm gc}_{r, {\textsf M}}  }  \Big[\, \eta_A\,;\, \Big(\sum_{x\in A}
[\, \eta_x - \varrho_\varphi (x/n) \,]\, \Big)^2\,\Big]
\, \Big\} \,,
\end{equation*}
an expression which extends to product inhomogeneous measures the
formula for the first order correction in the equivalence of
ensembles.  We obtained this formula inserting the constant ${\mathtt s}_A$
inside the expectation and then replacing $\varrho_\varphi (y/n) - 1$
by $\varrho_\varphi (y/n) - \eta_y$, which is allowed due to the
presence of the function $\eta_A$ inside the expectation.
<!-- end remark-33 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{s42}
Let $h$ be a local function, and $J\colon {\mathbb T}^d \to {\mathbb R}$ a
continuous function, and fix $0<\delta < 1/2$. Then, there exists a
finite constant ${\mathfrak a}_2={\mathfrak a}_2(\delta)$, depending only on ${\mathfrak r}$,
$h$ and $\delta$, such that
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k},{\textsf M}}  }  \Big [\,
\Big( \sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\,  \big\{ \tau_x h
-  E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}} [\tau_x h] \,\big\}
\Big)^2  \, \Big]
\,\le\,
{\mathfrak a}_2 \, \Vert J\Vert^2_\infty \, \, r_1^d
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{r_2}$, $\delta \le {\textsf M}/|B_{{\mathtt k}}| \le
1-\delta$, $r_1\ge 1$, $r_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
The expectation appearing in the statement of the corollary is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{x, y \in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\, J(y/n)\, 
E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k},{\textsf M}}  }  \Big [\,
\big\{ \tau_x h -  E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}} [\tau_x h] \,\big\}
\,
\big\{ \tau_y h -  E_{\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}} [\tau_y h] \,\big\}
\, \Big]\,.
\end{equation*}
By Proposition \ref{s12b}, in the previous formula, we may replace all
expectations with respect to the canonical measure
$\nu^{\rm c}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$ by ones with respect to the
grand-canonical measures $\nu^{\rm gc}_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M}}$ at a cost
bounded by ${\mathfrak a}_2(\delta) \, r_1^{-d}$. After this replacement, all
non-diagonal terms vanish. As there are only $O(r_1^d)$ diagonal
terms, the corollary is proved.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{s18}
For each $q\ge 1$, $\delta>0$, there exists a finite constant ${\mathfrak a}_1
= {\mathfrak a}_1(q, \delta)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\max_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{{\mathtt t}_3}}
\sup _{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta}
\max_{{\mathtt k}\in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}} }
\max_{A}\,
\Big | \, E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \,   \eta_{A}  \,\big] 
\; -\; E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \, \eta_{A}  \,\big]
\, \Big( \, 1 \,+\, \frac{1}{\Gamma_{2,{\mathtt j}}} \,
{\mathtt T}_{1, {\mathtt j} , A}  \,\Big)
\, \Big|
\; \le \; \frac {{\mathfrak a}_1}{({\mathtt t}_1 {\mathtt t}_2)^{2d}}
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathtt t}_1\ge 2$, ${\mathtt t}_2\ge 2$. In this formula,
${\textsf m} = {\textsf M}/|\Sigma^+_{{\mathtt t}_1 {\mathtt t}_2}|$, and the last maximum
is carried over all subsets $A$ of $B_{{\mathtt k}}$ with $q$ elements.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{s71}
For each $\delta>0$, there exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak a}_1 ={\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)$ such that
\begin{gather*}
\max_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{{\mathtt t}_3}}
\sup _{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta}
\max_{{\mathtt k}' \neq {\mathtt k}\in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}} }
\Big | \, E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \,   ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}) \,
({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}'}  - {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}'})  \,\big] 
\, \Big|
\; \le \; \frac {{\mathfrak a}_1}{({\mathtt t}_1 {\mathtt t}_2)^{d}}\,,
\\
\max_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{{\mathtt t}_3}}
\sup _{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta}
\max_{{\mathtt k}\in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}} }
\Big | \, E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \,   ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})^2  \,\big] 
\, \Big|
\; \le \; \frac {{\mathfrak a}_1}{{\mathtt t}_1^{d}}
\end{gather*}
for all ${\mathtt t}_1\ge 2$, ${\mathtt t}_2\ge 2$.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Rewrite the expectation appearing in the statement of the corollary as
\begin{gather*}
\frac{1}{|B_{{\mathtt k}}|^2}\, \sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt k}}}\,
\sum_{y\in B_{{\mathtt k}'}}
\big\{\, E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \, \eta_x\, \eta_y   \,\big]
\,-\,
E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }  [ \, \eta_x\,]
\,
E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }  [ \, \eta_y   \,]\,\big\}\,.
\end{gather*}
Replace the canonical measures by the grand canonical ones, at a cost,
according to \eqref{178}, of order ${\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)/({\mathtt t}_1 {\mathtt t}_2)^{d}$. With the grand canonical measures replacing the canonical
ones, the previous sum vanishes. This completes the proof of the first
assertion. The same proof applies to the second assertion. The
difference is that we have diagonal terms which are roughly estimated
by $1$, providing a worse estimate of order ${\mathtt t}_1^{-d}$ only.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{s15}
Fix $0<\delta<1/2$.  There exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak a}_1 = {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta, {\mathfrak r})$, depending only on $\delta$ and
${\mathfrak r}$, such that
\begin{align*}
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, \vartheta} (x/n) \,-\, \vartheta \, & =\,
\chi(\vartheta)\, H^{(1)}_{2, {\mathtt j}} (x/n)
\,+\, \chi(\vartheta)\, (1- \vartheta)\, H^{(2)}_{2, {\mathtt j}} (x/n)
\\
& +\, \chi(\vartheta) \, (\vartheta - \bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}})\,
H^{(3)}_{2, {\mathtt j}} (x/n) \,+\, \chi(\vartheta) \, H^{(4)}_{2, {\mathtt j}} (x/n)
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{(3)}_n (x) \,,
\end{align*}
for all $x \in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}$, ${\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}$,
$\delta \le \vartheta \le 1-\delta$,
where
\begin{equation*}
\max_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}}\, \max_{x \in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}}
\big |\, {\mathfrak R}^{(3)}_n (x) \,\big|
\,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_1 \,
\, ( \, 1+ \Vert \rho\Vert_{C^3}\,)^6
\, \Big( \frac{s_1s_2}{n}\Big)^3\,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Recall that ${\mathfrak a}_1$ represents a finite constant depending only on
$\delta$ and ${\mathfrak r}$ whose value may change from line to line.  For
three non-negative integers $i$, $p$, $q$, ${\mathfrak R}^{p,q}_{n,i}(x)$
represents a remainder such that
\begin{equation*}
\max_{ {\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3} }
\max_{x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} |\, {\color{blue} {\mathfrak R}^{p,q}_{n,i}(x)} \, | \,\le\,
{\mathfrak a}_1\, ( \, 1+ \Vert \rho\Vert_{C^i}\,)^p\, \epsilon^q_n \,,
\quad
\text{where}\quad {\color{blue} \epsilon_n} := \frac{ s_1s_2}{n} \, \cdot
\end{equation*}

Fix $\delta \le \vartheta \le 1-\delta$.  Write
$\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (y/n)$ as $F (\rho (y/n))$, where
$F(a) = a / \{ a + e^{- \Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)} (1-a) \}$.  By
\eqref{50} and a Taylor expansion,
\begin{align}
\label{61}
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} 
(x/n) - \vartheta \, =\,
& -\,  \frac{1}{ |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}}
F' (\rho (x/n))\,
\big\{\, \rho  (y/n)
- \rho  (x/n) \,\big \}
\\
& -\, \frac{1}{2}
\,  \frac{1} { |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}}
F'' (\rho   (x/n))\,
\big\{\, \rho (y/n)
- \rho  (x/n) \,\big \}^2
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{3,3}_{n,1} (x) \,.
\nonumber
\end{align}
Note that
\begin{equation*}
F' (\rho (x/n))\,=\,
e^{-\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}\, 
\Big( \frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n)}
{\rho (x/n)} \Big) ^2 \,, \;\;
F'' (\rho (x/n))\,=\, -\, 2\, 
e^{-\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}\,
[\, 1 - e^{-\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)} \,]\, 
\Big( \frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n)}
{\rho (x/n)} \Big) ^3 \,.
\end{equation*}
Hence, by \eqref{56b}, \eqref{98}, 
\begin{equation}
\label{165}
\max_{ {\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3} }
\max_{x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} |\, F' (\rho (x/n))\, | \,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_1\,,
\quad
\max_{ {\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3} }
\max_{x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} |\, F'' (\rho (x/n))\, | \,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_1\,.
\end{equation}
The bound on the remainder in \eqref{61} follows from \eqref{98},
the explicit formula for $F'''(\cdot)$, and from the fact that
${\mathfrak r} \le \rho(\cdot) \le 1-{\mathfrak r}$.

We examine the first term on the right-hand side of \eqref{61}.  By
the formula for $F' (\rho (x/n))$, and since
$\sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} (y-x_{2, {\mathtt j}})=0$, a Taylor expansion
yields that this expression can be written as
\begin{gather*}
\Big(\, \frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n) } { \rho (x/n) }
\Big)^2
e^{- \Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}
\, \Big\{ \frac{x-x_{2, {\mathtt j}}}{n}\cdot \nabla \rho (x/n) \,-\,
\frac{1}{ 2\, |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}}
\frac{y-x}{n} \cdot \nabla^2\rho (x/n)\, \frac{y-x}{n} \,\Big\}
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{1,3}_{n,3} (x) \,.
\end{gather*}
The same reasons as above provide the bound for the remainder.  By
\eqref{98} and \eqref{59}, in the main term of the previous displayed
equation we may replace the chemical potential
$\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)$ by
$\overline{\Phi}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)$ at a cost
${\mathfrak R}^{3,3}_{n,2} (x)$.  Therefore, the first term on the right-hand
side of \eqref{61} is equal to
\begin{gather}
\label{164}
\Big(\, \frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n) } { \rho (x/n) }
\Big)^2
e^{-\overline{ \Phi}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}
\, \Big\{ \frac{x-x_{2, {\mathtt j}}}{n}\cdot \nabla \rho (x/n) \,-\,
\frac{1}{ 2\, |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}}
\frac{y-x}{n} \cdot \nabla^2\rho (x/n)\, \frac{y-x}{n} \,\Big\}
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{3,3}_{n,3} (x)  \,.
\end{gather}

We now examine the square of the ratio
$\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n) /\rho (x/n)$ in the previous
formula. Add and subtract $\vartheta$ to
$\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n) $, expand the square, use
\eqref{61} and \eqref{165} to get that
\begin{gather*}
\Big(\, \frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n) } { \rho (x/n) }
\Big)^2 \,=\,
\frac{\vartheta^2}{\rho (x/n)^2} 
\,+\, 2\, \vartheta\,  \frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n)^2}{\rho (x/n)^4}\,
e^{- \Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}\,
\frac{x-x_{2, {\mathtt j}}}{n}\cdot \nabla\rho(x/n) \,
+\, {\mathfrak R}^{3,2}_{n,2} (x) \,.
\end{gather*}
By \eqref{57}, we may further replace
$\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n)$ by its average over
$D_{2, {\mathtt j}}$, which is equal to $\vartheta$, at a cost
${\mathfrak R}^{2,2}_{n,1} (x) $. Finally, replace $\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}$ by
$\overline{\Phi}_{2, {\mathtt j}}$ at an extra cost
${\mathfrak R}^{3,3}_{n,2} (x)$.  In conclusion,
\begin{gather*}
\Big(\, \frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n) } { \rho (x/n) }
\Big)^2 \,=\,
\frac{\vartheta^2}{\rho (x/n)^2} 
\,+\, 2\, \frac{\vartheta^3}{\rho (x/n)^4}\,
e^{- \overline{\Phi}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}\,
\frac{x-x_{2, {\mathtt j}}}{n}\cdot \nabla\rho(x/n) \,
+\, {\mathfrak R}^{3,2}_{n,2} (x) \,.
\end{gather*}

Hence, by \eqref{63}, \eqref{164}, which is equal to the first
term on the right-hand side of \eqref{61}, is given by
\begin{equation}
\label{166}
\begin{aligned}
& \chi(\vartheta)\,
\frac{\bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}} }{1 - \bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}} }\,
\frac{x-x_{2, {\mathtt j}}}{n} \cdot     \frac{ \nabla \rho (x/n) } { \rho (x/n)^2 }
\,+\,
2\, \chi(\vartheta)\, (1- \vartheta)\,
\frac{1} { \chi(\bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}} )^2} \,
\Big( \frac{x-x_{2, {\mathtt j}}}{n} \cdot  \nabla \rho (x/n)  \Big)^2 
\\
&\quad \,-\, \frac{1}{ 2}\, \frac{\chi(\vartheta)}
{\chi (\bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}})} \,
\frac{1}{  |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}}
\frac{y-x}{n} \cdot \nabla^2\rho (x/n)\, \frac{y-x}{n} 
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{6,3}_{n,3} (x)  \,.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In the second term of the first line we replaced $\rho (x/n)^{-4}$ by
$\bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}}^{-4}$ at a cost ${\mathfrak R}^{6,3}_{n,1} (x)$, and in
the first term of the second line, we replaced $\rho (x/n)^{-2}$ by
$\bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}}^{-2}$ at a cost ${\mathfrak R}^{3,3}_{n,2} (x)$.

We turn to the second term in \eqref{61}.  Since $F''(\rho (x/n))$, in
the formula above \eqref{165}, can be written as
$- \, 2 \, [\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n)/\rho (x/n) ]^3$
$e^{-\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}\, [1-e^{-\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}
(\vartheta)}]$, the second term in \eqref{61} is equal to
\begin{align*}
& e^{-\overline{\Phi}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}\,
[\, 1- e^{-\overline{\Phi}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)}\, ] \,
\frac{\vartheta^3} {\rho (x/n)^3}\,
\,  \frac{1} { |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} \,
\Big( \frac{y-x}{n} \cdot  \nabla \rho (x/n)  \Big)^2
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{4,3}_{n,2} (x) 
\\
&\quad
=\,
\frac { \chi(\vartheta) }  { \chi (\bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}})^2}\,
(\vartheta - \bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}})\, 
\,  \frac{1} { |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} \,
\Big( \frac{y-x}{n} \cdot  \nabla \rho (x/n)  \Big)^2
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{5,3}_{n,2} (x)  
\,.
\end{align*}
To obtain the term on the left-hand side of the equality, we performed
many changes.  We replaced $\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta} (x/n)$ by
its spatial average, which is $\vartheta$, at a cost
${\mathfrak R}^{3,3}_{n,1} (x)$, in view of \eqref{57}. Recalling \eqref{59},
we also changed $\Phi_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)$ by
$\overline{\Phi}_{2, {\mathtt j}}(\vartheta)$ at a cost
${\mathfrak R}^{4,4}_{n,2} (x)$. Finally we applied a Taylor expansion to the
squared term and recalled the bounds \eqref{98} to obtain a remainder
of type ${\mathfrak R}^{2,3}_{n,2} (x)$. To obtain the identity, we replaced
$\rho (x/n)^{-3}$ by $\bar\rho_{2, {\mathtt j}}^{-3}$ at a cost
${\mathfrak R}^{5,3}_{n,1} (x)$, and we used equation \eqref{63}.

To complete the proof of the lemma, it remains to recall \eqref{61},
\eqref{166}, and the previous formula which yields the second term in
\eqref{61}.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- remark-34: body_md -->
\label{rm5}
Setting $s_1$ to be $1$, turns the set $D_{2,{\mathtt j}}$ into a set of width
$s_2$. Hence, taking $s_2=\ell_1$, $s_3=L_2$, where $\ell_1$, $L_2$ are the
quantities introduced at the beginning of Section \ref{sec4}, Lemma
\ref{s15} becomes a statement on $\varrho_{{\mathtt k},\vartheta} (\cdot)$,
${\mathtt k}\in \Sigma^+_{L_2}$, the density profiles considered in the
second part of Section \ref{sec4}.  The next two corollaries are used
in that section.
<!-- end remark-34 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{s35}
Let $s_1=1$.  For each $0<\delta<1/2$, finite subset $A$ of ${\mathbb Z}^d$,
function $J$ in $C^1({\mathbb T}^d)$, there exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak a}_{3, 3}$, also  depending on $\delta$, such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\,
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M} }} [\, \tau_x \eta_A\,] \,
=\, |B_{{\mathtt k}}^o| \, J_{{\mathtt k}}\, \Big\{\, {\textsf m}^{|A|}
\,+\, {\textsf m}^{|A|-1}\,
\frac{\chi({\textsf m})} {\chi(\bar\rho_{{\mathtt k}})}\,
\sum_{y\in A} \frac{y}{n}\cdot (\nabla \rho)(x_{{\mathtt k}}/n)\,\Big\} 
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
for all $\delta \le {\textsf m}\le 1-\delta$.  Here
${\textsf m} = {\textsf M}/|B_{{\mathtt k}}|$, and
\begin{equation*}
\max_{{\mathtt k} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3}}
\max_{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1- \delta } 
|\, {\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})\, | \,\le\,  {\mathfrak a}_{3, 3}\, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1} \,
\, (s_2/n)^2\, s^d_2 \,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Rewrite the expectation appearing on the left-hand side of the
corollary's statement as
$\prod_{y\in A} \varrho_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf m}} ((y+x)/n)$ and apply
Lemma \ref{s15} with $s_1=1$ to get that the left-hand side is equal
to
\begin{equation*}
|B^o_{{\mathtt k}}| \, J_{{\mathtt k}}\, {\textsf m}^{|A|}
\,+\, \chi({\textsf m})\, {\textsf m}^{|A|-1}
\frac{\bar\rho_{{\mathtt k}}} {1-\bar\rho_{{\mathtt k}}}\,
\sum_{y\in A} \sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)
\frac{x+y-x_{{\mathtt k}}}{n}\cdot
\frac{(\nabla \rho)([x+y]/n)}{\rho([x+y]/n)^2} 
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n 
\end{equation*}
where
$|\, {\mathfrak R}_n\, | \,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_{3, 3}\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty \,
(s_2/n)^2\, s^d_2$.  Note that $|x+y-x_{{\mathtt k}}|/n \le s_2/n$. We may
therefore replace $J(x/n)$ by $J_{{\mathtt k}}$ at a cost bounded by
${\mathfrak a}_{3, 1} \, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1}\, (s_2/n)^2 \, s_2^d$, and
$(\nabla \rho)([x+y]/n) /\rho([x+y]/n)^{2}$ by
$(\nabla \rho)(x_{{\mathtt k}}/n) / \bar\rho_{{\mathtt k}}^{2}$ at a cost
${\mathfrak a}_{3, 2} \, \Vert J\Vert_{\infty}\, (s_2/n)^2 \, s_2^d$.  After
these replacements, to complete the proof it remains to observe that
$\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} (x-x_{{\mathtt k}})=0$ by symmetry.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{s31}
Let $s_1=1$.  Fix $0<\delta < 1/2$, a finite subset $A$ of ${\mathbb Z}^d$,
and a function $J$ in $C^1({\mathbb T}^d)$. There exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$, also depending on $\delta$, such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} J(x/n)\,
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M} }}  [\, \tau_x \eta_A\,] \,
\frac{1} {\Gamma_{{\mathtt k}}}\, {\mathtt T}^{(1)}_{{\mathtt k}, x+A} \, 
=\,  \frac{|B^o_{{\mathtt k}}|}{|B_{{\mathtt k}}|} \,
J_{{\mathtt k}}\, {\mathtt q}_{A} ({\textsf m})  
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
where ${\textsf m} = {\textsf M}/|B_{{\mathtt k}}|$, and 
\begin{equation*}
\max_{{\mathtt k} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3}} 
\max_{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1- \delta } 
\big|\, {\mathfrak R}_n ({\mathtt k})\, \big |
\,\le\,  {\mathfrak a}_{3,3} \, \Vert J\Vert_{C^1}\, \Big\{ \frac{1}{n}
\,+\,  \Big( \frac {s_2}{n} \Big)^2\,\Big\} \,.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
The proof is similar to the one of Corollary \ref{s35}.  If the
expectation was carried out with respect to a Bernoulli product
measure with density ${\textsf m}$, the first order term corresponds to
that in Remark \ref{s70}. To assess the error, expand 
$E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf M} }} [\, \tau_x \eta_A\,] $ and each
term in the definition of ${\mathtt T}^{(1)}_{{\mathtt k}, A}$ by using Lemma
\ref{s15}. A long but simple computation, similar to the one presented
in the previous proof, yields the result. The main observation is that
the sums $\sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} (x-x_{{\mathtt k}})$,
$\sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt k}}} (x-x_{{\mathtt k}})$ vanish by symmetry.  For
example, it follows from this remark and the expansion established in
Lemma \ref{s15} that
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{ | B_{{\mathtt k}}|} \sum_{x\in B_{{\mathtt k}}}
F(\varrho_{{\mathtt k}, {\textsf m}} (x/n)) \,=\,
F({\textsf m}) \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n 
\end{equation*}
for some error ${\mathfrak R}_n$ bounded by ${\mathfrak a}_{3,3} (s_2/n)^2$. It also
follows from this remark that
$|B^o_{{\mathtt k}}|^{-1} \sum_{x\in B^o_{{\mathtt k}}} (x+y-x_{{\mathtt k}})/n =
y/n$, what explains the term $1/n$ in the error; for instance, the
first order term in Corollary \ref{s35} divided by $|B_{{\mathtt k}}|$ is
of order $1/n$.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{s20b}
Fix $0<\delta<1/2$.  There exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}$, also  depending on $\delta$,
such that
\begin{align*}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} ]
\,-\, {\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}
\, & =\,
\chi({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})\, {\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n
\,,
\end{align*}
where
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue} {\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}} \,=\, H^{(1)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  \,+\,
{\mathtt Y}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}\,, \quad
{\color{blue} {\mathtt Y}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}} \,=\, 
(1- {\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})\, H^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} 
\, +\, 
({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}} - \bar\rho_{2,{\mathtt j}})\,
H^{(3)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}
+\, H^{(4)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  \,,
\end{equation*}
\vskip -.3 truecm
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue} H^{(1)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  } \,:=\,
\frac{\bar\rho_{2,{\mathtt j}}}{1 - \bar\rho_{2,{\mathtt j}}} \,
\frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}}
\frac{x - x_{2,{\mathtt j}}}{n} 
\cdot     \frac{ \nabla \rho (x/n) } { \rho (x/n)^2 }\,,
\\
{\color{blue} H^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  } \,:=\, 
\frac{2} {\chi( \bar\rho_{2,{\mathtt j}})^2} \,
\frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}}
\Big( \frac{x - x_{2,{\mathtt j}}}{n} 
\cdot  \nabla \rho (x/n)  \Big)^2\,,
\end{gather*}
\vskip -.3 truecm
\begin{gather*}
{\color{blue} H^{(3)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  } \,:=\,
\frac { 1 }  { \chi (\bar\rho_{2,{\mathtt j}})^2}\,
\frac{1} { |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} 
\sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}}
\Big( \frac{y-x}{n} \cdot  \nabla \rho (x/n)  \Big)^2 \,,
\end{gather*}
\vskip -.3 truecm
\begin{align*}
{\color{blue} H^{(4)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  } \,:=\,
-\, \frac{1}{ 2}\, \frac{1} { \chi(\bar\rho_{2,{\mathtt j}})} \,
\frac{1} { |D_{2, {\mathtt j}}| } \frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} 
\sum_{y\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}}
\frac{y-x}{n} \cdot \nabla^2\rho (x/n)\, \frac{y-x}{n} \,,
\end{align*}
and $|\, {\mathfrak R}_n \,| \,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_{3,3} \, (s_1s_2 /n)^3$ for all
${\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}$, ${\mathtt k}\in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}$,
$\delta \le {\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}} \le 1-\delta$.
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{s38}
Fix a smooth function $F\colon {\mathbb R} \to {\mathbb R}$, $0 < \delta <
1/2$. Then, there exists a constant ${\mathfrak a}_1 = {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta, F)$ such
that
\begin{equation*}
\Big | \, F(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})\,-\,
F ({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}) \, - \,  F'({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})
\, \chi({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})\,  {\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}
\,-\, \frac{1}{2}\,  F''({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})\,
\big[\, \chi({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})\, H^{(1)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}
\big]^2 
\,\Big| \, \le \, {\mathfrak a}_1  \, \Big(\, 
\frac{s_1s_2}{n} \,\Big)^3
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}$, ${\mathtt k} \in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}$,
$\delta \le {\textsf M}/|D_{2,{\mathtt j}}|\le 1-\delta$, $s_1$, $s_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{s17}
Fix $0<\delta <1/2$, and $p\ge 1$. Then, there exists a constant
${\mathfrak a}_1 = {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta, p)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\max_{{\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}}
\sup _{\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta}\,
\max_{{\mathtt k}\in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}} }
\Big | \, 
E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p\,\big]  \; -\;
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p \,\big] \,
\Big( \, 1 \,-\, \frac{ p\, (p-1) }{ (s_1 s_2)^d}
\, \frac{(1-{\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})^2}
{2\, \chi({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})} \,\Big)
\, \Big|
\; \le \; \frac {{\mathfrak a}_1}{(s_1s_2)^d}
\,\Big(\, 
\frac {s_1s_2} {n} \,+\,
\frac {1}{s_1^d} \,\Big)
\end{equation*}
for all $s_1\ge 2$, $s_2\ge 2$. In this formula, ${\textsf m} = {\textsf M}/|D_{2, {\mathtt j}}|$.
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
By definition, 
\begin{equation*}
{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p \,=\, \frac{1}{s_1^{dp} }
\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_p} \eta_{x_1} \cdots \eta_{x_p} \,,
\end{equation*}
where the sum is carried over all sites $x_1 \dots, x_p$ in
$D_{{\mathtt k}}$. Apply Corollary \ref{s18} to $A = \{x_1, \dots, x_p\}$.
Mind that the number of elements of $A$ might be strictly less than
$p$. The first order term in Corollary \ref{s18} is
$E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [ \, \eta_A \,] $. Summing over
$x_1, \dots, x_p$ yields
$E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [ \, {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p \,] $.

We turn to the second order term.  By Lemma \ref{s15} and a
straightforward calculation (cf. Remark \ref{s70} and
${\mathtt p}''_A({\textsf m}) = |A|\big(|A|-1\big){{\textsf m}}^{|A|-2}$), there
exists a finite constant ${\mathfrak a}_1=  {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\Big |\, \frac{1}{\Gamma_{2,{\mathtt j}}} \, {\mathtt T}^{(1)}_{2, {\mathtt j} , A} \,+\,
\frac{ |A|\, (|A|-1) }{ (s_1 s_2)^d}
\, \frac{(1-{\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})^2}
{2\, \chi({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})} 
\, \Big| \,\le\,  {\mathfrak a}_1 \, \frac{1}{(s_1 s_2)^d}\,
\frac{s_1s_2}{n}\,\cdot 
\end{equation*}
Hence, in Corollary \ref{s18}, the second order term in the expansion
of $E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [ \, \eta_A \,]$ is equal to
\begin{equation*}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [ \, \eta_A \,] \,
\frac{1}{\Gamma_{2,{\mathtt j}}} \, {\mathtt T}^{(1)}_{2, {\mathtt j} , A}
\,=\,
-\, \frac{1}{s_1^{dp} }
\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_p}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2, {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [ \,  \eta_{x_1} \cdots \eta_{x_p} \,]
\frac{ |A|\, (|A|-1) }{ (s_1 s_2)^d}
\, \frac{(1-{\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})^2}
{2\, \chi({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})}  \, +\,
R_n\,,
\end{equation*}
where $A = \{x_1, \dots, x_p\}$, and
$|R_n|\le {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta, p) \, (s_1 s_2)^{1-d} \,
n^{-1}$.

The number of sets $A$ with non-distinct sites is bounded above by
$C_0 s_1^{d(p-1)}$. Then, considering only the case where all sites
are distinct we get an extra error bounded by
$s_1^{-d} \, (s_1 s_2)^{-d}$. If all sites are distinct $|A|=p$. After
replacing $|A|$ by $p$ we may reconsider all terms in the sum by a
further error of order $s_1^{-d} \, (s_1 s_2)^{-d}$.  This completes
the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- lemma-38: body_md -->
\label{s22}
Fix $0 < \delta < 1/2$, $p\ge 1$. Then, there exists a constant
${\mathfrak a}_{3,3} = {\mathfrak a}_{3,3} (\delta, p)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\Big|\, E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p ] - 
{\textsf Q}_p (\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})
\,\Big| \, \le \, \frac{{\mathfrak a}_{3,3} }{s_1^{d}}   \, \Big\{\, 
\frac{1 }{s_1^{2d}} \,+\, \Big(\frac{s_1}{n}\Big)^2 \,\Big\}
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}$, ${\mathtt k} \in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}$,
$\delta \le {\textsf M}/|D_{2,{\mathtt j}}|\le 1-\delta$, $s_1$, $s_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end lemma-38 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
Fix $p\ge 2$, and write
\begin{equation*}
{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p \,=\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^{p} }
\,\Big\{
\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_p} \eta_{x_1} \cdots \eta_{x_p} \,+\,
\, c_1\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-1}} \eta_{x_1} \cdots \eta_{x_{p-1}}
\,+\,
\, c_2\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-2}} \eta_{x_1} \cdots \eta_{x_{p-2}}
\, \Big\}  \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_r \,.
\end{equation*}
Here and below, ${\mathfrak R}_r$ represents a remainder which satisfies the
bound $|{\mathfrak R}_r | \le C_0 s_1^{-3d}$ for some finite constant $C_0$
depending only on $p$. In this formula, the sums are carried out over
all distinct sites $x_1 \dots, x_q$ in $D_{{\mathtt k}}$, and
$c_{1} = p(p-1)/2$, $c_2 = c_{2,1}+ c_{2,2}$,
$c_{2,1} = p(p-1)(p-2)/ 6$, $c_{2,2} = p(p-1)(p-2)(p-3)/8$.  Note
that $c_1$ is $p$ choose $2$, $c_{2,1}$ $p$ choose $3$, and
$c_{2,2}$ three times $p$ choose $4$. By definition of
$\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j},\vartheta } (\cdot) $, and since
$\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}$ is a product measure, taking
expectation in the previous formula yields that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}}
\big[ {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p\,\big]  \,=\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^{p} }
\,\Big\{ &
\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_p} \varrho (x_1/n) \cdots \varrho (x_p/n)   \,+\,
\, c_1\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-1}} \varrho (x_1/n)  \cdots
\varrho (x_{p-1}/n)
\\
&\quad 
\,+\,
\, c_2\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-2}} \varrho (x_1/n)  \cdots
\varrho (x_{p-2}/n )
\, \Big\}  \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_r \,,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
where
$\varrho (\cdot) = \varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}} }
(\cdot)$.

Similarly, by definition of $\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}$,
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^p \,=\, 
\frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^{p} }
\,\Big\{ & 
\sum_{x_1, \dots, x_p} \varrho (x_1/n) \cdots \varrho (x_p/n)   \,+\,
\, c_1\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-1}} \varrho (x_1/n) ^2 \varrho (x_2/n)\cdots
\varrho (x_{p-1}/n)
\\
& +\,
\, c_{2,1}\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-2}} \varrho (x_1/n)^3  \varrho
(x_2/n) \cdots \varrho (x_{p-2}/n )
\\
& +\, c_{2,2}\, \sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-2}} \varrho (x_1/n)^2  \varrho
(x_2/n)^2 \varrho (x_3/n) \cdots \varrho (x_{p-2}/n )
\, \Big\}  \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_r \,.
\end{align*}

Subtract the right-hand side of the two previous equations.
The first terms cancel. The difference of the second ones is equal to
\begin{align*}
\frac{c_1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^{p} }
\sum_{x_1, \dots, x_{p-1}} \chi(\varrho (x_1/n))
\, \varrho (x_2/n)\cdots
\varrho (x_{p-1}/n) \,,
\end{align*}
where the sum is carried out over all distinct sites $x_1 \dots, x_{p-1}$
in $D_{{\mathtt k}}$. This expression is equal to
\begin{align*}
& \frac{c_1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \chi(\varrho (x/n))  \,\Big)\,
\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)  \,\Big)^{p-2}
\\
&\quad
-\, \frac{c_1 (p-2) }{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \chi(\varrho (x/n))\,
\varrho (x/n) \,\Big)\,
\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)  \,\Big)^{p-3}
\\
&\quad
-\, \frac{c_3 }{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \chi(\varrho (x/n))\,\,\Big)\,
\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)^2 \,\,\Big)\,
\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |}
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)  \,\Big)^{p-4} \, +\, {\mathfrak R}_r\,,
\end{align*}
where, $c_3 = c_1 (p-2)(p-3)/2 = 2\, c_{2,2}$, and
$c_1(p-2)= 3\, c_{2,1}$. By \eqref{85}, we may replace in the previous
formula $f (\varrho (x/n))$ by
$f(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})$ at a cost bounded by
${\mathfrak a}_{3,3}(\delta) \, (s_1/n)^2$. Hence, by definition of
$\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}$, the previous expression is
equal to
\begin{align*}
& \frac{c_1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\chi(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})\, 
\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^{p-2}\,
-\, \frac{c_1 (p-2) }{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\chi(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})\,
\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^{p-2}
-\, \frac{c_3 }{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\chi(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})\,
\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^{p-2}\,
\, + \, {\mathfrak R}_{r}
\, + \, {\mathfrak R}_{n,r}\,,
\end{align*}
where $|{\mathfrak R}_{n,r}| \le {\mathfrak a}_{3,3}(\delta) \,  s_1^{-d} (s_1/n)^2$.

An analogous argument yields that the difference of the third terms in
the expansion of
$E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}} [ {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p\,] $ and
$\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^p$ is equal to
\begin{align*}
& \frac{c_{2,1}}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\Big( \, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \chi(\varrho (x/n))\, [ 1 + \varrho (x/n))]   \,\Big)
\, \Big( \, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)  \,\Big)^{p-3}
\\
& \quad +\, \frac{c_{2,2}}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\Big( \, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \chi(\varrho (x/n))  \,\Big)
\, \Big( \, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)  \,\Big)^{p-3} 
\\
& \quad +\, \frac{c_{2,2}}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\Big( \, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \chi(\varrho (x/n))  \,\Big)
\Big( \, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)^2  \,\Big)
\, \Big( \, \frac{1}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |} \,
\sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \varrho (x/n)  \,\Big)^{p-4} \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_r \,.
\end{align*}
Apply \eqref{85} once more to obtain that this expression is equal to
\begin{align*}
\frac{c_{2,1}}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\chi(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})\, [ 1 +
\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} ] \, \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j},
{\mathtt k}}^{p-3} \,+\,
\frac{c_{2,2}}{ |D_{{\mathtt k}} |^2} \,
\chi(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}) \,
[\, 1 + \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \, ]\, 
\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^{p-3}   \,+\, {\mathfrak R}_r  \, + \, {\mathfrak R}_{n,r}\,.
\end{align*}
To complete the proof, it remains to recollect all previous estimates.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label{s39}
Fix $0 < \delta < 1/2$, $p\ge 1$. Then, there exists a constant
${\mathfrak a}_{3,3} = {\mathfrak a}_{3,3}(p, \delta)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} J_{{\mathtt k}} \,
E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p ]
\, &=\, s_2^d\, J_{2,{\mathtt j}}\, {\textsf Q}_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})
\,+\, {\textsf Q}'_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \,
\chi ({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})\,
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}  [\, J_{{\mathtt k}} - J_{2, {\mathtt j}}\,] \,
{\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  \\
& +\, \frac{1}{2}\, {\textsf Q}''_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \,
\chi({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})^2\,  \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}  J_{{\mathtt k}} \,
H^{(1)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \,
({\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  + {\mathtt Y}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} )
\\
& +\, \frac{1}{6}\, {\textsf Q}'''_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \,
\chi({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})^3 \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}  J_{{\mathtt k}} \,
[\,H^{(1)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \,]^3\,
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
where
\begin{equation*}
|\, {\mathfrak R}_n | \, \le \, {\mathfrak a}_{3,3} \,
\Vert J\Vert_\infty\,  s_2^d\, \Big\{ \, \Big( \frac{s_1s_2 }{n} \Big)^4
\,+\,  \frac{1 }{s_1^{d}}   \, \Big[ \, 
\frac{1 }{s_1^{2d}} \,+\, \Big(\frac{s_1 }{n} \Big)^2\,\Big] \Big\}
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}$, 
$\delta \le {\textsf M}/|D_{2,{\mathtt j}}|\le 1-\delta$, $s_1$, $s_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
According to Lemma \ref{s22},
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} J_{{\mathtt k}} \, E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p ]
\,=\, 
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} J_{{\mathtt k}}\,
{\textsf Q}_{p} (\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}) \,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{(1)}_n
\,,
\end{equation*}
where
$|{\mathfrak R}^{(1)}_n|\le {\mathfrak a}_{3,3}(\delta)\, (s_2/s_1)^{d} \, \{\,
s_1^{-2d} \,+\, (s_1/n)^{2} \}$.

Fix a smooth function $F\colon [0,1]\to {\mathbb R}$. By Lemma \ref{s20b},
$\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}$ is of order
$s_1s_2/n$. Therefore, by a Taylor expansion,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} J_{{\mathtt k}}\, F(\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})
\, & =\, F({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} J_{{\mathtt k}}\, 
\,+\, F'({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}
[\, J_{{\mathtt k}} \, - J_{2,{\mathtt j}}\,]\,
[\, \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}} \,]
\\
& +\, \sum_{i=2}^3 \frac{1}{i!}\, 
F^{(i)} ({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \, \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} J_{{\mathtt k}}\, 
[\, \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}} \,]^i
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}^{(2)}_n \,,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
where $F^{(i)}$ represents the $i$-th derivative of $F$, and
$|{\mathfrak R}^{(2)}_n|\le {\mathfrak a}_{3,3}\, \Vert J\Vert_\infty\, s_2^d\,
(s_1s_2/n)^4$. Moreover, in the second term on the right-hand side we
were allowed to introduce $J_{2,{\mathtt j}}$ because the sum
$\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} [\, \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}} \,]$ vanishes. To complete the proof, it
remains to recall the statement of Lemma \ref{s20b} to replace in the
previous formula
$\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}} $ by
$\chi ({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})\, {\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} + {\mathfrak R}_n$.
<!-- end proof-62 -->
<!-- corollary-16: body_md -->
\label{s30b}
Fix $0<\delta <1/2$, and $p\ge 1$. Then, there exists a constant
${\mathfrak a}_{3,3} = {\mathfrak a}_{3,3} (p, \delta)$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{110}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}} J_{{\mathtt k}} \,
E_{\nu^{\rm c} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} } [{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}^p ]
\, &=\, s_2^d\, J_{2,{\mathtt j}}\, {\textsf Q}_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})
\,+\, {\textsf Q}'_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \,
\chi ({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})\,
\sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}  [\, J_{{\mathtt k}} - J_{2, {\mathtt j}}\,] \,
{\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  \\
& +\, \frac{1}{2}\, {\textsf Q}''_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \,
\chi({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})^2\,  \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}  J_{{\mathtt k}} \,
H^{(1)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \,
({\mathtt Y}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  + {\mathtt Y}^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} )
\\
& +\, \frac{1}{6}\, {\textsf Q}'''_p({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}) \,
\chi({\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}})^3 \sum_{{\mathtt k}\in\Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}}  J_{{\mathtt k}} \,
[\,H^{(1)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \,]^3
\\
&- \, \frac {1}{2}\, s_2^d\, J_{2,{\mathtt j}}\, \frac{ p\, (p-1) }{ (s_1 s_2)^d}
\, \chi({\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}})  \, {\textsf m}_{2,{\mathtt j}}^{p-2}
\,+\, {\mathfrak R}_n
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation*}
|\, {\mathfrak R}_n | \, \le \, {\mathfrak a}_{3,3} \, \Vert J\Vert_\infty
\, s_2^d\, \Big\{ \, \Big(
\frac{s_1s_2 }{n} \Big)^4
\,+\,  \frac{s_1s_2 }{n} \, \frac{1} {(s_1s_2)^d } \, 
\,+\,  \frac{1 }{s_1^{d}}   \, \Big[ \, 
\frac{1 }{s_1^{2d}} \,+\, \frac{1 }{(s_1s_2)^{d}} \,+\,
\Big(\frac{s_1 }{n} \Big)^2\,\Big] \Big\}
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathtt j}\in \Sigma^+_{s_3}$, 
$\delta \le {\textsf M}/|D_{2,{\mathtt j}}|\le 1-\delta$, $s_1$, $s_2\ge 1$.
<!-- end corollary-16 -->
<!-- lemma-39: body_md -->
\label{s10}
For each $0<\delta<1/2$, there exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak a}_1 = {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\nu^{\rm c} _{2,  {\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}
\big[\, \{\eta : \eta_x = \xi_x
\;\forall x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}\,\}\,\big]
\,\le\,
{\mathfrak a}_1 \,
\nu^{\rm gc} _{2, {\mathtt j},  {\textsf M}} 
\big[\, \{\eta : \eta_x = \xi_x
\;\forall x\in D_{{\mathtt k}} \,\}\,\big]
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3} $, ${\mathtt k} \in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}$,
$\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1-\delta$, $\xi \in \{0,1\}^{D_{{\mathtt k}} }$, and
$s_1\ge 2$, $s_2\ge 2$. Here,
${\textsf m} = {\textsf M}/|D_{2,{\mathtt j}} |$.
<!-- end lemma-39 -->
<!-- proof-63: body_md -->
By definition of the canonical measure, the left-hand side of the
equation appearing in the statement of the lemma is equal to
\begin{equation*}
\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} 
\big[\, \{\eta : \eta_x = \xi_x
\;\forall x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}\,\}\,\big] \;
\frac{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} 
\big[\, \sum_{x\in D_{2,{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}}  \eta_x = {\textsf M} -
|\xi|\, \big]}
{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}  \big[\, \sum_{x\in D_{2,{\mathtt j}}}   \eta_x =
{\textsf M} \,\big]}\,,
\end{equation*}
where
${\color{blue} D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} } = D_{2,{\mathtt j}} \setminus D_{{\mathtt k}}$, ${\color{blue} |\xi| } = \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}} \xi_x$. It remains to bound
the previous ratio. This is done with the help of the local central
limit theorem.

Since the chemical potential of the product measure has been chosen
for the density of particles on $D_{2, {\mathtt j}}$ to be
${\textsf m} = {\textsf M}/|D_{2, {\mathtt j}} |$, see \eqref{50}, by Theorem
\ref{s29} with $\Sigma^+_r = D_{2, {\mathtt j}}$,
\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{2\pi \, \Gamma_{2, {\mathtt j}}} \, \nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}  \big[\,
\sum_{x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}}   \eta_x = {\textsf M} \,\big]
\,=\, 1 \,+\, \frac{\sqrt{2\pi} }{|D_{2, {\mathtt j}} |^{1/2}}\,
q_{1,L, \varnothing}(0) \,+\, O\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{2, {\mathtt j}} |}\,\Big)\,,
\end{equation*}
where
${\color{blue} \Gamma_{2, {\mathtt j}}} := \sum_{x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}} \chi (\,
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}} (x/n)\,)$,
$\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}} (x/n)$, $x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}}$, is the
density profile defined in \eqref{97}, $L = |D_{2, {\mathtt j}} |$, and
$q_{1,L, A}(\cdot) $ has been introduced in \eqref{78}.  As
$q_{1,L, \varnothing}(0)=0$, by Theorem \ref{s29}, the right-hand side
is bounded below by $1/2$ for $s_1s_2$ sufficiently large, uniformly
in $\delta \le {\textsf m} \le 1 -\delta$, ${\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3} $.

We turn to the numerator. By the same Theorem \ref{s29},
\begin{equation*}
\sqrt{2\pi \, \Gamma_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}} \, \nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}  \Big[\,
\sum_{x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}}   \eta_x = {\textsf M} - |\xi| \,\Big]
\,=\, e^{-z^2/2} \,+\, \frac{\sqrt{2\pi} }{|D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} |^{1/2}}\,
q_{1, L, D_{{\mathtt k}}}(z) \,+\, O\Big(\, \frac{1}{ |D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} |}\,\Big)\,,
\end{equation*}
where
${\color{blue} \Gamma_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}} := \sum_{x\in D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}}
\chi\big(\, \varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}} (x/n)\,\big)$,
\begin{equation*}
z\,=\,
\frac{1}{ \sqrt{\Gamma_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} } } \,
\Big\{\, \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}}}
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}} (x/n) \,
-\, |\xi |\, \Big\}\,.
\end{equation*}
The first term on the right-hand side in the penultimate displayed
equation is bounded by $1$. By the definition \eqref{78} of
$q_{1,L, D_{{\mathtt k}}}(\cdot)$, the second term is bounded by
$C_0\, |D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}|^{-1/2}\, H_3(z)\, \lambda_{3, L,
D_{{\mathtt k}}} (\varphi)$. Here, $\varphi$ is the chemical potential
selected in \eqref{21b} to get \eqref{50} with ${\textsf m}$ instead of
$\vartheta$.  By \eqref{79}, the formula for the third Hermite
polynomial, and the one above for $z$, this expression is less than or
equal to
$C_0\, \Gamma_{2,{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^{-2} \, |D_{{\mathtt k}}|\, \sum_{x\in
D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}} \, \gamma_{3, x}(\varphi)$, where, recall,
$\gamma_{3,x} (\varphi)$ is the third cumulant of a Bernoulli
distribution with density $\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}} (x/n)$.  By
\eqref{56b}, and the explicit expressions for the cumulants of a
Bernoulli distribution,
$C_0\, \Gamma_{2,{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}^{-2} \, |D_{{\mathtt k}}|\, \sum_{x\in
D_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}} \, \gamma_{3, x}(\varphi) \leq {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)$. Actually, it is bounded by
${\mathfrak a}_1(\delta) |D_{{\mathtt k}}|/ \Gamma_{2,{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}$, but this
better bound does not improve the estimate.  To complete the proof for
$s_1s_2$ sufficiently large, it remains to recollect all previous
estimates.

For the other cases, note that, for each
fixed $s_1$, $s_2$, the
right-hand side of the equation appearing in the statement of the lemma
is bounded away from $0$, uniformly in $\delta \le {\textsf m}\le
1-\delta$. Thus,  to extend the result for small $s_1s_2$, it
is enough to adjust the constant ${\mathfrak a}_1$.
<!-- end proof-63 -->
<!-- corollary-17: body_md -->
\label{s25}
For each $0<\delta<1/2$, there exists a finite constant
${\mathfrak a}_1={\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\nu^{\rm c} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}
\big \{ \, \big | \,{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \big | \; \ge 
\;   a \big\}
\; \le \;  {\mathfrak a}_1  \exp \big\{ - (a^2/2) \,s_1^d \, \big\}
\end{equation*}
for all ${\mathfrak a}_1\,  (s_1 s_2)^{-d} \le a\le 1$,
${\mathtt j} \in \Sigma^+_{s_3}$, ${\mathtt k} \in \Lambda_{{\mathtt j}}$,
$\delta \le {\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}} \le 1-\delta$, and
$s_1\ge 2$, $s_2\ge 2$.
<!-- end corollary-17 -->
<!-- proof-64: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{s10}, 
\begin{equation*}
\nu^{\rm c} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}
\big \{ \, \big | \,{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \big | \; \ge 
\;   a \big\}
\,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_1 \, 
\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}
\big \{ \, \big | \,{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \big |
\; \ge  \;   a \big\}
\end{equation*}
for some finite constant ${\mathfrak a}_1 = {\mathfrak a}_1(\delta)$. By Lemma
\ref{s17} with $p=1$,
$| \, \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} - {\textsf m}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} \,
| \,\le\, {\mathfrak a}_1\,  (s_1s_2)^{-d}$. Thus, the previous expression is less
than or equal to
\begin{equation*}
{\mathfrak a}_1 \, \nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}
\big \{ \, \,{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} 
\; \ge  \;   a/2 \,  \big\}
\,+ \,
{\mathfrak a}_1 \, \nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}}
\big \{ \, \,{\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}} - \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}} 
\; \le  \;   -\, a/2 \,  \big\}\,
\end{equation*}
provided $a \ge 2 \,{\mathfrak a}_1 \, (s_1s_2)^{-d}$. These two expressions
are estimated in the same way. We present the details for the first
one.

We proceed as in the classical proof of the upper bound large
deviations for i.i.d. random variables. There is just an extra
difficulty coming from the fact that the variables are not identically
distributed.  Recall the notation introduced at the beginning of
Sections \ref{sec9}, \ref{sec12}.  By Chebyshev exponential
inequality, the first term of the previous displayed equation is
bounded by
\begin{equation}
\label{81}
\begin{aligned}
& {\mathfrak a}_1 \, 
e^{ -\theta \, s_1^d \, (a/2)}
\, E_{\nu^{\rm gc} _{2,{\mathtt j}, {\textsf M}} }
\big [ \,
e^{  \theta\, s_1^d\,  ({\textsf m}_{{\mathtt k}}
- \widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}})  } \big]
\\
&\quad
\,=\, {\mathfrak a}_1\, 
\exp -\, s_1^d \,
\Big\{  \theta \, [ (a/2)  + \bar\varrho_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}]  \,-\,   
\frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}} } \ln \big[\,
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, e^\theta + 1 -
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, \big] \, \Big\} 
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
for every $\theta>0$. In this formula, we adopted the notation
introduced at the beginning of this section, and replaced
$\widetilde{{\textsf m}}_{{\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}$ by
${\color{blue} \bar\varrho_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}} := |D_{{\mathtt k}}|^{-1} \sum_{x\in
D_{{\mathtt k}} } \varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}} (x/n)$, where
${\textsf m} = {\textsf m}_{2, {\mathtt j}}$.

It is easily seen that the expression inside braces is strictly
concave in $\theta$. Let $\theta (a)$ be the parameter which maximizes
the expression, so that
\begin{equation}
\label{80}
(a/2)  + \bar\varrho_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}  \,=\,   
\frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}} }
\frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, e^{\theta(a)} }
{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, e^{\theta (a)} + 1 -
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) } \;\cdot
\end{equation}
Note that $\theta$ depends on ${\textsf m}$ and $\rho(\cdot)$.  By
definition of $\bar\varrho_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}$, $\theta(0)=0$.  With
this notation, the expression inside braces on the right-hand side of
\eqref{81} becomes
\begin{equation*}
R(a)\,:=\, 
\theta(a)  \, [ (a/2)  + \bar\varrho_{2, {\mathtt j}, {\mathtt k}}]  \,-\,   
\frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}} } \ln \big[\,
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, e^{\theta(a)} + 1 -
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, \big] \,.
\end{equation*}
Since $\theta(0) =0$, $R(0)=0$. A computation yields that
$R'(a)= \theta(a)/2$. In particular, $R'(0)=0$, and $R''(a) = (1/2)
\, \theta'(a)$. By \eqref{80},
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2}   \,=\,  \theta'(a)\, 
\frac{1}{|D_{{\mathtt k}}|} \sum_{x\in D_{{\mathtt k}} }
\chi ( \rho_x(a))   \, \quad \text{where}\;\;
\rho_x(a)  \,=\, 
\frac{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, e^{\theta(a)} }
{\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) \, e^{\theta (a)} + 1 -
\varrho^{(2)}_{{\mathtt j}, {\textsf m}}(x/n) } \;\cdot
\end{equation*}
Thus, $1/2 \le (1/4) \, \theta'(a)$, so that  $\theta'(a) \ge 2$, and 
$R''(a) \ge 1$, which completes the proof of the corollary.
<!-- end proof-64 -->
<!-- lemma-40: body_md -->
\label{s89}
Fix ${\mathtt r}\in {\mathbb R}$.  A sequence of measures $({\mathbb Q}_n:n\ge 1)$ on
$L^1(0, T; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})$ is tight if there exists
${\mathtt r}'< {\mathtt r}$ such that for all $\epsilon>0$,
\begin{gather}
\tag{A}
\lim_{A\to\infty} 
\limsup_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb Q}_{n} \Big[ \, \sup_{0<t_1<t_2<T} \Big\|\int_{t_1}^{t_2}
{\mathtt x} (t)  \, dt \, \Big\|_{{\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}'}} >A \,\Big ] \,=\,  0\,,
\\
\lim_{h\to 0} 
\limsup_{n\to\infty}  {\mathbb Q}_{n}
\Big[ \,  \int_0^{T-h}
\Vert {\mathtt x}(t+h) - {\mathtt x}(t) \Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}dt
> \epsilon  \, \Big] = 0\;.
\tag{B}
\end{gather}
<!-- end lemma-40 -->
<!-- lemma-41: body_md -->
\label{s63}
Fix ${\mathtt r}\in {\mathbb R}$.  A sequence of measures $({\mathbb Q}_n:n\ge 1)$ on
$L^1(0, T; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})$ is tight if there exist
${\mathtt r}'< {\mathtt r}$ and $0<\sigma<1$ such that
\begin{gather}
\tag{A}
\lim_{A\to\infty} 
\limsup_{n\to\infty} {\mathbb Q}_{n} \Big[ \, \sup_{0<t_1<t_2<T} \Big\|\int_{t_1}^{t_2}
{\mathtt x} (t)  \, dt \, \Big\|_{{\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}'}} >A \,\Big ] \,=\,  0\,,
\\
\lim_{A\to\infty} 
\limsup_{n\to\infty}  {\mathbb Q}_{n}
\Big[ \,  \Vert {\mathtt x} \Vert_{\dot W^{\sigma, 1} (0, T ; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})}  > A  \,
\Big] = 0\;.
\tag{B}
\end{gather}
<!-- end lemma-41 -->
<!-- lemma-42: body_md -->
\label{s57}
Suppose that there exist a finite constant $C_0$ and $b>0$ such that
\begin{equation*}
\sup_{n\ge 1}  \,
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}} \big[ \,  
\Vert {\mathtt x} (t) - {\mathtt x}(s)\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}\, \big] \, \le \,
C_0\, |t-s|^b
\end{equation*}
for all $0\le s<t\le T$. Then, condition {\rm (B)} of the previous lemma is
fulfilled for $0<\sigma<b$.
<!-- end lemma-42 -->
<!-- proof-65: body_md -->
Fix $0<\sigma<b$.  By Chebyshev's inequality and the definition of the
norm $\Vert \,\cdot\, \Vert_{\dot W^{\sigma, 1} (0, T ; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})} $,
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb Q}_{n} \Big[ \,
\Vert {\mathtt x} \Vert_{\dot W^{\sigma, 1} (0, T ; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})}  >A \,\Big ]
\,\le\,
\frac{1}{A}\,
\int_0^T \int_0^T
\frac{1} {|t-s|^{1+\sigma}}\,
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}} \big[ \,  
\Vert {\mathtt x} (t) - {\mathtt x}(s)\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}\, \big]
\;ds\,dt\,.
\end{equation*}
By hypothesis, the right-hand side is bounded by $(2C_0/A) [a
(1+a)]^{-1} T^{1+a}$, where $a=b-\sigma$. As this bound does not
depend on $n$ and vanishes as $A\to\infty$, condition {\rm (B)} of
Lemma \ref{s63} holds.
<!-- end proof-65 -->
<!-- lemma-43: body_md -->
\label{s64}
Suppose that there exist a sequence $\{\beta_m : m\in{\mathbb Z}^d\}$ and
$b>0$ such that
\begin{align*}
\sup_{n\ge 1}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n} } \Big[ \,    \, |\, \< {\mathtt x} (t) - {\mathtt x}(s) ,\, \phi_m\>\, | \,
\Big] \,\le\, \beta_m \, |t-s|^b
\end{align*}
for all $m\in{\mathbb Z}^d$, $0\le s<t\le T$ and
\begin{align*}
\sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d} \beta_m \, \gamma_m^{-{\mathtt r}/2}\,  \omega^{-1/2}_m
\,<\,\infty\,. 
\end{align*}
Then, condition {\rm (B)} of the Lemma \ref{s63} is fulfilled for
$0<\sigma<b$.
<!-- end lemma-43 -->
<!-- proof-66: body_md -->
Taking expectations in \eqref{236} and applying Fubini yields that
\begin{equation}
\label{223}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}} \big[ \,
\Vert {\mathtt x} (t) - {\mathtt x}(s)\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}\, \big]
\;\le\;
\sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d} \gamma_m^{-{\mathtt r}/2}\,  \omega^{-1/2}_m \,
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n} } \Big[ \, |\, \< {\mathtt x} (t) - {\mathtt x}(s) ,\, \phi_m\>\, |
\, \Big] 
\end{equation}
for all $0\le s < t\le T$ and $n\ge 1$.

By assumption, the right-hand side of \eqref{223} is less than or
equal to $C_0 \, |t-s|^b$ for some finite constant $C_0$. This bound
holds for all $n\ge 1$ and $0\le s\le t \le T$. This proves that the
condition of Lemma \ref{s57} holds.
<!-- end proof-66 -->
<!-- lemma-44: body_md -->
\label{s66}
Condition (A) in Lemmata \ref{s89} and \ref{s63} holds provided
\begin{equation}
\label{158}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}}  \Big[ \, \sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d}
(\gamma^{-{\mathtt r}'}_m/\omega_m)^{1/2}
\,  \int_{0}^{T}
\big|\,  \< {\mathtt x} (t)  ,\, \phi_m\> \big | \, \, dt \, \Big ]
\,<\, \infty \,.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-44 -->
<!-- proof-67: body_md -->
By definition of the
${\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}'}$-norm, 
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb Q}_{n} \Big[ \, \sup_{0<t_1<t_2<T} \Big\|\int_{t_1}^{t_2}
{\mathtt x} (t)  \, dt \, \Big\|_{{\mathcal H}_{-{\mathtt r}'}} >A \,\Big ]
\, & \le\, 
{\mathbb Q}_{n}  \Big[ \, \sup_{0<t_1<t_2<T}  \sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d}
\gamma^{-{\mathtt r}'}_m\,  \Big|\,  \int_{t_1}^{t_2}
\< {\mathtt x} (t)  ,\, \phi_m\> \, dt \, \Big |^2 > A^2 \,\Big ]
\\
& \le\, 
{\mathbb Q}_{n}  \Big[ \, \sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d}
\gamma^{- {\mathtt r}'}_m\,  \sup_{0<t_1<t_2<T}   \Big|\,  \int_{t_1}^{t_2}
\< {\mathtt x} (t)  ,\, \phi_m\> \, dt \, \Big |^2 > A^2 \,\Big ]\,.
\end{align*}
Recall the definition of the sequence $\{\omega_m : m\in {\mathbb Z}^d\}$
and the argument employed in the previous lemma to estimate this
expression by
\begin{align*}
& \sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d} {\mathbb Q}_{n}  \Big[ \, 
(\gamma^{- {\mathtt r}'}_m/\omega_m)
\,  \sup_{0<t_1<t_2<T}   \Big|\,  \int_{t_1}^{t_2}
\< {\mathtt x} (t)  ,\, \phi_m\> \, dt \, \Big |^2 > A^2 \,\Big ]
\\
& =\,
\sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d} {\mathbb Q}_{n}  \Big[ \, 
(\gamma^{-{\mathtt r}'}_m/\omega_m)^{1/2}
\,  \sup_{0<t_1<t_2<T}   \Big|\,  \int_{t_1}^{t_2}
\< {\mathtt x} (t)  ,\, \phi_m\> \, dt \, \Big | > A \,\Big ]
\,.
\end{align*}
By Chebyshev's inequality this expression is less than or equal to
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{A} \, E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}}  \Big[ \, \sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d}
(\gamma^{-{\mathtt r}'}_m/\omega_m)^{1/2}
\,  \int_{0}^{T}
\big|\,  \< {\mathtt x} (t)  ,\, \phi_m\> \big | \, \, dt \, \Big ]\,.
\end{align*}
By \eqref{158}, the $\limsup_n$ of this expression vanishes as
$A\to\infty$. This completes the proof of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-67 -->
<!-- corollary-18: body_md -->
\label{s67}
Fix ${\mathtt r}\in {\mathbb R}$, and a sequence of measures $({\mathbb Q}_n:n\ge 1)$ on
$L^1(0,T ; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})$.  Suppose that there exists
${\mathtt r}'< {\mathtt r}$ such that
\begin{equation}
\tag{A}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}}  \Big[ \, \sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d}
(\gamma^{-{\mathtt r}'}_m/\omega_m)^{1/2}
\,  \int_{0}^{T}
\big|\,  \< {\mathtt x} (t)  ,\, \phi_m\> \big | \, \, dt \, \Big ]
\,<\, \infty \,.
\end{equation}
Suppose, furthermore, that there exist a sequence
$\{\beta_m : m\in{\mathbb Z}^d\}$ and $b>0$ such that
\begin{align}
\tag{B}
\sup_{n\ge 1}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n} } \Big[ \,    \, |\, \< {\mathtt x} (t) - {\mathtt x}(s) ,\, \phi_m\>\, | \,
\Big] \,\le\, \beta_m \, |t-s|^b
\end{align}
for all $m\in{\mathbb Z}^d$, $0\le s<t\le T$ and
\begin{align}
\label{239}
\sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d} \beta_m \, \gamma_m^{-{\mathtt r}/2}\,  \omega^{-1/2}_m
\,<\,\infty\,. 
\end{align}
Then, the sequence $({\mathbb Q}_n:n\ge 1)$ on $L^1(0,T; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})$ is
tight.
<!-- end corollary-18 -->
<!-- corollary-19: body_md -->
\label{s90}
Fix ${\mathtt r}\in {\mathbb R}$, and a sequence of measures $({\mathbb Q}_n:n\ge 1)$ on
$L^1(0,T ; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})$.  Suppose that there exists
${\mathtt r}'< {\mathtt r}$ such that condition \eqref{158} holds, and that
there exist sequences $\{\beta_m : m\in{\mathbb Z}^d\}$ and
$\{b_n: n\geq 1\}$ such that $\lim_n b_n=0$, and
\begin{align}
\tag{B}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n} } \Big[ \,    \, |\, \< {\mathtt x} (t+h) - {\mathtt x}(t) ,\, \phi_m\>\, | \,
\Big] \,\le\, \beta_m \, (h + b_n)
\end{align}
for all $m\in{\mathbb Z}^d$, $n\ge 1$, $0<h<T$, $0<t< T-h$, and
\begin{align*}
\sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d}\beta_m \, \gamma_m^{-{\mathtt r}/2}\,  \omega^{-1/2}_m
\,<\,\infty\,. 
\end{align*}
Then, the sequence $({\mathbb Q}_n:n\ge 1)$ on $L^1(0,T; {\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}})$ is
tight.
<!-- end corollary-19 -->
<!-- proof-68: body_md -->
Let
\begin{equation*}
{\mathfrak b} \;:=\; \sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d}\beta_m \, \gamma_m^{-{\mathtt r}/2}\,
\omega^{-1/2}_m \;<\; \infty\,,
\end{equation*}
which is finite by assumption.  It is enough to check conditions {\rm
(A)} and {\rm (B)} of Lemma \ref{s89}.  Condition {\rm (A)} holds by
Lemma \ref{s66}.

We turn to condition {\rm (B)} of Lemma \ref{s89}. Recall the estimate
\eqref{223}.  Fix $0<h<T$ and $n\ge 1$.  Applying \eqref{223} with the
pair $(t, t+h)$ in place of $(s,t)$, and then the hypothesis {\rm
(B)}, we obtain, for all $0<t<T-h$,
\begin{equation}
\label{224}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}} \big[ \,
\Vert {\mathtt x} (t+h) - {\mathtt x}(t)\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}\, \big]
\;\le\;
\sum_{m\in {\mathbb Z}^d} \gamma_m^{-{\mathtt r}/2}\,  \omega^{-1/2}_m \, \beta_m \,
( h + b_n) \;=\; {\mathfrak b} \, ( h + b_n) \,.
\end{equation}

By Chebyshev's inequality and Fubini's theorem, for every
$\epsilon>0$,
\begin{equation*}
{\mathbb Q}_{n}
\Big[ \,  \int_0^{T-h}
\Vert {\mathtt x}(t+h) - {\mathtt x}(t) \Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}\, dt
> \epsilon  \, \Big]
\;\le\;
\frac{1}{\epsilon}\, \int_0^{T-h}
E_{{\mathbb Q}_{n}} \big[ \,
\Vert {\mathtt x} (t+h) - {\mathtt x}(t)\Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}\, \big] \; dt \,.
\end{equation*}
By \eqref{224}, the right-hand side is bounded by
$(T/\epsilon)\, {\mathfrak b}\, ( h + b_n)$.  As $b_n\to 0$,
\begin{equation*}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}  {\mathbb Q}_{n}
\Big[ \,  \int_0^{T-h}
\Vert {\mathtt x}(t+h) - {\mathtt x}(t) \Vert_{{\mathcal H}_{- {\mathtt r}}}\, dt
> \epsilon  \, \Big]
\;\le\; \frac{T\, {\mathfrak b}}{\epsilon}\; h \,,
\end{equation*}
